advice: The simplest fix for 'um' and 'ah' is to stay silent where the filler would go.
quote: Replace verbalized pauses with silence.

source.author: Lisa B. Marshall
source.title: Um, How Do I Stop, Ya Know, Using Um and Ah?

advice: Most people don't realize how often they hesitate. Listening back to your own recordings every day trains you to notice a filler just before you say it.
drill: Record yourself in different settings and listen to at least five minutes a day for 14 days, noting every hesitation.

source.author: Lisa B. Marshall
source.title: Um, How Do I Stop, Ya Know, Using Um and Ah?

advice: In conversation, 'um' holds your turn. In a speech nobody will cut in, so you don't need to fill the gap. Simply reminding yourself of this can cut fillers.

source.author: Lisa B. Marshall
source.title: Um, How Do I Stop, Ya Know, Using Um and Ah?

advice: Short, simple sentences put less load on your brain, so you hesitate and trip less.

source.author: Lisa B. Marshall
source.title: Um, How Do I Stop, Ya Know, Using Um and Ah?

advice: Find the situations where your fillers jump, such as Q&A or touchy topics, and watch your speech more closely there.
drill: Compare filler counts from a prepared section and an unscripted Q&A section of the same practice.

source.author: Lisa B. Marshall
source.title: Um, How Do I Stop, Ya Know, Using Um and Ah?

advice: If you write your speech out, write it the way you talk. Better still, speak it first and transcribe that. Drop words you tend to stumble over.
drill: Talk through your speech aloud, transcribe the recording, and edit that instead of a written draft.

source.author: Lisa B. Marshall
source.title: Um, How Do I Stop, Ya Know, Using Um and Ah?

advice: Unplanned speech is naturally full of hesitations, so a few are normal. Aim to cut them down, not to get rid of every one.

source.author: Lisa B. Marshall
source.title: Um, How Do I Stop, Ya Know, Using Um and Ah?

advice: An automatic transcript makes your fillers easy to count, because you can search it for each one.
drill: Get a transcript of a practice run and search it for each of your filler words to count them.

source.author: Yue Yin
source.credentials: Professor of educational psychology, University of Illinois Chicago
source.title: Less Filler, More Substance

advice: To tell whether a word is a filler, read the sentence without it. If the meaning doesn't change, it was filler.
quote: If the sentence remains clear without it, then it's likely a filler word.

source.author: Yue Yin
source.credentials: Professor of educational psychology, University of Illinois Chicago
source.title: Less Filler, More Substance

advice: If one section keeps pulling out crutch words, rewrite or rehearse just that section until you can say it cleanly.
drill: Split your speech into sections and repeat the hardest one until you get through it with no fillers.

source.author: Yue Yin
source.credentials: Professor of educational psychology, University of Illinois Chicago
source.title: Less Filler, More Substance

advice: Slow down most when moving from one point to the next. That's where you need thinking time and where fillers creep in.

source.author: Yue Yin
source.credentials: Professor of educational psychology, University of Illinois Chicago
source.title: Less Filler, More Substance

advice: With practice you can feel a filler coming and swap in a pause. A filler draws attention to itself and a moment of silence doesn't.

source.author: Joel Schwartzberg
source.title: 9 Surprising Ways You Can Benefit From a Pause

advice: Fillers come in three kinds: sounds (um, uh, ah, mm), words (basically, actually, literally) and phrases ('I think that', 'you know'). Watch for all three.

source.author: Andrew Dlugan
source.title: How to Stop Saying Um, Uh, and Other Filler Words

advice: Ask a listener to count each filler you use and tell you how much it distracted them.
drill: Have a friend tally your fillers by type during a practice talk, then compare the count with how distracting they found it.

source.author: Andrew Dlugan
source.title: How to Stop Saying Um, Uh, and Other Filler Words

advice: Fillers go up when preparation goes down. Being well prepared and well rested means fewer words to invent on the spot.

source.author: Andrew Dlugan
source.title: How to Stop Saying Um, Uh, and Other Filler Words

advice: Don't pack in more content than your time allows. Too much material makes you rush, and rushing breeds fillers.

source.author: Andrew Dlugan
source.title: How to Stop Saying Um, Uh, and Other Filler Words

advice: An audience won't jump in the moment you go quiet. You can stop and think silently and they'll understand.
quote: You just need to … think, and your audience will understand.

source.author: Andrew Dlugan
source.title: How to Stop Saying Um, Uh, and Other Filler Words

advice: Go back to your first assessment from time to time and check your progress. Is your filler count down, your pace slower, and are you pausing instead?
drill: Re-record the same talk every few weeks and compare filler counts with your first recording.

source.author: Andrew Dlugan
source.title: How to Stop Saying Um, Uh, and Other Filler Words

advice: Opening a sentence with 'Well…', or adding phrases like 'As I said before', is filler too.

source.title: Lengthen the List of Filler Words

advice: Feedback works best right away. Pointing out a filler 45 minutes later does little, so practice with live cues such as a bell or clicker.
quote: Telling someone they said an um 45 minutes ago is worthless.
drill: Have a practice partner tap a pen or ring a bell each time you use a filler.

source.author: Kate McClare
source.title: Counting on the Ah-Counter

advice: Telling yourself 'pause instead' often fails because the 'um' is already out. Speak in short bursts of words with small breaks between them instead.
quote: When you chunk you get into a rhythm: burst of words/break/burst of words/break….
drill: Practice chunking in everyday conversation until it feels natural, then use it in speeches.

source.author: Olivia Mitchell
source.title: How to eliminate filler words

advice: Explain your speech casually to a friend, a pet or a wall. It shows you your natural style and helps you speak without the nervous 'ums'.
drill: Give the whole speech conversationally to a pet or a wall before showing it to a coach.

source.author: Jordan Phillips
source.title: Commentary Extemp Starter Kit

advice: Research suggests 'uh' signals a short delay and 'um' a longer one. Lots of 'um' means you're doing heavy planning mid-sentence, so plan the idea before you start speaking.

source.author: Herbert H. Clark, Jean E. Fox Tree
source.title: Using uh and um in spontaneous speaking

advice: In experiments, occasional fillers actually helped listeners recall a story better than a fluent version, while coughs of the same length hurt recall. One stray 'uh' isn't a disaster, so don't stop over it.

source.author: Scott H. Fraundorf, Duane G. Watson
source.title: The disfluent discourse: Effects of filled pauses on recall

advice: Listeners recognized the next word faster after any short delay, whether it was 'um' or silence. A silent pause gives you the same benefit without the filler.

source.author: Martin Corley, Robert J. Hartsuiker
source.title: Why Um Helps Auditory Word Recognition: The Temporal Delay Hypothesis

advice: Treat the end of a sentence like a full stop. Finish with a firm pause instead of sliding into 'and', 'so' or 'uh'.
quote: punctuate the end of the sentence through a decisive pause

source.title: Verbal Delivery (Chapter 8)

advice: You may have fillers you can't hear yourself, like 'kind of'. Ask someone who listens to you often.
drill: Ask a classmate to name the one filler you use most.

source.title: Verbal Delivery (Chapter 8)

advice: Practice until you can get through the speech without fillers. Slow down so you have time to think before speaking, and learn which fillers you use.

source.title: WC117: Public Speaking Tools

advice: Speakers fill silence because they're afraid of seeming inarticulate. A calm pause actually comes across better than a filler and shows confidence.

source.title: Cutting Out Filler Words

advice: Everyone adds 'uh' or 'you know' sometimes, and stress, excitement or rushing make it worse. Calming down and slowing down reduce these slips.
quote: We all have times when we do not speak smoothly. We may add 'uh' or 'you know' to what we say.

source.title: Stuttering

advice: Use pauses so you aren't searching for words mid-sentence. If you do lose a word, wait silently instead of saying 'er' or 'um'.

source.author: Andrew Dlugan
source.title: Speech Pauses: 12 Techniques to Speak Volumes with Your Silence

advice: A nasal-only "mh" or "mm" is a real filled pause, but most speakers never use it, and those who do use it as a personal habit. If your recordings show a lot of "mm" before you start a sentence, treat it as your signature filler and target it the same way you would target "um".
quote: the choice of the form of the filled pause (either uh, um or mh) seems highly idiosyncratic
drill: Listen to a 2-minute recording and tally three columns separately: uh, um, and closed-mouth mm/mh. Work on whichever column is your personal favorite first.

source.author: Mathilde Hutin, Junfei Hu, Liesbeth Degand
source.credentials: Institute for Language and Communication, University of Louvain
source.title: Uh, um and mh: Are filled pauses prone to conversational convergence?

advice: People don't pick up each other's filler style in conversation, so your "uh", "um" or "mh" habit comes from you, not from the people around you. Don't wait for a better speaking environment to fix it. Change it through your own practice.
quote: These results indicate that filled pauses do not seem prone to conversational convergence

source.author: Mathilde Hutin, Junfei Hu, Liesbeth Degand
source.credentials: Institute for Language and Communication, University of Louvain
source.title: Uh, um and mh: Are filled pauses prone to conversational convergence?

advice: If you can't remove a filled pause completely, keep it short. In a study of business presentations, speakers whose filled pauses were long sounded less competent, and the researchers recommend keeping each one to a single syllable, about 400 ms or less.
quote: The longer the FPs of a speaker are the less competent s/he sounds in the ears of listeners
drill: Record yourself answering three unprepared questions. Find every filled pause in an audio editor and mark any that last longer than about half a second. Practice cutting those drawn-out "uuuh"s down to a quick blip or to silence.

source.author: Oliver Niebuhr, Kerstin Fischer
source.title: Do not Hesitate! - Unless You Do it Shortly or Nasally: How the Phonetics of Filled Pauses Determine Their Subjective Frequency and Perceived Speaker Performance

advice: Not all hesitation sounds cost the same. Speakers whose filled pauses were mostly nasal ('um' or a closed-mouth 'mmh') got higher performance ratings, and listeners underestimated how often speakers with short filled pauses hesitated.
quote: consisted mainly ("um") or entirely ("mmh") of a nasal segment.

source.author: Oliver Niebuhr, Kerstin Fischer
source.title: Do not Hesitate! - Unless You Do it Shortly or Nasally: How the Phonetics of Filled Pauses Determine Their Subjective Frequency and Perceived Speaker Performance

advice: For a realistic benchmark, German-speaking managers giving business presentations averaged about six filled pauses per minute, with a range of 1 to 13. Your listeners' sense of how many you use depends on how long each one lasts, not only on the count.
quote: The average Total FP Count was 6.33 FPs per minute, which is typical for German speakers

source.author: Oliver Niebuhr, Kerstin Fischer
source.title: Do not Hesitate! - Unless You Do it Shortly or Nasally: How the Phonetics of Filled Pauses Determine Their Subjective Frequency and Perceived Speaker Performance

advice: Tongue clicks (the little "tsk" sound) can be a filler of their own. In one analysis of an expert keynote, the speaker clicked about nine times a minute, always in the gaps between phrases and often next to an "uhm", as a sign of hesitation.
quote: clicks are used as hesitation markers
drill: Play back a recording with headphones and listen only for clicks, not words. Count them per minute, then compare the count against your um/uh count.

source.author: Jürgen Trouvain, Zofia Malisz
source.title: Inter-speech Clicks in an Interspeech Keynote

advice: Clicks tend to arrive late in a pause, just before you start talking again, and often together with a sharp audible in-breath. To cut both, take your breath early and quietly at the start of the pause, so you aren't gasping and clicking right before the next phrase.
quote: Our observations suggest a link between click production and ingressive airflow
drill: Read a paragraph aloud. At each period, inhale silently through the nose right away, then wait a beat before speaking. Listen back for any click or gasp just before each new sentence.

source.author: Jürgen Trouvain, Zofia Malisz
source.title: Inter-speech Clicks in an Interspeech Keynote

advice: A click followed by an in-breath at the start of a turn is probably the sound of gearing up to talk. If your recordings show one before nearly every sentence, make sure you're ready to speak before you open your mouth.
quote: This kind of click is probably a result of gearing up to talk

source.author: Richard Ogden
source.title: Sounds and actions in conversation (slides; draws on Ogden 2013, Clicks and Percussives in English conversation)

advice: Listeners don't hear clicks only as annoyance. In English conversation, clicks also mark stance and manage the talk, for example during a word search. A click during a search for a word tells the audience you're stuck, so treat it like an "uh" and replace it with a clean silent pause.
quote: We build on previous work which shows that clicks are also used in the management of sequences of talk.

source.author: Richard Ogden
source.credentials: Department of Language and Linguistic Science, University of York
source.title: Clicks and percussives in English conversation

advice: Clicks (a 'tsk' sound) often mark the start of a new sequence in conversation, working together with changes in pitch, loudness and glottalisation. If you hear clicks at your transitions, a clear silent pause and a change in pitch can signal the new point more cleanly.
quote: These findings challenge the traditional view that clicks function only paralinguistically in English.

source.author: Melissa Wright
source.title: Clicks as Markers of New Sequences in English Conversation
source.publisher: 16th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences, Saarbrücken

advice: In word searches ("what's the name of it?"), clicks typically come together with "uh" or "um", and how often people click varies a lot from person to person. If you're a heavy clicker, your clicks probably cluster at the moments you're searching for a word.
quote: Click usage varied substantially by individual speaker, but also seemed to interact with dialect and speech style.
drill: Practise a 'name five things' drill (five rivers, five authors) aloud. Whenever you can't find a word, close your lips and stay silent rather than clicking or saying uh.

source.author: Julia Moreno
source.title: "What's the name of it? [!]": Phonetic clicks in word search strategies in Glasgow

advice: The longer you hold an "mmm" or "hmm", the more thinking it signals to the listener. If you need a moment, a quick, short hum signals far less deliberation than a long, drawn-out "hmmmmm".
quote: In general, duration appears to correlate with thought

source.author: Nigel Ward
source.title: Pragmatic Functions of Prosodic Features in Non-Lexical Utterances

advice: Vowel-less sounds like "mm" and "hh" mostly show up as back-channels, the small noises a listener makes while someone else is talking. When you're the one holding the floor, keep them out of your own speaking turn.
quote: Most of these were in back-channel positions, and many were sounds without vowels, such as mm and hh.

source.author: Nigel Ward
source.title: Pragmatic Functions of Prosodic Features in Non-Lexical Utterances

advice: "Uh-huh", "mm" and "oh" are common in English conversation, and they help control the flow of talk and convey attitude. Because they are so automatic, you will probably have to hear them in a recording before you notice them in your own speech.
quote: In human dialogs these sounds are important in conversation control and for conveying attitudes.

source.author: Nigel Ward
source.title: The Challenge of Non-lexical Speech Sounds
source.publisher: International Conference on Spoken Language Processing (ICSLP)

advice: "Mm-hm" and "uh huh" are continuers: the listener's way of saying "keep going" and passing up a turn. They belong to the listening role. In cross-examination or Q&A, use them while the other person talks, not as the opening of your own answer.
quote: a continuer is a recognizable indication that the speaker is expected to proceed.

source.author: Shimako Iwasaki
source.title: Continuer

advice: An audible in-breath before you answer is normal, and it's more likely before longer answers. In conversation, answerers usually start inhaling right after the question ends. Take that breath on purpose as your thinking moment, rather than covering the gap with "um".
quote: longer responses are more often preceded by an inbreath
drill: Have a partner fire ten quick questions at you. After each one, inhale deliberately and quietly through your nose, then start your answer on the out-breath, with no filler.

source.author: Francisco Torreira, Sara Bögels, Stephen C. Levinson
source.title: Breathing for answering: the time course of response planning in conversation

advice: Habitual throat clearing is an audible filler, and it's also hard on your vocal cords and can turn into a cycle. When you feel the urge, swallow hard instead. It clears mucus without the noise or irritation.
quote: Frequent throat-clearing is very hard on your vocal cords.
drill: For one week, every time you notice the urge to clear your throat while practising, swallow hard instead. Tally the substitutions to build awareness.

source.credentials: Speech-Language Pathology Regional Voice Program, Rockyview General Hospital (reprinted by Calgary COPD & Asthma Program)
source.title: How to Look After Your Voice
source.publisher: University of Calgary, Cumming School of Medicine

advice: Keep water at the podium as your planned alternative to throat clearing. Pausing to take a sip and swallow with effort replaces a noisy "ahem", and it gives you a natural silent pause at the same time.
quote: Take a sip of water and/or swallow with effort instead of clearing your throat or coughing.

source.credentials: Speech-Language Pathology Department, The Montreal Children's Hospital
source.title: Instructions for a healthy voice

advice: Habit reversal treats filled pauses, tongue clicks and overused "like" together. First learn to catch each one as it happens (awareness training), then practise a competing response in its place. All six participants cut all three habits right after the training.
quote: simplified habit reversal training that consisted of awareness training and competing response training
drill: Awareness step: watch your recording and raise a finger every time you hear um, a click, or 'like'. Competing step: give a new 1-minute talk and, whenever you feel one coming, close your lips and hold a brief silent pause instead.

source.author: Carolyn Joanne Mancuso
source.credentials: M.A. thesis, University of South Florida
source.title: Using Habit Reversal to Decrease Filled Pauses and Nervous Habits in Public Speaking
source.publisher: University of South Florida Digital Commons

advice: Just learning to recognise your own filled pauses, tongue clicks and "like" can reduce them, even without a replacement behavior. Expect to need refreshers, though. In the study, booster sessions were needed for further gains.
quote: Awareness training resulted in meaningful reductions in target behaviors for all participants.
drill: Schedule a 5-minute awareness booster each week: replay 60 seconds of your latest practice and tally clicks, ums and likes before you rehearse again.

source.author: Claire Spieler, Raymond Miltenberger
source.title: Using awareness training to decrease nervous habits during public speaking
source.publisher: Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis (via MetaTOC)

advice: Self-paced computer training can work as well. Studying definitions and audio examples (and non-examples) of filled pauses and tongue clicks, then passing a short identification quiz, cut speakers' disfluencies to low rates right away.
quote: Following asynchronous AT, speech disfluencies immediately decreased to low rates for all participants.
drill: Make your own 'spot the filler' quiz: cut ten 5-second clips from your recordings and label each as clean, filled pause, click, or misused word. Score yourself until you get every one right.

source.author: Christopher J. Perrin, Jonathon Metz, Tracy L. Kettering
source.title: Effects of Asynchronous Training on Public Speaking Speech Disfluencies (poster)

advice: An "um" at the start of your answer to a question shapes how you're judged. Overhearers rated answers with an um, a silent pause, or both more negatively, and a short, clean gap before the answer most positively. In Q&A, aim to start your answer promptly and without filler.
quote: Ums before long pauses show advance knowledge of delays.
drill: Have a partner ask 10 questions. Start each answer with a short restatement ('The main reason is...') within about a second, with no um.

source.author: Jean E. Fox Tree
source.title: Interpreting pauses and ums at turn exchanges

advice: Discourse markers like "you know", "I mean" and "oh" are common in conversation but almost absent from polished prepared speeches, and overusing "like" lowered job applicants' chances. When you want to sound like your ideas are fully formed, cut back on "you know" and "I mean".
quote: Predictably, inaugural speeches contain no you knows, I means, or ohs

source.author: Jean E. Fox Tree
source.title: Discourse Markers across Speakers and Settings

advice: "You know" asks listeners to fill in what you left unsaid, and "I mean" warns them you're about to revise what you just said. A run of "I mean"s is really a string of restarts. Settle the point before you say it rather than correcting it out loud.
quote: We believe that you know and I mean have basic meanings, like other stereotypical words.
drill: Transcribe a 2-minute answer and mark every 'I mean'. For each one, rewrite the sentence so the revised version comes first, then say it again with no correction.

source.author: Jean E. Fox Tree, Josef C. Schrock
source.title: Basic Meanings of You Know and I Mean

advice: "Like" isn't scattered at random. When speakers retell a story, they reuse it in the same spots, mostly before quantities such as times and occasionally before names, where it signals loose wording. Look for your "like"s before numbers and give the number directly.
quote: Like was, however, recycled before some names and times.
drill: Tell the same 1-minute story three times. Each time, notice whether 'like' lands before a number or time ('like ten minutes'), and on the next retelling say the figure directly ('about ten minutes' or just 'ten minutes').

source.author: Jean E. Fox Tree
source.title: Placing Like in Telling Stories

advice: Fillers are like hazard lights: they signal an underlying speaking problem, such as needing time to find a word or change direction. They aren't the problem itself, so work on planning and word-finding rather than just banning 'um'.
quote: The problem is the illegal parking, or the lack of available valid parking, not the use of the lights.

source.author: Jean E. Fox Tree
source.title: Functional Spontaneous Speech Phenomena
source.publisher: Perspectives on Fluency and Fluency Disorders 17(2)

advice: Speakers have real control over "uh" and "um". People use fewer of them in formal settings and when speaking in time with a metronome. Treat filled pauses as a habit you can manage, not an automatic reflex.
quote: To summarize, speakers have selective control over uh and um.
drill: Read a short passage, then talk off-script for one minute while a metronome ticks at a slow, steady beat. Note how your filler count changes when you speak to a steady pulse.

source.author: Herbert H. Clark, Jean E. Fox Tree
source.credentials: Stanford University; University of California, Santa Cruz
source.title: Using uh and um in spontaneous speaking

advice: Stretching a filler ('uhhhh') tells listeners a delay is already under way, a signal separate from choosing 'uh' or 'um'. If a filler slips out, keep it short rather than holding it and advertising that you are still stuck.
quote: Uh and um, we have argued, are not merely "filled pauses", audible counterparts to silent pauses.

source.author: Herbert H. Clark, Jean E. Fox Tree
source.credentials: Stanford University; University of California, Santa Cruz
source.title: Using uh and um in spontaneous speaking

advice: Listeners tend to read "um" as anxiety or poor preparation, even when it isn't, and ums affect impressions even when listeners don't consciously notice them. Speech with no pauses at all made the best impression, so preparation that removes the need to hesitate beats simply swapping fillers for silence.
quote: ums can be, but are not always, processed automatically

source.author: Nicholas Christenfeld
source.title: Does it hurt to say um?

advice: Filler sounds depend on the language. Spanish speakers typically use "eh" and "em" instead of English "uh" and "um", and bilinguals' fillers shift with their contact with English. Bilingual speakers should listen for each language's fillers separately in their recordings.
quote: If, however, you're eavesdropping on Spanish speakers, chances are good that you'll hear ehs and ems instead.

source.author: Daniel Erker, Lee-Ann Marie Vidal-Covas
source.title: What We Say When We Say Nothing at All: Clues to Contact-Induced Language Change in Spanish Conversational Pause-Fillers
source.publisher: Instituto Cervantes at FAS, Harvard University (Estudios del Observatorio 80)

advice: Almost every language has filled pauses, and they sound alike: a neutral vowel, sometimes ending in a nasal (French "euh", Mandarin "en", Swedish "ohm"). Japanese mostly uses word-like "ano" and "eto". Fillers are a universal part of speech, not a personal flaw.
quote: With a few exceptions, filled pauses exist in every language, and are weirdly similar.

source.author: Dan Nosowitz
source.title: The Mystery and Occasional Poetry of, Uh, Filled Pauses

advice: In trilingual Cantonese-English-Mandarin speech, 'uh' was the most common filled pause in all three languages, while 'um' and the closed-mouth 'm' showed up more in English (about 26% and 10% of filled pauses) than in Cantonese or Mandarin (5-6% for 'm'). Check which filler you favor in each language you speak.
quote: A preference for uh was found for all three languages

source.author: Grace Wenling Cao, Peggy Mok
source.credentials: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
source.title: The Acoustics of cross-linguistic filled pauses in Cantonese-English-Mandarin trilingual speech

advice: Speaking in a second language changes your fillers. Dutch students used "um" more in English than in Dutch, and individual speakers varied a lot. If you speak in a second language, count your fillers in that language separately.
quote: Hesitation behavior is a relatively unconscious part of language

source.author: Meike de Boer, Willemijn Heeren
source.title: Individual variation in filled pauses in the native and second language

advice: Fillers also do language-specific work: in Japanese they reflect how a speaker is engaging with the listener, and in British English "um" marked bigger problems than "uh". Fillers are used to communicate, so cut them where they say something unhelpful about you, rather than mechanically.
quote: Overall, our data supports the Filler-As-Words hypothesis that filled pauses are used communicatively.

source.author: Ye Tian, Takehiko Maruyama, Jonathan Ginzburg
source.title: Self Addressed Questions and Filled Pauses: A Cross-linguistic Investigation

advice: Stretching a syllable ("theeee...", "andddd") works the same way as an "euh" or "um": in French spontaneous speech, filled pauses and lengthening behaved alike, while silent pauses alone were never heard as hesitation. Listen for drawn-out words as hidden fillers.
quote: silent pauses by themselves never serve as hesitation markers
drill: In your transcript, flag any word you held longer than normal (often 'and', 'the', 'so'). Re-record those sentences saying the word at normal length, followed by a short silent pause.

source.author: Estelle Campione, Jean Véronis
source.title: Pauses and hesitations in French spontaneous speech

advice: Speakers are more likely to say "um" right before introducing something new, so the moment you bring up a new name, term or example is a high-risk spot. Rehearse your new-term introductions until they come out cleanly.
quote: An initial "um" was over twice as likely to precede a new than an old referent.

source.author: Dale J. Barr
source.credentials: Beckman Institute, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign
source.title: Trouble in Mind: Paralinguistic Indices of Effort and Uncertainty in Communication

advice: Pair each crutch word with a small physical action, such as tapping your leg whenever you say "like". The action makes the habit noticeable in the moment. Once you can feel a filler coming, stay deliberately silent instead.
drill: During a 3-minute practice talk, tap your thigh every time you say your crutch word. In the next round, try to catch it before it comes out and replace it with silence.

source.author: Noah Zandan
source.title: How to Stop Saying "Um," "Ah," and "You Know"

advice: Fillers aren't all judged equally. One communication professor suggests that if you need a filler, "like" or "I mean" is judged less harshly than "uh" or "um", and fillers mid-sentence stand out less than ones at the start or end of a thought.
quote: "A balanced way to use filler words might be to use a few, but not too many," Fraundorf says.

source.author: Susmita Baral
source.title: Can't Quit Saying 'Um' and 'Ah'? Just Learn How to Use Them Better

advice: Don't open your speech with "So". It's the weakest possible first word, and starting nearly every sentence with it turns it into a crutch. Save "so" for real cause-and-effect and the occasional rhythmic beat.
quote: Also, if you start virtually every sentence with "so," that is bad as well.
drill: Record your first 30 seconds three times. If the first word is 'So', 'Okay so' or 'Um', restart until the first word is part of your actual message.

source.author: Bill Brown, DTM
source.title: So, What's So Bad About So?

advice: If you talk fast and fill gaps with crutch words, telling yourself to "slow down" rarely works. Add deliberate pauses and speak a bit louder instead. Both steady your pace and leave less room for filler.
quote: insert more deliberate pauses and raise your volume; both are countermeasures to fast talking.

source.author: Joel Schwartzberg
source.credentials: Presentation coach; author of The Language of Leadership and Get to the Point!
source.title: Drop Those Crutches

advice: Ask your feedback partner for more than a tally. Have them name which crutch words you use and flag any word you repeat more than five times. A specific named crutch is much easier to target than a total count.
quote: The Ah-Counter says "five-plus" to indicate any speaker who uses a crutch word more than five times.

source.author: Joel Schwartzberg
source.credentials: Presentation coach; author of The Language of Leadership and Get to the Point!
source.title: Drop Those Crutches

advice: A useful benchmark is about one filler per minute. The average speaker uses roughly five. To practice, record yourself casually describing your day from start to finish and replace each filler with a silent beat.
quote: To practice, set up a video to record, and talk about what you did from the beginning to the end of the day.
drill: Record a 3-minute 'my day' monologue, count fillers per minute, and repeat daily until you're near one per minute.

source.author: Noah Zandan
source.credentials: CEO and co-founder of Quantified Communications
source.title: How to Stop Saying 'Um,' 'Ah,' and 'You Know' (reprint hosted by Rutgers Food Science graduate program)

advice: Don't rely on auto-generated transcripts to count your fillers. Many transcription services silently delete 'um' and 'uh', which makes you look more fluent than you are. Review the actual audio or video instead.
quote: many transcription services automatically cut out filler words!

source.author: Team Duarte
source.title: Why you should absolutely avoid using filler words (and how to actually stop)

advice: Fillers cluster in two places: the start of a sentence and the gap between ideas. Watch those two spots in particular and use a silent pause there instead.
quote: There are two places where filler words commonly appear: at the beginning of a statement and in between ideas.

source.author: Steven D. Cohen
source.credentials: Instructor, Harvard Division of Continuing Education; faculty, Johns Hopkins Carey Business School
source.title: Tips on Public Speaking: Eliminating the Dreaded “Um”

advice: 'Um' and 'uh' tend to show up right before hard-to-find words, such as abstract, technical or unfamiliar ones. Choosing more familiar wording and practicing until the material feels familiar removes many fillers at their source.
quote: we need to make things more familiar, make things less difficult and make things less abstract
drill: Mark the 5 hardest words or terms in your speech. Practice saying the sentences that contain them until each comes out without a filler in front.

source.author: Valerie Fridland (guest), Matt Abrahams (host)
source.credentials: Fridland: professor of sociolinguistics, University of Nevada; Abrahams: lecturer in strategic communication, Stanford GSB
source.title: “Um, Like, So”: How Filler Words Can Be Effective in Communication
source.publisher: Stanford Graduate School of Business (Think Fast, Talk Smart)

advice: To sound authoritative, aim to sound fully rehearsed even when you're speaking off the cuff. In this conversation about authority, Pfeffer also advises avoiding filler words and ums or ahs as much as possible.
quote: You want to speak as if even though it's not rehearsed, it's been completely rehearsed

source.author: Jeffrey Pfeffer (guest), Matt Abrahams (host)
source.credentials: Pfeffer: professor of organizational behavior, Stanford GSB
source.title: How We Gain — or Give Away — Authority While Speaking
source.publisher: Stanford Graduate School of Business (Think Fast, Talk Smart)

advice: Running through a speech once more right away doesn't reduce filled pauses much. In one study, waiting about a week before repeating the task cut 'um' and 'uh' the most, so space your rehearsals out over several days.
quote: Filled pauses were impervious to the effects of a single repetition of the task.
drill: Practice the same speech on day 1 and again on day 7, then compare filler counts between the two recordings.

source.author: Gavin Bui, Mohammad Javad Ahmadian, Ann-Marie Hunter
source.title: Spacing effects on repeated L2 task performance

advice: Give yourself a limited filler budget during practice. When you go over it, the speech ends and you start again, trying to get further each time.
quote: have a friend watch you and end your speech when you’ve used filler words X amount of times.
drill: Set a limit (for example, 3 fillers). A partner stops you when you reach it, and you restart the speech, aiming to get further each time.

source.author: Joshua Hu
source.credentials: Ethos Debate intern; four-year NSDA Policy and Lincoln-Douglas debater; NSDA Nationals qualifier
source.title: How to Improve Fluency and Clarity in Speaking

advice: Build filler-free fluency with a random word generator: talk about the word it gives you for five minutes without stumbles or filler words.
drill: Use a random word generator and speak on the word for 5 minutes without any stumbles or filler words.

source.title: Delivery Part 1: Pronunciation & Fluency

advice: Nervous speakers tend to speed up, and speed brings more fillers. Deliberately slowing your pace gives your thinking time to catch up, so you need fewer 'ums' to cover the gaps.
quote: Speaking at a slower pace will help reduce the use of filler words.

source.title: Eliminate Filler Words
source.publisher: California State University, San Bernardino (Speaking Center)

advice: Don't aim for absolute zero. Saying 'um' two or three times in a speech may go unnoticed, but 'like' gets no such allowance and quickly becomes distracting.
quote: You might be able to get away with saying "um" as many as two or three times in your speech before it becomes distracting.

source.title: Stand Up, Speak Out: The Practice and Ethics of Public Speaking, Section 14.4 'Practicing for Successful Speech Delivery'

advice: Where a filler lands may matter as well as whether you say one. In this study, sentences with no 'um' were rated most acceptable, and listeners repeated sentences more accurately when 'um' sat in its usual spot (such as a clause boundary) than in an unusual one.
quote: Filled pauses often occur at clause boundaries

source.author: Minna Kirjavainen, Ludivine Crible, Kate Beeching
source.title: Can filled pauses be represented as linguistic items? Investigating the effect of exposure on the perception and production of um

advice: Give yourself a specific replacement for the filler: a silent pause. In this study, speakers learned to notice their disfluencies and were told to pause silently in their place, and all four cut their disfluencies afterwards. Earlier work had already suggested that teaching a replacement response may work better than awareness alone.
quote: results suggested that teaching a competing response (CR) may produce better outcomes.
drill: Give a 2-minute talk to a partner. Each time you feel an 'um' coming, close your lips and pause silently instead, then carry on. Have your partner tally fillers and silent pauses separately.

source.author: Brittany Pawlik, Christopher J. Perrin
source.title: Reducing speech disfluencies during public speaking using brief habit reversal

advice: Fewer fillers in practice sessions may not carry over to a real presentation. All four speakers in this study reduced their disfluencies after training, but carry-over to presenting in front of a class was shown for only one participant. Rehearse your filler-free delivery in front of real audiences too.
quote: For 1 participant, generalized effects were demonstrated when presenting in front of a class.

source.author: Brittany Pawlik, Christopher J. Perrin
source.title: Reducing speech disfluencies during public speaking using brief habit reversal

advice: Habit reversal training has a growing research base for cutting filled pauses in public speaking: one journal alone published seven studies of it between 2016 and 2022. If you want a method with research behind it, it is a good place to start.
quote: From 2016 to 2022, the Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis published 7 studies

source.author: James K. Luiselli
source.title: Public speaking disfluencies: A review of habit reversal training and research

advice: Start with the cheapest step: write a precise description of your own fillers. For 4 of 9 speakers in this study, a response description alone was enough to reduce disfluencies, and when it worked by itself it may have been more efficient than the full training package.
quote: Response description was sufficient at reducing speech disfluencies for 4 of 9 participants.
drill: Write a one-line definition for each of your fillers (for example: 'um' = any 'uh'/'um'/'er' sound between words), with two examples and one non-example, and read it before every practice run.

source.author: Stephanie M. Ortiz, Meghan A. Deshais, Raymond G. Miltenberger, Kenneth F. Reeve
source.title: Decreasing nervous habits during public speaking: A component analysis of awareness training

advice: If a definition isn't enough, add detection practice in stages. Some speakers in this study needed to spot their disfluencies in videos, and others also needed to detect them live during practice. The training was delivered virtually, and for most participants the reductions lasted through follow-up.
quote: Reductions were maintained during follow-up and generalization probes for most participants.

source.author: Stephanie M. Ortiz, Meghan A. Deshais, Raymond G. Miltenberger, Kenneth F. Reeve
source.title: Decreasing nervous habits during public speaking: A component analysis of awareness training

advice: When you work on one filler, keep counting the others and your speaking rate too. Awareness training alone cut targeted filler words for every student in this study, but how untargeted fillers and speech rate changed alongside them differed from person to person.
quote: covariation between targeted filler words and secondary dependent variables was idiosyncratic across participants.
drill: On each practice recording, tally your target filler, every other filler word, and your words per minute, so you can see if a new crutch replaces the old one.

source.author: Christina C. Montes, Megan R. Heinicke, Danielle M. Geierman
source.title: Awareness training reduces college students' speech disfluencies in public speaking

advice: Train your filler awareness in two stages: first spot fillers on a video of yourself, then catch them live while you practise speaking. Live practice alone was enough for some students in this study, but doing video then live training in sequence was more likely to produce a marked change.
quote: a treatment package including the sequential application of both video and in vivo training is more likely to result in marked behavior change.
drill: Watch a recording of yourself and mark every filler. Then give the same talk live and raise a finger each time you hear one leave your mouth.

source.author: Christina C. Montes, Megan R. Heinicke, M. Alexander Guendulain, Elizabeth Morales
source.title: A component analysis of awareness training for reducing speech disfluencies

advice: Teams can cut fillers together. In this study, university students in small groups trained to notice disfluencies and pause silently instead, with a group contingency (a reward the whole group shared). Disfluencies dropped meaningfully, and the reductions held when they later presented to a small audience.
quote: Brief habit reversal combined with an interdependent group contingency resulted in a meaningful reduction in speech disfluencies
drill: In a club or team practice, set a shared filler target for everyone's speeches combined, and give the group a reward only when the team total comes in under it.

source.author: Christopher J. Perrin, Sarah A. Hensel, Durie L. Lynch, Lisa R. Gallegos, Kendall Bell, Kristen Carpenter
source.title: Using brief habit reversal and an interdependent group contingency to reduce public-speaking speech disfluencies

advice: The replacement silent pause tends to fade after training ends. In this study, every speaker used more silent pauses after training, but only one kept using them at a high level. Keep practising the deliberate pause after your fillers drop, or it may slip away.
quote: Relative to baseline, competing responses increased for all participants but only remained high for 1 participant following training.

source.author: Christopher J. Perrin, Sarah A. Hensel, Durie L. Lynch, Lisa R. Gallegos, Kendall Bell, Kristen Carpenter
source.title: Using brief habit reversal and an interdependent group contingency to reduce public-speaking speech disfluencies

advice: You don't need zero fillers. When listeners rated speeches with 0, 2, 5 or 12 disfluencies per minute, a rate of 5 per minute did not hurt perceived effectiveness, while high rates (notably 12 filler sounds per minute) did. Aim for five or fewer per minute.
quote: A low, but nonzero, rate of disfluencies (5 per minute) did not adversely affect perceived effectiveness.

source.author: Matthew M. Laske, Florence D. DiGennaro Reed
source.title: Um, so, like, do speech disfluencies matter? A parametric evaluation of filler sounds and words

advice: Prioritise filler sounds over filler words. In this study, adding disfluencies hurt how effective a speaker seemed in most rating categories, and filler sounds in particular did, especially at high rates. Work on your filler sounds first.
quote: Increased disfluencies, particularly filler sounds, significantly affected perceptions across most categories,

source.author: Matthew M. Laske, Florence D. DiGennaro Reed
source.title: Um, so, like, do speech disfluencies matter? A parametric evaluation of filler sounds and words

advice: The payoff from awareness training goes beyond the filler count. After training, students said they used fewer verbal fillers and felt their overall public speaking had improved, and the effects generally held in front of a small audience.
quote: participants indicated not only decreased use of verbal fillers, but also improved overall public speaking ability posttreatment.

source.author: Claire Spieler, Raymond Miltenberger
source.title: Using awareness training to decrease nervous habits during public speaking

advice: Listen for 'thee' where you would normally say 'thuh'. In a large corpus of conversation, 81% of 'thee' pronunciations were followed by a break in speech, compared with about 7% for 'thuh'. A 'thee' is a hidden filler that warns you're about to get stuck.
quote: Fully 81% of the instances of thiy in the corpus were followed by a suspension of speech
drill: In a recording, mark every 'thee' you said before a consonant and check whether a pause, 'um' or restart followed.

source.author: Jean E. Fox Tree, Herbert H. Clark
source.title: Pronouncing "the" as "thee" to signal problems in speaking

advice: Speakers chose 'thee' when they anticipated a major problem, usually with the noun that came next, such as finding the word or choosing it. If your 'thee's cluster before certain names or terms, rehearse those nouns until they come out ready.
quote: They chose THIY when they anticipated a major problem and THUH when they didn’t.

source.author: Jean E. Fox Tree, Herbert H. Clark
source.title: Pronouncing "the" as "thee" to signal problems in speaking

advice: Being an expert doesn't shield you from fillers. In this study, the same spontaneous clips with 'um' and 'uh' left in made speakers seem less ready and less certain than versions with them removed, whether listeners thought the speaker was a professor or a student.
quote: We find that filled pauses led to lower perceived readiness and certainty, regardless of speaker expertise (Experiment 1).

source.author: Jonathan Him Nok Lee, Anna Papafragou
source.title: Disfluency in Spontaneous Speech: Social Attribution and Behavioral Consequences
source.publisher: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society

advice: Fillers can cost you the next chance to speak. Listeners were less likely to choose to ask a disfluent speaker again, and this was explained by the speaker seeming less ready. In interviews and Q&A, prepare enough that you sound ready.
quote: listeners were less likely to choose to ask disfluent speakers again

source.author: Jonathan Him Nok Lee, Anna Papafragou
source.title: Disfluency in Spontaneous Speech: Social Attribution and Behavioral Consequences
source.publisher: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society

advice: Not every filler plays the same role. In French speech, fillers fell into two patterns: at the start of a unit together with a discourse marker, or in the middle clustered with other hesitation markers. The authors link these to fluent and disfluent uses. When reviewing recordings, note where each filler sits and what comes with it, rather than counting them all as equal.
quote: initial position clustered with a discourse marker vs. medial position clustered with other hesitation markers

source.author: Loulou Kosmala, Ludivine Crible
source.title: The dual status of filled pauses: evidence from genre, proficiency and co-occurrence

advice: Filler coaching doesn't have to happen in person. In this study, simplified habit reversal was delivered face to face to one college student and over telehealth to two others, and it generally reduced all the targeted behaviours. Habit-reversal coaching over a video call can work.
quote: SHR was generally effective in decreasing all targets

source.author: Danielle Marie Geierman
source.credentials: MA thesis, Psychology, California State University, Sacramento
source.title: Evaluating collateral effects of habit reversal on idiosyncratic speech disfluencies and nervous habits

advice: When you count fillers on a video, also note what was happening each time: moving from one topic to the next, being asked a question, or glancing down at your notes. Knowing your trigger moments tells you exactly where to plan a slow breath instead.
quote: Do they occur when you are wrapping up one topic and moving onto the next?
drill: Watch a recording and write each filler on a list under one of three headings: transition, answering a question, or looking at notes. Practise a slow inhale in place of the filler in the most common category.

source.title: Is Your Presentation Filled with Um's? A method to reduce filled pauses when speaking in front of a group

advice: Nerves show up as fillers and repeated words. In this study of student interpreters, the more anxious ones said more 'er' and 'um' and repeated more words and phrases, and more disfluencies went with lower scores. The author's remedy is more chances to speak in public.
quote: In particular, more anxious interpreters tended to have more fillers, such as er and um, and more repetitions of words and phrases.

source.author: Nan Zhao
source.title: Speech Disfluencies in Consecutive Interpreting by Student Interpreters: The Role of Language Proficiency, Working Memory, and Anxiety

advice: Don't apologize for a slip. Keep going as if you meant it, or make light of it, because saying 'sorry' points out the mistake.
quote: The audience doesn't know you've made a mistake until you tell them you've made a mistake.

source.author: Allison Shapira
source.title: Don't say "I'm Sorry" during your speech

advice: When you're tempted to say 'I'm sorry' after a stumble, pause, breathe, smile and carry on.

source.author: Allison Shapira
source.title: Don't say "I'm Sorry" during your speech

advice: Anything that draws attention to a mistake, not just the word 'sorry', makes it bigger. Act relaxed and push ahead, because your slip looms larger to you than to them.
quote: Never explain, never apologize.

source.title: How to Handle Public Speaking Mistakes (Hint: No Regrets)

advice: If you start over at every slip in practice, you're training yourself to stop. Rehearse recovering and carrying on instead.
drill: Do full run-throughs with one rule: whatever goes wrong, don't stop or restart from the top.

source.title: Public Speaking Tip 6: Don't Worry, You WILL Make Mistakes!

advice: Practice mistakes on purpose so a real one doesn't throw you.
quote: Practice recovering from mistakes. Intentionally mess up, then smoothly continue.
drill: Deliberately flub a word in each practice run and continue without restarting.

source.title: How to Overcome Your Fear of Public Speaking

advice: Instead of saying 'Sorry, let me rephrase', use language simple enough, and a clear enough structure, that you don't need to rephrase.

source.title: Avoid These Common Speech Mistakes

advice: Don't apologize for being nervous. Take a moment instead, because your nerves are less visible than you think.

source.title: Avoid These Common Speech Mistakes

advice: Research on everyday speech found people are more likely to start a phrase, stop, and repeat its first word when the phrase is long or complex. Plan the whole phrase before you commit to the first word.

source.author: Herbert H. Clark, Thomas Wasow
source.title: Repeating Words in Spontaneous Speech

advice: Repeats usually happen on small opening words like 'I', 'the' or 'a', as in 'I uh I wouldn't…'. If you catch yourself, pause silently before the phrase instead of firing off its first word.
drill: Listen to a recording and circle every repeated 'I', 'the' or 'a'. Re-record those sentences with a silent breath before them.

source.author: Herbert H. Clark, Thomas Wasow
source.title: Repeating Words in Spontaneous Speech

advice: Speakers restart a phrase to make it sound continuous again, and the longer the break, the more likely a restart. Keeping hesitations short reduces the urge to start over.

source.author: Herbert H. Clark, Thomas Wasow
source.title: Repeating Words in Spontaneous Speech

advice: If you actually misspoke, take a breath, acknowledge it briefly and restate the point. Make it quick, but make your meaning clear.

source.title: How to Recover When You've Blown It

advice: Everyone trips over words sometimes, and it isn't worth derailing your talk. If the bit you fumbled wasn't crucial, let it go and move on.

source.author: Linda Ugelow
source.title: How to recover from public speaking mistakes

advice: Tongue twisters build steadier articulation. Start slowly and crisply, then speed up only as far as you can stay clear.
drill: Say a tongue twister slowly with crisp word endings, then speed up. When you trip, drop back to a slower speed.

source.author: Susan Dugdale
source.title: 44 Diction Exercises (Tongue Twisters) for Clear Speech

advice: Repeating a whole word or phrase, or revising mid-sentence, is a normal disfluency. See a speech-language pathologist if repeats come with tension, blocks or avoidance.

source.title: Stuttering

advice: Avoid long run-on sentences. They're easy to lose track of and end up restarting.

source.author: Steven J. Palkovitz
source.title: Guidelines for Public Speaking

advice: Small stumbles mostly go unnoticed, so carry on as if nothing happened. Rushing makes you trip more, so slow down.

source.title: Worries About Stumbling Over Your Words Or Being Inarticulate

advice: After a blank or a slip, picking up where you left off almost always works better than going back over what you said.

source.title: Mind Goes Blank During a Presentation? Here's How to Recover

advice: The flub rarely loses the room. Stopping to say 'let me start that over' is what makes you look rattled. Absorb the mistake and keep going.
drill: In your next rehearsal, promise yourself you won't stop or apologize for any error.

source.author: Topher Keene
source.title: Use the Mistake: Turn a Flub Into a Character Choice

advice: Rehearse the hard bits and rewrite phrases you keep tripping over before the real performance.
drill: Read your script aloud, mark every phrase you trip on, and either drill it or reword it.

source.title: Vocal Warm-Up Exercises: Ten Tips to Tame That Tripping Tongue

advice: Editing phrases like "I mean" and "you know" signal what kind of repair is coming. Fixing a slip yourself, right away, is better than leaving it for the listener to untangle. When you do restart, make it one clean, fast correction rather than a chain of them.
quote: She signals the type of repairs she is making by means of editing terms.

source.author: Herbert H. Clark
source.title: Managing problems in speaking

advice: Restarts and self-corrections tend to be the last fluency problem to fade with practice. In one study, pauses at the ends of clauses shrank by the second run-through and mid-clause pauses kept shrinking until the fourth, but self-repairs only dropped after the fourth performance, so don't judge your restarts after just a couple of tries.
quote: self-repairs decreased only after the fourth performance
drill: Deliver the same 2-minute speech six times in a row, recording each one. Count restarts on recordings 1, 3 and 6 to watch the late drop.

source.author: Craig Lambert, Judit Kormos, Danny Minn
source.credentials: Curtin University; Lancaster University; Kitakyushu University
source.title: Task Repetition and Second Language Speech Processing
source.publisher: Studies in Second Language Acquisition (Cambridge University Press)

advice: In competition, a short fluency break costs less than stopping to apologize and restart. Practice on purpose: when you misspeak, fix the word in flow and keep going instead of starting the sentence over.
quote: you should always always always practice moving on after a MAJOR mistake in your speech.
drill: During practice, have a partner call out 'wrong!' at random moments. Correct yourself mid-sentence and continue without going back to the start of the sentence.

source.title: Delivery Part 1: Pronunciation & Fluency

advice: Expect a few stumbles in every round and set a limit you can realistically hit, instead of aiming for zero. Some judges keep a tally, so the goal is to keep restarts rare and recover quickly instead of spiraling after one.
quote: you want to stumble less than three times in a round
drill: Score each practice speech by counting stumbles. Aim for under three per speech, then lower the target once you hit it consistently.

source.title: Strategy: Fluency in Extemporaneous Speaking

advice: To find out how often you restart and leave sentences unfinished, write out a recording of your speech word for word, including every 'uh', every repeated start and every half sentence. Seeing them on paper shows patterns that you don't hear while you're speaking.
quote: transcribe the entire speech, word for word, complete with all the 'uhs,' stuttering, and sentence fragments
drill: Record one rebuttal or speech, transcribe it exactly, and highlight every restart and abandoned sentence in one color and every filler in another.

source.author: Jason Baldwin
source.credentials: Graduate philosophy student, University of Notre Dame; coordinator of the LD division, Kentucky Institute
source.title: LD Rebuttals as Speeches
source.publisher: Rostrum (National Forensic League), Rostrum Library archive at University of Vermont

advice: Listeners' fluency judgments depend mostly on how you pause and how fast you go. Occasional self-corrections count for surprisingly little, so a quick, clean repair is better than freezing to avoid one.
quote: repair measures contributed only very little

source.author: Hans Rutger Bosker, Anne-France Pinget, Hugo Quené, Ted Sanders, Nivja H. De Jong
source.title: What makes speech sound fluent? The contributions of pauses, speed and repairs

advice: Say your presentation a little differently on every practice run. The goal is to keep it conversational instead of memorizing exact phrases.
quote: Every time you say your presentation, say it differently.
drill: Run your speech three times, changing the wording of each main point on purpose while keeping the order the same.

source.title: 8 Key Points for Perfect Presentation Practice

advice: When you slip, think of it as a missed take in a film and move straight on to your next point. Stopping to replay or fix the mistake turns a small stumble into a long pause.
quote: Finally, like an athlete, if you miss a shot, don't dwell on it – instead, focus on the next play.

source.author: Think:Act
source.title: Matt Abrahams on speaking well when on the spot

advice: Bracing for a hard word you're dreading can make you trip over the easy words around it. Keep your attention on the whole sentence instead of waiting for that one spot.
quote: The irony is that the difficult name is usually pronounced flawlessly,

source.author: Peter Stewart
source.title: 0651 – When To Expect Verbal Trips and Slips
source.publisher: Get A Better Broadcast, Podcast and Voice-Over Voice (podcast)

advice: If you feel a word getting stuck, start its first sound with the lips, tongue and jaw barely touching and hold that sound a moment, then finish the rest of the word at normal speed. A loose, stretched-out start is less likely to turn into a forced restart.
quote: Prolongation is starting the first sound of the word with a very light contact with your articulators
drill: Pick 10 words you often trip on. Say each one three times, holding the first sound lightly for about half a second, then saying the rest of the word crisply.

source.author: Dorvan H. Breitenfeldt
source.title: Advice to Those Who Stutter (Chapter 2)

advice: Don't push hard against a word you are afraid of. Start moving your mouth and letting air and sound flow at the same moment, so you glide into the first syllable rather than crashing into it and starting over.
quote: try to ease out of your blocks by sliding into the first syllable of the word

source.author: Lon L. Emerick
source.title: Advice to Those Who Stutter (Chapter 1)

advice: Rushing to answer straight away invites false starts. Before you answer a question, and between phrases, silently count to two so time pressure doesn't push you into speech you haven't planned.
quote: using a count of two in their minds as a guide
drill: Have a partner ask you quick factual questions (your address, a phone number, today's plans). Count 'one, two' in your head before every answer.

source.author: Hugo H. Gregory
source.title: Advice to Those Who Stutter (Chapter 4)

advice: Avoid 'launching' habits such as a throwaway sound, a 'well', or swapping in an easier word to get yourself going. These tricks feel helpful, but they make speaking harder over time. Begin the real first word instead.
quote: use a sound or some trick to get speech started

source.author: Lon L. Emerick
source.title: Advice to Those Who Stutter (Chapter 1)

advice: An 'easy onset' means letting a little breath flow out before your voice switches on, so the first sound starts softly instead of with a hard catch in the throat. Build the skill in steps: sounds first, then words, then phrases, then everyday sentences.
quote: Exhale (as if sighing) on a prolonged /h/ sound: 'hhhhhh.'
drill: Sigh out 'hhhh' and let it fade into a vowel ('hhh-ah'). Next, put a faint /h/ before vowel-starting words ('h-apple', 'h-under'), then use the same gentle start at the beginning of each phrase in a short paragraph.

source.author: Adult Speech Therapy
source.credentials: Site written by speech-language pathologists (bio lists Alisha Kleindel, SLP instructor at Midwestern University)
source.title: Easy Onset for Voice Therapy and Stuttering

advice: Words that start with p, b, t, d, k or g can't be eased in with breath. For these, let the lips or tongue touch only lightly as you form the first sound, which cuts the tension that leads to a jammed start.
quote: To decrease tension when saying plosives, practice light articulatory contacts.
drill: Say pairs like 'pen/Ben', 'two/do', 'cot/got' first with a firm press and then with a feather-light touch, so you can feel the difference.

source.author: Adult Speech Therapy
source.credentials: Site written by speech-language pathologists (bio lists Alisha Kleindel, SLP instructor at Midwestern University)
source.title: Easy Onset for Voice Therapy and Stuttering

advice: After you stumble on a word, take a short pause, notice where you tensed up, relax that spot, and say the word once more smoothly before going on. This turns a messy restart into a single calm do-over.
quote: Cancellations are a stuttering technique that can be used after a disfluency

source.author: Leanne Sherred
source.title: 7 Strategies to Help Improve Fluency and a Stutter

advice: As a practice exercise, read sentences giving every syllable the same stress and length, as if keeping time with a metronome, while still letting your pitch move naturally. The steady beat smooths out stops and starts.
quote: saying a sentence with equal stress on each syllable.
drill: Set a metronome to about 120 bpm and read a paragraph one syllable per click. Then read it again at normal speed and keep the same evenness.

source.author: Leanne Sherred
source.title: 7 Strategies to Help Improve Fluency and a Stutter

advice: Get in ahead of a stumble. When you sense a word coming that you might trip on, change how you start it, softer and slower, before you say it, rather than fixing it afterward.
quote: If you feel a stutter coming, you adjust how you start the word to reduce tension.

source.author: Alexis Irazoque
source.title: Fluency Shaping vs. Stuttering Modification: Which Stuttering Strategy Is Best?

advice: Building in regular pauses slows a rushed, jumbled delivery better than telling yourself to 'talk slower'. Learn the habit on printed text first by stopping at every comma and period, and start each new sentence smoothly.
quote: Adequate pausing will slow down his speech more than any exhortation to talk slowly
drill: Underline the first word of each sentence in a printed paragraph. Read it aloud, starting each underlined word gently and silently counting 'one-two' at every comma.

source.author: David A. Daly
source.credentials: Ed.D.; ASHA Fellow; Specialty Certification in Fluency Disorders
source.publisher: Minnesota State University, Mankato (International Cluttering Online Conference archive)

advice: Fast talkers tend to lose control and clarity as their sentences get longer. Practise pausing on short statements first, then work up step by step to longer and more complex ones.
quote: clutterers' rate of speech increases and speech intelligibility suffers as they produce longer sentences.
drill: Week 1: pause cleanly within 5-word sentences. Week 2: 10-word sentences. Week 3: two-clause sentences. Move up only when the pauses stay steady.

source.author: David A. Daly
source.credentials: Ed.D.; ASHA Fellow; Specialty Certification in Fluency Disorders
source.publisher: Minnesota State University, Mankato (International Cluttering Online Conference archive)

advice: Mark your practice text with pause points at phrase breaks, about every three to five words, and stop briefly at each one. Once this feels natural, shorten the pauses so your speech still sounds conversational.
quote: Place the asterisks at phrase boundaries, so that the client will be pausing after every 3 to 5 words.
drill: Put an asterisk at every phrase boundary in a paragraph and read it with a clear pause at each mark. Over several sessions, shrink the pauses until listeners can barely notice them.

source.author: Kenneth Logan
source.title: Helping Clients Who Clutter Regulate Speaking Rate
source.publisher: Minnesota State University, Mankato (International Cluttering Online Conference archive)

advice: To slow down without sounding choppy, stretch the sounds inside words a little instead of only adding gaps. This helps most with long multisyllable words, which come out more accurately at a controlled speed.
quote: Speakers can reduce articulation rate by increasing the duration of individual speech sounds.
drill: Time yourself reading a passage at roughly one second per syllable, then two-thirds of a second, then slightly slower than normal. Pay most attention to the long words.

source.author: Kenneth Logan
source.title: Helping Clients Who Clutter Regulate Speaking Rate
source.publisher: Minnesota State University, Mankato (International Cluttering Online Conference archive)

advice: Practise controlled speech on tasks that get harder to formulate, step by step: first listing, then reading, retelling, explaining, and finally persuading. Each step adds planning load, so you build fluency before the hardest kinds of speaking.
drill: Do one minute of each in order: list items in a category, read a paragraph aloud, retell it, explain how something works, argue for a position. Keep pausing at the same quality throughout.

source.author: Yvonne van Zaalen, Isabella Reichel
source.title: An Introduction to Cluttering: A Practical Guide for Speech-Language Pathology Students, Clinicians, and Researchers

advice: If you tend to blur or drop syllables (especially unstressed ones) in longer words, practice tapping each syllable as you say the word to build syllable awareness.
drill: Tap one finger per syllable as you say long words such as 'statistically', 'responsibility' and 'particularly', first slowly and then at conversational speed.

source.author: Yvonne van Zaalen, Isabella Reichel
source.title: An Introduction to Cluttering: A Practical Guide for Speech-Language Pathology Students, Clinicians, and Researchers

advice: Monitor yourself by checking for what went right, such as well-placed pauses, rather than only counting stumbles. In this case, the client made five recordings a day and analyzed two of them, checking against a narrow question such as whether every syllable could be heard.
quote: focuses not on moments of disfluency or reduced intelligibility but on moments of adequate pausing
drill: Record five 30-second clips a day. Pick two and mark every spot where you paused well, then note one place where a pause would have prevented a stumble.

source.title: An Adolescent Confronted With Cluttering: The Story of Johan
source.publisher: Perspectives of the ASHA Special Interest Groups

advice: Disfluencies per word rise sharply as utterances get longer, because each long sentence demands more planning on the fly. Break complex ideas into a series of shorter spoken units so you have less to plan at once.
quote: Spoken disfluencies are strikingly sensitive to the increased planning demands of generating progressively longer utterances.

source.author: Sharon Oviatt
source.title: Predicting and Managing Spoken Disfluencies During Human-Computer Interaction
source.publisher: Human Language Technology: Proceedings of a Workshop held at Plainsboro, New Jersey

advice: Giving your talk a set structure takes planning work off you while you speak, and in this research structured formats removed most disfluencies. Answer within a fixed frame (for example: point, reason, example) rather than making up the shape as you go.
quote: That is, 70% of all disfluencies were eliminated by using a more structured form.
drill: Answer five practice questions using the same three-slot frame each time, and compare the recording with five answers given without a frame.

source.author: Sharon Oviatt
source.title: Predicting and Managing Spoken Disfluencies During Human-Computer Interaction
source.publisher: Human Language Technology: Proceedings of a Workshop held at Plainsboro, New Jersey

advice: Expect more repeats and restarts in the parts of your talk that are hardest to put into words, such as describing abstract material, or when you are the one directing the explanation. Plan the wording for those sections ahead of time instead of improvising them.
quote: disfluencies are associated with an increase in planning difficulty

source.author: Heather Bortfeld, Silvia D. Leon, Jonathan E. Bloom, Michael F. Schober, Susan E. Brennan
source.title: Disfluency rates in conversation: Effects of age, relationship, topic, role, and gender

advice: When you notice a slip, you don't have to cut off that instant and leave a gap. Fluent speakers tend to keep going until the correction is ready and then switch over cleanly, which makes the repair sound smoother.
quote: Speakers preferred fluency over accuracy.

source.author: Mandana Seyfeddinipur, Sotaro Kita, Peter Indefrey
source.title: How speakers interrupt themselves in managing problems in speaking: Evidence from self-repairs

advice: When you fix a slip, don't drop the corrected word in by itself. Go back a word or two to lead into it, so listeners can tell straight away which part of the sentence you are replacing.
quote: no later than upon hearing the very first word of the correction

source.author: Willem J. M. Levelt
source.title: Spontaneous self-repairs in speech: Processes and representations
source.publisher: Proceedings of the 10th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences (Foris)

advice: Keep a correction tight. Repeat your original wording and change only the word that was wrong, rather than rebuilding the whole sentence a new way.
quote: corrections for error are highly conservative, closely copying the wording of the original utterance.

source.author: Willem J. M. Levelt
source.title: Spontaneous self-repairs in speech: Processes and representations
source.publisher: Proceedings of the 10th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences (Foris)

advice: A misspoken word doesn't disappear from the listener's mind the moment you correct it, and traces of it stay. When a slip touches an important fact, say the corrected statement again in full so the right version is the one that sticks.
quote: the reparandum is not completely erased from the parse, but rather traces of the reparandum linger

source.author: Matthew W. Lowder, Fernanda Ferreira
source.title: Prediction in the processing of repair disfluencies

advice: A quick mid-word cutoff followed by a brief 'uh' and then the correct word does not confuse listeners. In experiments it helped them get to the right meaning faster. Make the fix quickly and calmly instead of stopping to apologize or explain.
quote: listeners selected the target object more quickly, and no less accurately.

source.author: Susan E. Brennan, Michael F. Schober
source.title: How Listeners Compensate for Disfluencies in Spontaneous Speech

advice: An occasional repeated word ('the the') gets noticed, but in brain-response studies it did not harm listeners' understanding or memory of the next word. Don't stop to fix a simple repetition. Just keep going.

source.author: Lucy J. MacGregor, M. Corley, David I. Donaldson
source.title: Not all disfluencies are are equal: The effects of disfluent repetitions on language comprehension

advice: How far ahead you plan before you start talking is partly your choice. Under pressure people begin before their thought is complete and finish planning mid-sentence, which makes the sentence itself take longer. When an idea is complicated, take a beat to plan its first part before you start.
quote: Speakers sometimes speak and plan simultaneously

source.author: Fernanda Ferreira, Benjamin Swets
source.title: How incremental is language production? Evidence from the production of utterances requiring the computation of arithmetic sums

advice: When you flub a line while recording or reading, don't start the whole section over. Stop, take a breath, let some of it out, and pick up again from the last complete sentence.
quote: Just stop, breathe, partially release that breath, and go back to the last whole sentence and start again.

source.author: Karen Schaefer
source.title: Voicing Your Script: Tips and Techniques

advice: Lots of stumbling usually means you are reading faster than you can handle. Slow down until the passage comes out clean, then bring the speed back up a little at a time.
quote: If you're stumbling a lot, maybe you're trying to read too fast.

source.author: Karen Schaefer
source.title: Voicing Your Script: Tips and Techniques

advice: If one phrase keeps tripping you up after practice, the wording may be the problem rather than you. Rewrite it into something you can say cleanly.
quote: If you still stumble, rewrite that phrase so you can read it cleanly.

source.author: Karen Schaefer
source.title: Voicing Your Script: Tips and Techniques

advice: After a stumble, the adrenaline rush makes you want to speed up, which usually leads to more slips. Do the opposite: slow down and pause briefly so your thoughts and your mouth can get back in sync.
quote: When you stumble across a word or a phrase don’t speed up. Slow down. Pause.

source.title: The Trick to Smoothing Out Stumbles

advice: Every speaker has a top efficient speed. Past it, stammering and backtracking actually slow you down. Find your own efficient rate and stay there, and you can often cover more material than someone racing past their limit.
quote: the resulting stammering ends up actually slowing the debater down.

source.author: David M. Cheshier
source.credentials: Assistant Professor of Communications and Director of Debate, Georgia State University

advice: When reading quickly from a page, guide your eyes with a fingertip kept a word or two ahead of what you are saying. This keeps your place and cuts down on stumbles from skipping or misreading.
quote: racing your finger a couple words ahead of what you're speaking at the moment

source.author: David M. Cheshier
source.credentials: Assistant Professor of Communications and Director of Debate, Georgia State University

advice: Clarity drills, such as speaking with a pencil in your mouth, carry over best when you alternate: about twenty seconds of the drill, then twenty seconds of normal speech, then back to the drill. That way you don't slip into a 'drill mode' that never shows up in your real delivery.
quote: then speaking normally for twenty seconds, then back to the drill.
drill: Read for 20 seconds while over-articulating every syllable, then 20 seconds normally, and alternate for 3 minutes.

source.author: David M. Cheshier
source.credentials: Assistant Professor of Communications and Director of Debate, Georgia State University

advice: To build stop-free delivery, practise with a partner who stops you at every flub or break, and then restart the speech from the very beginning. The cost of going back to the start keeps you focused on a clean run.
drill: Start Stops: a monitor calls 'stop' at every fluency break or flub, and you begin again from the introduction until you finish one clean run.

source.author: Brittany Stanchik
source.title: Congressional Debate Practice Drills

advice: Once you can get through a speech, switch to a gentler version of the drill. Your partner still stops you to name a habit, but you make the fix and carry on from that spot, which builds in-the-moment correction without starting over.
quote: The speaker does not have to start all over once they make a mistake
drill: Relaxed Start Stops: pick a focus (such as fluency), have a monitor interrupt with a quick correction, and continue from that point while applying it.

source.author: Brittany Stanchik
source.title: Congressional Debate Practice Drills

advice: Type up a recording of your speech word for word and mark every break and long pause. Then look for where they cluster, for example at transitions, in evidence, or in certain sentence types, so you can fix the cause and not just the symptom.
quote: Notice the fluency breaks- where do they happen the most?
drill: Record 3 minutes, transcribe it with a symbol at each break or long pause, and list the three spots where breaks cluster most.

source.author: Brittany Stanchik
source.title: Congressional Debate Practice Drills

advice: For a phrase you keep tripping on, draw hash marks between the words so you can see exactly where each one ends. Then say that phrase over and over until it rolls off your tongue.
quote: I will repeat a word or phrase I am stumbling on numerous times.

source.author: Justine Reiss
source.title: Working Wednesday: How to Deal With Tricky Words and Phrasing
