advice: Make up your own tongue twister from the exact words you usually trip on. Practise it slowly, speed up only after a clean run, and drop back to slow the moment you slip.
quote: The key with tongue twisters as diction exercises is to only speed up once you’re in control of the words.
drill: Write one sentence packed with your personal trouble words. Say it slowly five times in a row, speed up only after five clean reps, and slow down after any mistake.

source.author: Lili Wexu
source.credentials: Actor, voiceover talent and announcer with 20+ years of experience
source.title: The Best Diction Exercises for Actors

advice: Practise hard words with a pencil held sideways between your teeth. The obstacle forces your tongue to find exact positions, and that precision carries over once you remove the pencil.
quote: The pencil creates an obstruction that forces my tongue to be clear about where it should be.
drill: Read a paragraph slowly with a pencil across your teeth, then read it again without the pencil and listen for the sharper consonants.

source.author: Lili Wexu
source.credentials: Actor, voiceover talent and announcer with 20+ years of experience
source.title: The Best Diction Exercises for Actors

advice: Match the fix to the size of the slip. If you trip on a single word, just say that word again and move on. If a whole phrase comes out jumbled, briefly say you'll read it again and redo it once.

source.author: Kim Stewart
source.title: Be heard: Presentation skills for radio readers

advice: Before reading aloud, go through the text and mark how words group into meaning units, and pick out the hard names, words and acronyms. Say those aloud several times beforehand so they don't catch you out live.
quote: Prepare their pronunciation by speaking them aloud several times.

source.author: Kim Stewart
source.title: Be heard: Presentation skills for radio readers

advice: Lay out spoken notes or scripts with one complete thought per line and a blank line between thoughts. This makes it easy for your eyes to find the next idea without losing your place.
quote: I try to keep every line self-contained – and one line.

source.title: How NPR's Carrie Johnson found her radio voice

advice: If you skip a line or say things out of order, don't backtrack and restart the passage. The audience has no script to compare against. Carry on, and add anything essential later with a bridge such as 'what I haven't told you yet is...'.
quote: Remember, the audience doesn't know what you've planned.

source.author: Caren S. Neile
source.title: Overcoming Embarrassing Moments Onstage

advice: In an analysis of 959 natural self-repairs, speakers usually stopped as soon as they noticed trouble, except that a word that was correct tended to be finished first. So if the word coming out is wrong, cut it off right there. If it is right and you just want to rephrase, finish the word and then switch.
quote: interrupting follows detection promptly, with the exception that correct words tend to be completed.
drill: Read a list of short descriptions aloud while a partner calls out 'change' at random moments. If the word you are saying is wrong, stop mid-word. If it is fine, finish it and then rephrase.

source.author: Willem J. M. Levelt
source.title: Monitoring and self-repair in speech

advice: Levelt found that whether a repair sounds well formed depends on how it relates to the original, and he linked this to how two items joined by 'and' or 'or' relate. A quick check for a correction: the original bit and the fix should fit together the way the two halves of an 'X or Y' phrase would ('turn left' / 'right' works, 'turn left' / 'the second street' doesn't).
quote: A bi-conditional well-formedness rule links this relation to a corresponding relation between the conjuncts of a coordination.
drill: Record yourself describing a route or a diagram, then listen for each self-correction. Write the original and the repair with 'or' between them. Where that reads badly, practise saying the corrected sentence so the fix lines up with the part it replaces.

source.author: Willem J. M. Levelt
source.title: Monitoring and self-repair in speech

advice: In 1,525 repairs by callers to a radio talk show, many corrections started after the cut-off sooner than any model predicted, showing that people can plan a correction while they are still talking. A repair doesn't need a long silent gap, so aim to slide from the cut-off straight into the fix.
quote: Many of the cut-off-to-repair times observed were faster than would be predicted by any model in the literature.

source.author: E. R. Blackmer, J. L. Mitton
source.title: Theories of monitoring and the timing of repairs in spontaneous speech

advice: In a study of 368 natural repairs of sound slips, the corrected word was more often sped up than slowed down compared with the slip, and most repairs were not over-pronounced. You don't need to stretch out or over-enunciate a correction; these speakers usually said the fix at least as fast as the slip.
quote: most repairs cannot be described as hyper-articulated on the grounds of their temporal organisation

source.author: Leendert Plug, Paul Carter
source.title: Timing and tempo in spontaneous phonological error repair

advice: Repairs that start early, before the wrong word is finished, come with shorter gaps before the correction than repairs that start late. So listen to yourself closely as you speak. Catching a slip partway through the word tends to go with a quicker fix.
quote: early repairs are associated with shorter offset-to-repair intervals than late ones
drill: Read tongue-twister sentences at a slightly fast pace. Each time you slip, stop as soon as you hear it, mid-word if you can, and say the right word at once. Count how many of your stops came mid-word rather than after the whole word.

source.author: Leendert Plug, Paul Carter
source.title: Timing and tempo in spontaneous phonological error repair

advice: In this study of speech errors, the correct word was the most common repair, but it was used less often when the error was caught late, after being heard aloud (about half a second after inner-speech monitoring), than when it was caught internally. When you fix a slip you have already said aloud, make sure the replacement is actually right instead of grabbing the first alternative.
quote: the time lag between self-monitoring internal and overt speech appears to be in the order of 500 ms.

source.author: Sieb Nooteboom, Hugo Quené
source.credentials: Utrecht Institute of Linguistics OTS, Utrecht University
source.title: Testing a Theory of Repairing Segmental Speech Errors

advice: Brain recordings showed that listeners register an abandoned sentence start (a false start) as a grammatical anomaly. Repeated words were processed differently, in a way the authors link to listeners often not consciously noticing repeats. So abandoned sentence frames are a habit worth targeting: settle how a sentence will begin before you launch it.
quote: listeners detect a syntactic anomaly when processing these items
drill: Record a two-minute answer to an impromptu question. Mark every sentence you started and then abandoned. Redo the answer, saying your first few words silently in your head before you start each sentence, and compare the counts.

source.author: Jan McAllister, Susan Cato-Symonds, Blake Johnson
source.title: Listeners' ERP responses to false starts and repetitions in spontaneous speech
source.publisher: Proc. ITRW on Disfluency in Spontaneous Speech (DiSS 2001), ISCA

advice: Listeners can usually tell a sentence has broken off as soon as they hear the first word after the break. In this small study they could still tell within one word when the speech was filtered so the words couldn't be made out. Listeners pick up a restart almost at once, so make it quick and clean instead of trying to hide it.
quote: listeners could usually detect disfluency when they heard the first word after the interruption

source.author: R. J. Lickley
source.title: Juncture Cues to Disfluency

advice: In natural conversation, disfluencies affect up to ten percent of words and over a third of utterances, and some speakers produce about three times the average. Measure your own baseline from a recording and work to bring it down, rather than comparing yourself to a flawless ideal.
quote: However, speakers vary considerably, with some speakers showing about three times the average rate.
drill: Transcribe one minute of yourself speaking off the cuff. Count restarts, repeats and fillers, divide by the number of words, and note the rate. Repeat weekly to see whether your rate drops.

source.author: Elizabeth Shriberg
source.title: To 'errrr' is human: ecology and acoustics of speech disfluencies
source.publisher: Journal of the International Phonetic Association

advice: Shriberg found that speakers lean toward either repeating words or abandoning starts, and the ones who abandon starts talk faster. She suggests faster speakers get ahead of their own planning and so must take back half-begun sentences. If your recordings show mostly abandoned starts rather than repeats, try easing your pace a little to give planning time to keep up.
quote: and thus often have to retract provisional starts and begin anew
drill: Record a two-minute impromptu answer at your usual pace and again about 10 percent slower. Count abandoned starts in each version to see whether slowing down reduces them for you.

source.author: Elizabeth Shriberg
source.title: To 'errrr' is human: ecology and acoustics of speech disfluencies
source.publisher: Journal of the International Phonetic Association

advice: Plan what to say like a telegram. First settle the few key content words of your point, then add the small linking words as you speak. This brochure recommends planning the 'what' before the 'how' for people whose fast speech comes out disorganised.
quote: the “what” can be taught as formulating a telegram
drill: For each practice question, jot three to five key words (the telegram), then say the full answer aloud building sentences around them. Gradually drop the written notes and just think the telegram before you speak.

source.author: Kenneth O. St. Louis
source.title: Cluttering: Some Guidelines

advice: Keep a short 'wrong' clip of your rushed, disorganised speech and a 'right' clip of you speaking clearly and under control. Listening to the two back to back several times a day trains your ear to notice the difference while you talk.
quote: listen to and compare these “wrong” and “right” speech samples several times a day
drill: Save a 20-second clip of a messy answer and a 20-second clip of a clean one. Play them back to back three times a day for a week before practice sessions.

source.author: Kenneth O. St. Louis
source.title: Cluttering: Some Guidelines

advice: If your mind goes blank: pause, take a calm sip of water, nod while you look at your notes, find your place and keep going.
quote: You don't need to tell the audience that you lost your place.
drill: In rehearsal, have a friend call 'blank!' at random moments and practice the sip, nod, find, continue routine.

source.author: Allison Shapira
source.title: What to do when your mind goes blank

advice: Don't memorize a script word for word. Practice from bullet points so that one forgotten line can't derail you.
drill: Deliver the speech three times from bullet points only, letting the wording change each time.

source.author: Allison Shapira
source.title: What to do when your mind goes blank

advice: Blanks often happen where two ideas aren't connected. Build a clear bridge from each point to the next.
drill: Practice aloud, mark every spot where you stall, and write a linking sentence for each.

source.author: Allison Shapira
source.title: What to do when your mind goes blank

advice: Print notes in a large font with plenty of white space, on one side of the page only, so you can find your place at a glance.

source.author: Allison Shapira
source.title: What to do when your mind goes blank

advice: If you notice you're rambling, pause, nod and use a bridge line such as 'Let me move on to a different point.' It looks deliberate.

source.author: Allison Shapira
source.title: What to do when your mind goes blank

advice: When you lose your thread, 'rewind': repeat your last sentence or phrase. It buys thinking time and often jogs what comes next.
quote: Repeat the last sentence or phrase. This gives your mind both time to think and a little 'restart' jolt.

source.author: Diane Windingland
source.title: What Was I Saying?

advice: If rewinding doesn't work, 'fast-forward': skip to the next part you do remember and carry on.

source.author: Diane Windingland
source.title: What Was I Saying?

advice: Link your sections by ending one point with the word or phrase that starts the next. It works as a built-in memory trigger.
drill: Rewrite each transition so the last words of one section become the first words of the next, then rehearse the transitions only.

source.author: Diane Windingland
source.title: What Was I Saying?

advice: Plan how you'll recover from a blank before the speech, the way you'd plan a fire drill, so you aren't improvising under stress.
drill: Write down your blank-recovery steps and practice them during a run-through.

source.author: Diane Windingland
source.title: What Was I Saying?

advice: A world champion speaker who blanked for seven seconds recovered by pausing, breathing deeply and turning his attention from himself to the audience.

source.author: Ed Tate
source.title: Seven Seconds of Terror

advice: Think of your talk as a conversation, not a recital. Then a missing line doesn't freeze you.
quote: Rather than focusing on delivering a memorized speech, I began thinking of the presentation as a conversation with 2,000+ of my best friends.

source.author: Ed Tate
source.title: Seven Seconds of Terror

advice: Keep your usual rehearsal routine on the day. Breaking it, or comparing yourself to the speaker before you, can set off a blank.

source.author: Ed Tate
source.title: Seven Seconds of Terror

advice: Going blank is a stress freeze, not a failure. Pause, look at the audience and restart with 'As I was saying…', repeating your last few sentences.
quote: Going blank onstage is a typical freeze response.

source.author: Katie Stoddart
source.title: Use Your Brain to Calm Your Speaking Nerves

advice: To cover a blank, invite the audience to take a breath with you. It buys you a few calm seconds to remember.
drill: Memorize the cue 'Go blank, let's breathe' and practice saying it smoothly.

source.author: Katie Stoddart
source.title: Use Your Brain to Calm Your Speaking Nerves

advice: Memorize at least your opening and closing lines and keep the middle conversational. Practice out loud, not just in your head.

source.title: How to Overcome Your Fear of Public Speaking

advice: If nothing comes back, it's fine to say briefly that you lost your place, check your notes, or ask the audience where you were. They care more about the recovery than the blank.
quote: The audience doesn't care that you've blanked, they care that you recover.

source.author: Karen Eber
source.title: How to Overcome Public Speaking Fear (And Stop Going Blank Onstage)

advice: For each section of your talk, decide in advance what you'll jump to if you blank and restarting doesn't help.
drill: Next to each section of your outline, write a 'go-to-next' point to fall back on.

source.author: Karen Eber
source.title: How to Overcome Public Speaking Fear (And Stop Going Blank Onstage)

advice: In conversation research, about four seconds of unexpected silence was enough to make people uncomfortable. Silences you didn't plan should stay well under that, unless you're clearly checking notes or pausing on purpose.

source.author: Namkje Koudenburg, Tom Postmes, Ernestine Gordijn
source.title: Disrupting the flow: How brief silences in group conversations affect social needs

advice: If you lose your place mid-speech, pause, breathe, look at your notes, then restart the sentence confidently. Most people won't notice a small reset.

source.title: 9 Common Mistakes in Public Speaking to Avoid

advice: Repeat a question before you answer it. Everyone hears it, and you get thinking time without dead air or fillers.

source.author: Steven J. Palkovitz
source.title: Guidelines for Public Speaking

advice: When your mind goes blank, go back to your core message. Restating it buys time to recover your next thought, and the audience doesn't know what you planned to say anyway.

source.author: Peter Dhu
source.title: What Do You Do If Your Mind Goes Blank When Public Speaking

advice: If you lose your place, ask the audience a quick show-of-hands question about what you just said. While they answer, glance at your notes and recall your next point.

source.title: How to Recover If You Lose Your Place During a Presentation: 8 Proven Strategies

advice: A pause to drink water or check your notes looks so normal that audiences rarely realize you're recovering.

source.author: Andrew Dlugan
source.title: Speech Pauses: 12 Techniques to Speak Volumes with Your Silence

advice: Great speakers often pause for two to three seconds or longer, and a pause makes you sound confident and in control. Keep a deliberate pause under about five seconds, the point past which the article says it may start to count against you.
quote: As long as the pause isn't too long (no more than five seconds), the audience won't hold it against you.
drill: Practice pausing for a silent count of three at key points, and use a stopwatch on your recording to check that no pause runs past five seconds.

source.author: Noah Zandan
source.credentials: CEO and co-founder of Quantified Communications
source.title: How to Stop Saying 'Um,' 'Ah,' and 'You Know' (reprint hosted by Rutgers Food Science graduate program)

advice: When a hard question leaves you needing time, say so briefly and then take the pause. Asking for a moment turns a long silence into a deliberate choice instead of an awkward gap.
quote: I want to take a moment to think about that.
drill: Have a partner ask tough cross-ex or Q&A questions. Practice saying a short 'let me think' line, pausing silently, and then answering.

source.author: Matt Abrahams and Shawon Jackson
source.credentials: Abrahams: lecturer, Stanford Graduate School of Business
source.title: Communication Tips from the Classroom and Around the World
source.publisher: Stanford Graduate School of Business (Think Fast, Talk Smart)

advice: Using pauses well is one of the most important delivery skills, but many speakers feel uneasy in silence and that unease shows. Comfort with pausing comes from practicing it on purpose until it no longer feels risky.
quote: In terms of timing, the effective use of pauses is one of the most important skills to develop.

source.title: Stand Up, Speak Out: The Practice and Ethics of Public Speaking, Section 14.4 'Practicing for Successful Speech Delivery'

advice: If you lose your place in an extemp speech, don't come to a dead stop. Keeping your voice moving through a bridge or a restatement usually brings the next point back, while a frozen silence tends to cause more stumbles.
quote: If you lose your place, keep speaking and it will come back to you.

source.title: Strategy: Fluency in Extemporaneous Speaking

advice: Don't always rehearse from the top. Start each run-through at a random section, so the middle and ending get as much practice as the opening and you can pick up from any point if you lose your place.
quote: start rehearsing each time at a random section and take it from there.
drill: Number your sections, roll a die or draw a card to choose a starting section, and deliver from there to the end. Do five random starts per session.

source.author: Caren S. Neile
source.title: Techniques To Remember Your Speech

advice: Split your speech into small self-contained units and learn them one at a time. If something throws you off, you only have to find the start of the current unit, not rebuild the whole speech in your head.
quote: So if he gets thrown off, he can more easily find his way back.
drill: Give each chunk a two-word label. Have a friend call out labels in random order and start speaking from that chunk within two seconds.

source.author: Caren S. Neile
source.title: Techniques To Remember Your Speech

advice: Keep your preview loose instead of announcing every point in exact order, because a detailed preview locks you in and turns a forgotten point into a visible gap. If you remember a skipped point later, bring it in with a phrase like "What I haven't told you is..." rather than stopping.
quote: But the more specific you are in your introduction, the more you are tied to what you planned to say.

source.author: Caren S. Neile
source.title: Techniques To Remember Your Speech

advice: For contest speeches, learn the text well enough that you aren't searching for the next words while you talk. A half-learned script splits your attention between remembering and delivering, and that split shows up as hesitations.
quote: If you don’t have it memorized, a part of your mind will be thinking about what words should come next.

source.author: Bill Brown
source.credentials: DTM; speech delivery coach, Gillette, Wyoming
source.title: Memorize Your Speeches and Avoid Interruptions

advice: Rehearse by pretending to explain each idea to a real person who needs it, instead of repeating the words by rote. Material learned for its meaning holds up better than memorized wording.
quote: students who studied material by imagining conveying its meaning to somebody else who needed the information
drill: Picture one specific listener, such as a younger sibling or a new teammate, and explain each section to them out loud without looking at your notes.

source.author: Eric Wargo
source.title: 'To be or, or … um … line!'

advice: Like actors, map your speech as a chain of intentions, noting what each section is trying to do and why it leads to the next one. When the exact words slip, the next intention is still there to pull you forward.
quote: To get inside the character, an actor will break a script down into a series of logically connected "beats" or intentions.
drill: Write one verb phrase per section in the margin ("warn them", "prove it", "reassure"). Then rehearse from those phrases alone.

source.author: Eric Wargo
source.title: 'To be or, or … um … line!'

advice: Use the method of loci (memory palace). Mentally place each main point at a spot along a route you know well, like your walk to school. While speaking, walk the route in your head to find the next point instead of stalling.
quote: To remember a piece of information, you "drop" it along the path and later retrace your steps and "pick it up."
drill: Choose five landmarks on a familiar route and attach one vivid image per main point. Walk the route in your head and say each point aloud at its landmark.

source.author: Yasemin Saplakoglu
source.title: Sherlock Holmes' famous memory trick really works

advice: Rehearse under some pressure, not only in a quiet room. Practicing with a moderate amount of stress makes the real high-stakes moment feel more familiar, so your mind is less likely to lock up.
quote: practicing under stress, even a moderate amount, helps a person feel comfortable later.
drill: Run your speech in front of two or three people, or on a timed video call, at least twice before the real event.

source.author: William Harms
source.title: Brain key to 'choking' under pressure

advice: Once a speech is well practiced, don't micromanage each word while you deliver it. Choking research shows that over-monitoring well-learned skills disrupts them, so put your attention on the message and the listener.
quote: Thinking too much about each specific part of the task can throw off well-practiced techniques.

source.author: William Harms
source.title: Brain key to 'choking' under pressure

advice: Shortly before a high-pressure performance, spend about 10 minutes writing specifically about what you're worried will go wrong. In the study, this freed up the working memory that worry was using, and anxious students performed better.
quote: Writing about your worries for 10 minutes before an upcoming exam leveled the playing field
drill: Ten minutes before your round, write nonstop about your specific fears for this speech, such as blanking or a hard question. Then close the notebook.

source.author: William Harms
source.title: Writing about worries eases anxiety and improves test performance

advice: Don't tell yourself to calm down. Relabel the jitters as excitement by saying "I am excited" out loud before you speak. In the study, this turned attention toward what could go well, and judges rated those speakers higher.
quote: independent judges found that excited people seemed more persuasive, competent, persistent, and confident.

source.author: Erin O'Donnell
source.title: Get excited to perform well

advice: If the exact wording vanishes, say the point in whatever plain words come to you and keep moving. Knowing what each part is trying to say is your safety net for when the scripted line is gone.
quote: If you know the point your character is trying to get across, you can always say something that keeps the play moving.
drill: Take a paragraph you know well and deliver it three times, using completely different words each time but the same point.

source.author: Lindsay Price
source.title: Advice to an Actor Who Forgets Their Lines

advice: When your mind goes blank, check whether you're holding your breath, which is common while you wait for the words to come. Breathe out fully, because the next line often comes back once you exhale.
quote: Actors will often hold their breath waiting for the line to come.

source.author: Lindsay Price
source.title: Advice to an Actor Who Forgets Their Lines

advice: Don't split rehearsal time evenly. Put at least half of it into the transitions and passages where you usually stall, since those are the spots most likely to fail under pressure.
quote: Spend at least 50 percent of your rehearsal time on the most difficult parts.
drill: Record one full run and mark every pause longer than two seconds. Next session, drill only those marked spots until they run smoothly three times in a row.

source.author: Rebecca Strassberg
source.title: How Do Actors Memorize Lines? Here's How 9 Professionals Do It

advice: While you rehearse, walk around the room and deliver each idea at a different physical spot, picturing it as vividly as you can. Tying each thought to a place gives you a cue for what comes next.
quote: Walk around your room and place each thought in a different spot as you do.

source.author: Rebecca Strassberg
source.title: How Do Actors Memorize Lines? Here's How 9 Professionals Do It

advice: In extemp prep, run through elements of your speech in isolation rather than the whole speech. Say each point tag and its sources out loud, and make sure your question and answer are memorized.
quote: The way to avoid these problems is to run through elements of your speech in isolation.
drill: In the last five minutes of prep, say your question, answer and each point tag with its source aloud three times, without notes.

source.title: Strategy: Maximizing Prep Time

advice: Train for no-lag speaking with a partner. One person talks, and the moment they stop, the other picks up the thread immediately, which builds the habit of always having a next sentence ready.
quote: One person starts by talking, and any time they stop, the other has to pick up the conversation without any lag.
drill: Five-minute rounds with a partner on a random topic. Count every handoff where the gap felt longer than a beat, and try to beat that count next round.

source.title: Impromptu Starter Kit

advice: Practice starting to speak immediately on a prompt you haven't planned, and work your way toward a thesis as you talk. This trains you out of freezing while you wait for a perfect opening.
quote: Have someone give you a word, and immediately start talking about the word until you come around to a thesis.
drill: Have a partner give you random words. Start talking within one second and stop once you have said a clear thesis sentence.

source.title: Impromptu Starter Kit

advice: Build and practice a small set of go-to transition phrases you can use in any speech. That way you aren't inventing connecting language under pressure, which is where speakers often stall between points.
quote: Practice with this language so that you aren't struggling to come up with something fresh in every speech.
drill: Write five transition templates (for example, "That leads to the bigger question of...") and use each one in a practice speech this week.

source.title: Middle School Competition Events – At A Glance: Extemporaneous Speaking

advice: In an impromptu, you don't have to start talking right away. It's fine to take a short, silent moment to think and choose your point before you begin.
quote: Fortunately, you don't have to start talking right away. It's OK to pause and think for 10 to 15 seconds.

source.author: Bill Brown
source.credentials: DTM; speech delivery coach, Gillette, Wyoming
source.title: Let's Talk Table Topics

advice: If a question stumps you, don't wait in silence for a full answer. Pick one important word from the question and build on it, or argue the opposite side, so you have something to say right away.
quote: You also can pick one significant word from the question and expound on that.
drill: Have a partner read odd questions aloud. For each, name the one word you'll build on within three seconds, then talk for 60 seconds.

source.author: Peggy Beach
source.credentials: DTM; freelance writer and communications instructor
source.title: Spontaneous Speaking

advice: For impromptu answers, open by stating your opinion on the topic. It gives you a first sentence you can say right away instead of stalling at the start.

source.author: Greg Lewis
source.title: The Two Sides of Table Topics

advice: Before you speak, prepare one "back-pocket" question related to your topic that you can ask the audience. If you go blank, asking it buys you time to collect your thoughts and avoids dead air.
quote: In advance of speaking, always have what I call a back-pocket question, a question you can pull out to ask your audience

source.author: Matt Abrahams
source.credentials: Lecturer, Stanford Graduate School of Business; host of Think Fast, Talk Smart
source.title: High-Stakes Communication: How to Manage Anxiety Speaking in Front of Others

advice: Worrying about going blank makes it more likely, so break the cycle. Have your recovery moves ready ahead of time, and remind yourself that a total blank is actually rare.
quote: because we get so nervous about blanking out, it makes blanking out more likely.

source.author: Matt Abrahams
source.credentials: Lecturer, Stanford Graduate School of Business; host of Think Fast, Talk Smart
source.title: High-Stakes Communication: How to Manage Anxiety Speaking in Front of Others

advice: Freezing often comes from judging every idea before you say it. Aim for an ordinary, obvious answer instead of a brilliant one, and treat small stumbles lightly so they don't stop you.
quote: And that is shoot for average and fail cheerfully.

source.author: Matt Abrahams (with guests Adam Tobin and Dan Klein)
source.credentials: Lecturer, Stanford Graduate School of Business
source.title: Speaking Without a Net: How to Master Impromptu Communication

advice: Keep a simple three-step template ready for on-the-spot answers: what the thing is, why it matters, and what should happen next. Moving through fixed steps means you always know what comes next and don't stall.
drill: Answer three random questions a day using only What / So what / Now what, saying one or two sentences for each step.

source.author: Stanford Seed (interview with Matt Abrahams)
source.title: How to 'Think Faster and Talk Smarter': a Masterclass with Matt Abrahams

advice: When a word is on the tip of your tongue, think of words that share its opening syllable. In the research described, words sharing the first syllable helped retrieval while words sharing only the first sound did not, and silently reading the words worked as well as saying them aloud.
quote: These results suggest that a word's initial phonology is the key to its retrieval.

source.title: Tip-of-the-Tongue States Yield Language Insights

advice: In this research, processing a word's sounds (participants pronounced words sharing sounds with the target) strengthened the weak memory link behind tip-of-the-tongue blanks and improved recall in both young and older adults. Saying hard names and technical terms aloud as you rehearse applies the same idea.
quote: Processing the phonology of a TOT target strengthens this weak connection and improves memory recall with both young and old adults.
drill: List every proper name and technical term in your speech and say each one aloud five times the day before and the morning of your talk.

source.title: New Research Explains 'Tip Of The Tongue' Experiences

advice: Keep dramatic pauses short, around two seconds, and put them at clear moments like your opening or right before a key line. Silences of about three seconds or more start to feel awkward, and listeners may think you've forgotten what comes next.
quote: However, if the silences are too long, the audience tend to believe that the speaker forgot what was supposed to be said.
drill: Record yourself doing one deliberate pause before your thesis. Measure it in an audio editor and aim for about 2 seconds, not 3 or more.

source.author: Carlos Concepcion
source.title: Creating Drama by [Insert Pause here] Creating Silence

advice: When the audience laughs or reacts, wait instead of talking over it. A long pause here is planned, not lost, so start again only as the laughter begins to fade.
quote: Respect the laugh zone by continuing to pause until the laughter starts to trail off.

source.author: Randy Lane
source.credentials: Owner, Randy Lane Company (radio and TV personality coach)
source.title: Dead Air: Friend Or Foe

advice: Broadcasters treat about three seconds of unplanned silence as the limit before someone has to speak. Use that as a rough ceiling for unplanned gaps, and if you reach it, say something, even a simple bridge sentence.
quote: Up to three seconds of silence is the most that should pass before the newsreader cuts in.

source.author: Peter Stewart
source.title: 0651 – When To Expect Verbal Trips and Slips
source.publisher: Get A Better Broadcast, Podcast and Voice-Over Voice (podcast)

advice: Speech anxiety shows up in your pauses. In an impromptu task, anxious speakers paused more often and for longer than calm speakers, so tracking how often and how long you pause is a measurable way to see whether your nerves are improving.
quote: paused more often and for a longer duration than the nonanxious group.
drill: Record a 2-minute impromptu speech each week. Count pauses over 2 seconds and add up their total length, then track both numbers over time.

source.author: Michael R. Lewin, Daniel W. McNeil, Jonathan M. Lipson
source.title: Enduring without avoiding: Pauses and verbal dysfluencies in public speaking fear
source.publisher: Journal of Psychopathology and Behavioral Assessment

advice: Rehearse by recalling your speech from memory, not by rereading the script. In the study, repeated recall greatly improved later memory, while extra rereading added nothing.
quote: Repeated studying after learning had no effect on delayed recall, but repeated testing produced a large positive effect.
drill: Close your notes and say your outline from memory. Check it against your notes, fix the gaps and repeat, spreading these recall rounds across several days.

source.author: Jeffrey D. Karpicke, Henry L. Roediger III
source.title: The Critical Importance of Retrieval for Learning

advice: If you're speaking somewhere other than where you practiced and your memory goes, picture the room where you rehearsed. Mentally bringing back the practice setting reduces the memory loss that a new environment can cause.
quote: as well as mental reinstatement of appropriate context cues at test, all reduce the effect of environmental manipulations.

source.author: Steven M. Smith, Edward Vela
source.title: Environmental context-dependent memory: A review and meta-analysis

advice: In some practice runs, picture an audience in front of you and perform as if it were the real thing. Casual run-throughs train a relaxed kind of attention that can fail you under real pressure.
quote: They should be advised to spend some of their time practicing as if they were performing

source.author: Nancy Bricard, Sherwyn M. Woods
source.title: Memory Problems for Musical Performers

advice: Move from script to keywords in stages. Start with a full-sentence outline, then cut it to partial sentences, then to just keywords and key phrases, and deliver the speech aloud at each stage before cutting further.
quote: Utilize partial memorization techniques (practice delivering the speech at each step)
drill: Day 1: deliver from the full-sentence outline. Day 2: deliver from partial sentences. Day 3: deliver from keywords only.

source.title: Tips for using limited speech notes
source.publisher: Public Speaking Center, University of Wisconsin–La Crosse

advice: Sketch your speech as a mind map, with the main topic in the center and branches for each point. If you lose your place, picturing how the branches connect helps you find the next point.
quote: Start with the main topic in the center and branch out to subtopics and supporting points.
drill: Draw the mind map from memory on a blank page before each rehearsal, then compare it with the original.

source.author: Robin Kermode
source.title: What To Do When You Go Blank

advice: A memory palace takes weeks of steady practice, not one evening. In this study, beginners trained 30 minutes a day for six weeks, and four months later they recalled about 50 words, compared with about 30 for a working-memory training group and about 27 for a no-training group. So start building your routes well before the season.
quote: participants completed 30 min of training each day for 40 days at home

source.author: I. C. Wagner, B. N. Konrad, P. Schuster, S. Weisig, D. Repantis, K. Ohla, S. Kühn, G. Fernández, A. Steiger, C. Lamm, M. Czisch, M. Dresler
source.title: Durable memories and efficient neural coding through mnemonic training using the method of loci

advice: Train the memory palace in small steps on a few fixed routes. Trainees in this study built four routes, used them to memorise random word lists, and got five more words each time they recalled a full list, and the gains were still there four months later.
quote: the memory training group showed significantly increased free recall performance after 4 months
drill: Pick one route with 10 stops. Each day, place a random word list along it and recall it aloud. When you get every word right, add five more stops or words. Then use the same route for your speech's main points.

source.author: I. C. Wagner, B. N. Konrad, P. Schuster, S. Weisig, D. Repantis, K. Ohla, S. Kühn, G. Fernández, A. Steiger, C. Lamm, M. Czisch, M. Dresler
source.title: Durable memories and efficient neural coding through mnemonic training using the method of loci

advice: Anxiety and excitement are both high-arousal states, so turning nerves into excitement is easier than forcing yourself to calm down. Say "I'm excited" out loud even if you don't believe it yet. Brooks reports that doing so raises genuine excitement, and speakers who did it gave longer speeches.
quote: Even if they don't believe it at first, saying 'I'm excited' out loud increases authentic feelings of excitement.

source.author: American Psychological Association (reporting research by Alison Wood Brooks)
source.title: Getting excited helps with performance anxiety more than trying to calm down, study finds

advice: When the next point vanishes, step back and briefly sum up what you've already covered. The recap gives you a moment to remember the missing point, and you can then present it as the point you've been building toward.
quote: So just to step back for a moment, I've already covered how X and Y are relevant
drill: In practice, have a partner call "blank!" at random moments. Each time, give a one-sentence recap of the points so far before continuing.

source.author: Matt Abrahams
source.title: Matt Abrahams: Presentations and the Art of the Graceful Recovery

advice: When you lose your place, don't strain to remember what comes next. Turn your attention to what you just said, because reorienting from your last point is more likely to get you moving again smoothly.
quote: you are more likely to continue smoothly if you reorient yourself by looking to what you said previously.

source.author: Matt Abrahams
source.title: Matt Abrahams: Presentations and the Art of the Graceful Recovery

advice: Being put on the spot can trigger fight-or-flight and make your brain feel foggy. Handle it on two fronts: slow, deep breathing for the physical symptoms, and keeping your attention on the present moment instead of on how things might turn out.
quote: Your fight or flight response kicks in—your heart pounds, your limbs shake, and your brain gets foggy.

source.author: Matt Abrahams
source.title: Think Faster, Talk Smarter: How to Speak Successfully When You're Put on the Spot

advice: Just before you go on, run through the first minute of your talk in your head. Knowing exactly how you'll open gives you confidence at the start.
quote: Go through the first minute of your talk in your mind.

source.title: Public Speaking: Tips for Day of Presentation

advice: For your first extemporaneous speeches, prepare far more material than you can use and don't worry about polish. If fear scrambles your thoughts, just keep talking, even restating the same idea in different words, until you feel in control again.
quote: keep on talking until self-possession and the mastery of every faculty have been fully restored.

source.author: William Pittenger
source.title: Extempore Speech: How to Acquire and Practice It
source.publisher: National School of Elocution and Oratory (Project Gutenberg edition)

advice: Being watched and judged can itself cause word-finding blocks. In this experiment, people who believed they were being evaluated reported more tip-of-the-tongue moments than people who didn't. So expect more blocks in front of judges than in solo practice, and do some rehearsals with someone watching.
quote: evaluative observation by a third party can be disruptive to word retrieval

source.author: Lori E. James, Christopher J. Schmank, Nichol Castro, Tony W. Buchanan
source.title: Tip of the Tongue States Increase Under Evaluative Observation

advice: Hesitations that fall between sentences or clauses are mostly about working out what to say next (conceptualizing), while those inside a clause or phrase are more about finding the words. So if your recordings show long gaps between sentences, work on knowing your next idea through a clearer structure and outline.
quote: disfluencies at syntactic boundaries are mostly related to conceptualizing
drill: Transcribe a recording and mark each pause over one second that falls between sentences. For each one, check whether you knew what your next point was; if not, tighten the outline at that spot.

source.author: Nivja H. De Jong
source.title: Fluency in Second Language Testing: Insights From Different Disciplines

advice: Use the AGD transition game to train yourself never to stall. A partner calls out unrelated topics one after another, and you have to link each one smoothly into your talk. You keep going until you stumble or pause too long, and you win by lasting three minutes.
quote: The speaker has to effectively link them together until they either stumble or pause for too long.
drill: A partner rattles off unrelated topics one after another; connect each to what you were saying without stopping. Goal: 3 minutes with no stumble or long pause.

source.author: Ananth Veluvali
source.title: Extemp Drill List

advice: Pauses between sentences are normal and fairly long. In work reported by these researchers, Goldman-Eisler found that 77.9% of sentences in spontaneous speech were separated by pauses longer than half a second. A pause of that size at a sentence end is ordinary, so don't try to squeeze it out.
quote: 77.9% of sentences in spontaneous speech are divided from each other by pauses longer than 500 msec

source.author: Geoffrey W. Beattie, B. L. Butterworth
source.credentials: University of Sheffield; University of Cambridge
source.title: Contextual Probability and Word Frequency as Determinants of Pauses and Errors in Spontaneous Speech

advice: Just suppressing silent pauses can backfire. When speakers were penalised for pausing, they paused less often but produced more filled hesitations, especially repetitions. The authors suggest that the demands of the task set how much you hesitate overall, so make the task easier through preparation instead of forcing yourself not to stop.
quote: a significant increase in the amount of filled hesitation, particularly in repetition, resulted

source.author: Geoffrey W. Beattie, R. J. Bradbury
source.title: An experimental investigation of the modifiability of the temporal structure of spontaneous speech

advice: Pause lengths tend to fall into three sizes: brief (under 0.2 s), medium (0.2-1 s), and long (over 1 s). In read and spontaneous speech in five languages, long pauses showed up only in the spontaneous speech. When you read a text aloud, a silence of more than a second falls outside what this study observed, so use one only on purpose.
quote: medium (200-1000 ms) and long (> 1000 ms) pauses, the latter occurring only in spontaneous speech.

source.author: Estelle Campione, Jean Véronis
source.title: A large-scale multilingual study of silent pause duration

advice: Pause briefly wherever a comma would go in writing, between clauses and between items in a list.
drill: Rewrite your script with one short clause per line and pause at the end of each line while rehearsing.

source.author: Andrew Dlugan
source.title: Speech Pauses: 12 Techniques to Speak Volumes with Your Silence

advice: Pause for a medium beat at the end of each sentence. Don't chain sentences together with 'and', because the audience loses the break.

source.author: Andrew Dlugan
source.title: Speech Pauses: 12 Techniques to Speak Volumes with Your Silence

advice: Take a longer pause when you move to a new point or start or finish a story, the way a paragraph break works in writing.

source.author: Andrew Dlugan
source.title: Speech Pauses: 12 Techniques to Speak Volumes with Your Silence

advice: To stress a key word, pause just before it and just after it. The first pause says 'listen' and the second says 'remember this'.

source.author: Andrew Dlugan
source.title: Speech Pauses: 12 Techniques to Speak Volumes with Your Silence

advice: After a rhetorical question, stay quiet long enough for people to think of an answer. Moving straight on frustrates them.

source.author: Andrew Dlugan
source.title: Speech Pauses: 12 Techniques to Speak Volumes with Your Silence

advice: Reading aloud tends to produce only short pauses. When you read from a script, make your pauses longer on purpose so it sounds natural.

source.author: Andrew Dlugan
source.title: Speech Pauses: 12 Techniques to Speak Volumes with Your Silence

advice: Keep your pause lengths consistent: comma pauses shorter than sentence pauses, and sentence pauses shorter than the pauses between points.

source.author: Andrew Dlugan
source.title: Speech Pauses: 12 Techniques to Speak Volumes with Your Silence

advice: When you mean to take a long pause, make it longer than feels comfortable.
quote: For long pauses, pause longer than you think is necessary, perhaps longer than is comfortable for you.

source.author: Andrew Dlugan
source.title: Speech Pauses: 12 Techniques to Speak Volumes with Your Silence

advice: Before your first word, take a deliberate silent beat and run your opening sentence through your head. It centers you and stops a stumbling start.
drill: Before each practice run, wait silently and mentally say your full first sentence before speaking.

source.author: Andrew Dlugan
source.title: Speech Pauses: 12 Techniques to Speak Volumes with Your Silence

advice: Ask for feedback on your pauses. Did they feel natural, were any awkward, was the overall pace right? Watching yourself on video helps too.
drill: Watch a recording and mark each pause that felt awkward or too long.

source.author: Andrew Dlugan
source.title: Speech Pauses: 12 Techniques to Speak Volumes with Your Silence

advice: Try a 'micro-pause' of a second or less right before your key word. It pulls drifting listeners back without sounding dramatic.
quote: Place the pause right before the key word.

source.title: Silence Is Golden

advice: Pausing lets your brain get ahead of your mouth, so you choose words first instead of rambling and correcting yourself.
quote: pausing allows your mind to script your mouth.
drill: Answer 'What do you like about your job?' aloud, then answer 'What do you dislike?' taking all the pauses you need. Compare the two answers.

source.author: Joel Schwartzberg
source.title: 9 Surprising Ways You Can Benefit From a Pause

advice: Speakers think they paused 'too much'. Audiences usually remember only one or two pauses, because silence is hard to notice.

source.author: Joel Schwartzberg
source.title: 9 Surprising Ways You Can Benefit From a Pause

advice: Use pauses to breathe quietly through your nose with your mouth closed, so the breath doesn't make a sound.
quote: Taking breaths while speaking is a secret between you and your body.

source.author: Joel Schwartzberg
source.title: 9 Surprising Ways You Can Benefit From a Pause

advice: Listeners need time to take in your point. Pause after important ideas instead of rushing into the next sentence.

source.author: Joel Schwartzberg
source.title: 9 Surprising Ways You Can Benefit From a Pause

advice: Pauses in conversation are mostly short (about 0.2 seconds) to medium (about 0.6 seconds). Skilled speakers deliberately hold some pauses for two to three seconds for effect.

source.title: Effective Pauses (SAGE Flex for Public Speaking)

advice: Pausing too often can make you sound unprepared. Save pauses for emphasis and for holding attention.

source.title: Verbal Delivery (Chapter 8)

advice: A pause that feels endless to you is usually short to the audience. Keep that in mind and let the silence sit.
quote: what seems like a long pause to me is probably a short pause to those in the audience.

source.title: Cutting Out Filler Words

advice: Pauses help when they fall at idea boundaries, but a pause in the middle of a sentence breaks the thought and sounds like hesitation. Finish the sentence first, then pause.
quote: Be careful, though, to avoid pauses at unusual times—in the middle of sentences, for example.
drill: Read a paragraph aloud and pause only at periods and between ideas. Then deliver it from memory and check the recording for any pause that falls inside a clause.

source.title: Public Speaking Presentations: Delivery

advice: Pauses inside sentences take several practice repetitions to disappear, longer than pauses at sentence ends. If you still hesitate in the middle of a sentence on the second run-through, keep repeating; in one study the improvement continued until about the fourth performance.
quote: midclause pauses decreased up to the fourth

source.author: Craig Lambert, Judit Kormos, Danny Minn
source.credentials: Curtin University; Lancaster University; Kitakyushu University
source.title: Task Repetition and Second Language Speech Processing
source.publisher: Studies in Second Language Acquisition (Cambridge University Press)

advice: Even one immediate repeat of a speech helps. In the second performance, speakers in one study talked faster and tended to make fewer pauses in the middle of clauses.
quote: task repetition led to a decrease in the number of pauses in the middle of a clause
drill: Immediately after a practice speech, give it again once and compare mid-sentence pauses between the two recordings.

source.author: Gavin Bui, Mohammad Javad Ahmadian, Ann-Marie Hunter
source.title: Spacing effects on repeated L2 task performance

advice: Breathe at your natural pauses between phrases, not in the middle of a thought. Gasping mid-sentence for air is a sign of an inexperienced speaker, so plan where your breaths go.
quote: pauses are normal places to breathe; breathless gasps often reflect inexperienced speakers.
drill: Mark breath points (/) in your script at phrase boundaries and practice breathing only at those marks.

source.author: Wayne C. Mannebach
source.credentials: Former director of debate and forensics, Ripon College; English teacher, St. Mary Central High School (Neenah, WI)
source.title: Facts Alone Are Not Enough: A Plea for Coordinated Voice and Message
source.publisher: Rostrum (National Forensic League), Rostrum Library archive at University of Vermont

advice: Be conscious of your pause patterns. Decide in advance where pauses belong and mark them in your speaker notes so they become a deliberate choice instead of hesitation.
quote: Write pause patterns into you speaker notes.
drill: Add a visible pause mark (for example ||) at transitions and after key lines in your notes, then practice following the marks exactly.

source.author: A. Susan Owen
source.title: Delivery Tips
source.publisher: Center for Speech and Effective Advocacy, University of Puget Sound

advice: When you listen to a recording of yourself, you may hear speech that comes out in choppy bursts with gaps between them. Smooth phrasing comes from lots of out-loud repetition, including using spare moments such as the commute or the shower to talk your material through.
drill: Each day, talk through one speech out loud during a routine activity, then record a full run and listen for choppy phrasing.

source.author: Martha B. Ebeling
source.credentials: Extemp coach, Dayton Oakwood High School (OH); coached 23 national qualifiers in extemp
source.title: Ten Commandments for Effective Extemporaneous Delivery
source.publisher: Rostrum (National Forensic League), Rostrum Library archive at University of Vermont

advice: Listeners judge how fluent you sound most closely by how often you stop silently inside a clause. Pauses in the middle of a clause tend to signal that you are still searching for words, so save your pauses for the ends of clauses.
quote: silent pause rate within a clause demonstrated the strongest correlation with L2 fluency ratings
drill: Record a one-minute impromptu answer, transcribe it, and mark every silent pause as either inside a clause or between clauses. Count only the inside-clause pauses, then redo the answer and try to move them to the clause breaks.

source.author: Jimin Kahng
source.title: The Effect of Pause Location on Perceived Fluency
source.publisher: Applied Psycholinguistics (Cambridge University Press); UNI ScholarWorks record

advice: Native speakers are not exempt. When researchers edited recordings so that the same pauses landed in different places, fluency ratings of both native and non-native speech changed, so where you pause matters, not just how much you pause.
quote: Findings suggest a significant role of pause location in perceived fluency.

source.author: Jimin Kahng
source.title: The Effect of Pause Location on Perceived Fluency

advice: If you need a pause, put it between clauses. In a listening experiment, sentences with a silence inside a clause were rated less fluent than the same sentences with the silence moved to a clause boundary.
quote: sentences with pauses within clauses were rated as less fluent than sentences with pauses between clauses
drill: Read one sentence twice: once pausing after the subject's first word ("The new / budget plan cuts funding"), once pausing at the clause break ("The new budget plan cuts funding, / and the board approved it"). Record both and compare how they sound.

source.author: Z. Houghton, M. Kato, M. Baese-Berk, C. Vaughn
source.title: Task-dependent consequences of disfluency in perception of native and non-native speech

advice: When untrained listeners rate fluency, pausing and speed explain most of their judgment and self-corrections explain very little. If you have limited practice time, fixing where and how long you pause will pay off more than worrying about an occasional restart.
quote: pause and speed measures best predicted the subjective fluency ratings

source.author: Hans Rutger Bosker, Anne-France Pinget, Hugo Quené, Ted Sanders, Nivja H. de Jong
source.title: What makes speech sound fluent? The contributions of pauses, speed and repairs
source.publisher: Language Testing (SAGE); Utrecht University research portal

advice: Learners stand out from native speakers mainly because they pause in the middle of clauses. Ready-made multi-word phrases had very few pauses inside them, so practising your stock phrases until they come out as one unit may help cut down on mid-sentence gaps.
quote: pause frequently in the middle of clauses rather than at the end
drill: List eight phrases you use a lot in speeches (for example "on the other hand," "the main reason is," "what this means for us"). Say each one ten times as a single, unbroken unit, then use three of them in a one-minute impromptu talk.

source.author: Parvaneh Tavakoli
source.title: Pausing patterns: differences between L2 learners and native speakers

advice: Different pause problems go with different skill levels. Frequent pauses at the ends of clauses separated low-rated speakers from mid-rated ones, while frequent mid-clause pauses separated mid-rated speakers from top ones. Once your sentence-to-sentence planning is smooth, the next step is getting rid of stops inside clauses.
quote: the number of mid-clause pauses differentiated mid and high-level performance

source.author: Kazuya Saito, Meltem Ilkan, Viktoria Magne, Mai Tran, Shungo Suzuki
source.title: Acoustic characteristics and learner profiles of low, mid and high-level second language fluency

advice: How often you pause mid-clause stays fairly steady from one speaking task to another, while how long those pauses last varies more. In unrehearsed interview-style answers, the number of mid-clause pauses was the measure that reliably told native from non-native speech, so count those pauses in your Q&A practice as well as in prepared speeches.
drill: Have a partner ask you five unseen questions. Record your answers and count the pauses that fall inside a clause, then compare that count with one from a rehearsed speech of the same length.

source.author: Amanda Huensch
source.title: Effects of speaking task and proficiency on the midclause pausing characteristics of L1 and L2 speech from the same speakers
source.publisher: Studies in Second Language Acquisition (Cambridge University Press)

advice: Every speaker is more likely to stop just before a rarer word. If your speech contains technical terms, names, or uncommon words, rehearse those exact words in context so that searching for them doesn't open a gap in the middle of a sentence.
quote: both L1 and L2 speakers are more likely to pause before lower frequency words as compared to higher frequency words
drill: Underline the five least common words in your speech. Practise each one inside the full phrase that leads into it (for example "the results of the meta-analysis") until there is no hitch before the word.

source.author: Nivja H. de Jong
source.title: Predicting pauses in L1 and L2 speech: the effects of utterance boundaries and word frequency
source.publisher: International Review of Applied Linguistics in Language Teaching (De Gruyter)

advice: How often you stop mid-clause in a second language depended mostly on how quickly you can retrieve words and build sentences in that language. How long your pauses last tended to mirror your first-language habits. Work on mid-clause stops through vocabulary and phrase practice, and don't expect your typical pause length to change much.

source.author: Jimin Kahng
source.title: Explaining second language utterance fluency: Contribution of cognitive fluency and first language utterance fluency

advice: In a study of second-language Finnish, the pauses that hurt ratings most were silences or fillers inside a short phrase and pauses right after a word you cut off halfway. A pause between two phrases, even inside a longer clause, did little harm, so keep each small phrase intact.
quote: silent and filled pauses within phrases and pauses after incomplete words significantly reduce the fluency

source.author: Heini Kallio, Mikko Kuronen, Liisa Koivusalo
source.title: The role of pause location in perceived fluency and proficiency in L2 Finnish
source.publisher: ISAPh 2022: Proceedings of the 4th International Symposium on Applied Phonetics

advice: Some pause spots break grammar: between "the" and its noun, or between a helping verb and the main verb ("will / announce"). In storytelling recordings, children paused in these places far more often than adults did. Adult pauses also grew longer around longer phrases, so keep small word pairs welded together and save pauses for the joints between phrases.
drill: Read a paragraph aloud and have a partner raise a hand whenever you pause right after "a/the/my" or right after "is/will/has/can." Reread until no hands go up.

source.author: Melissa A. Redford
source.title: A Comparative Analysis of Pausing in Child and Adult Storytelling

advice: Speakers plan well ahead: in this study, the length of the next phrase, and even the phrase after it, affected how long speakers paused. A pause before a long stretch of speech is part of normal planning, so you don't need to treat it as a fluency problem.
quote: speakers have a large lookahead in speech production, mediated by prosodic structure

source.author: Jelena Krivokapić
source.title: Speech Planning and Prosodic Phrase Length

advice: Pause lengths tend to follow the grammatical structure of a sentence, and speakers also tend to place pauses so the pieces on either side are of similar length. When a sentence needs a breath, take it at a grammatical joint near the middle rather than near one end.
quote: The linguistic surface structure of a sentence is a good predictor of the pause durations.

source.author: Harlan Lane, François Grosjean, Lysianne Grosjean
source.title: The Patterns of Silence: Performance Structures in Sentence Productions
source.publisher: Proceedings of the International Congress of Phonetic Sciences (ICPhS 1979)

advice: At slow and normal reading speeds, people time their breaths to fall in planned pauses at grammatical breaks. At fast speeds, the need for air takes over and decides where the pauses go. Rushing makes you gasp in the middle of phrases, so slow down enough to keep your breaths at the boundaries.

source.author: François Grosjean
source.title: Breathing, Pausing and Reading

advice: In read speech, nearly all breaths fall at grammatical boundaries. In spontaneous speech, a sizeable share land in the middle of a phrase because thinking up words on the spot is harder. When you speak without a script, rehearse your key sentences so your breaths stay at the phrase breaks.

source.author: Marcin Włodarczak, Mattias Heldner
source.title: Respiratory Constraints in Verbal and Non-verbal Communication

advice: Punctuation is a writing convention, not a map of where to pause. One sentence can hold several separate messages, so work out where each message starts and ends and mark those points as your pause spots.
quote: Your script will have punctuation for sure, but of course, that’s an ‘artificial articulatory construct’
drill: Choose a long sentence from your script and draw a slash (/) wherever one message ends and the next begins, regardless of commas. Read it with pauses only at your slashes.

source.author: Peter Stewart
source.credentials: Voice coach who has trained broadcasters for BBC Radio 1, BBC Radio 3 and Capital FM
source.title: 0186 – Marking Up For Phrases
source.publisher: Get A Better Broadcast, Podcast and Voice-Over Voice (podcast)

advice: If you run out of air before a sentence ends, you either took too small a breath, are trying to say too much on one breath, or are letting air leak out. The last words then come out weak or strained. Shorten the sentence or plan a breath at a phrase break, and treat the end of each sentence as part of the message.
quote: if your message is important, so are the end of your sentences.

source.author: Peter Stewart
source.title: 835 – Why Do I Run Out Of Breath?
source.publisher: Get A Better Broadcast, Podcast and Voice-Over Voice (podcast)

advice: Before you read a script aloud, mark your breaths and pauses with slashes, but use them sparingly. Add one only where a long sentence needs a breath, where a key idea needs separating, or where a beat before or after something important helps. Leave lines that already flow unmarked.
quote: we sometimes breathe in unnatural places or simply run out of air.
drill: Mark a script in pencil using the article's model: "Rain is likely through the weekend / with heavier storms expected Sunday night." Then read it aloud and erase any slash that made the line sound stiff.

source.title: Marking scripts can help you sound more natural on the radio

advice: Breath points don't have to fall only at commas or sentence ends; they can also fall at the key (operative) words of a sentence. Keep your lips slightly apart between phrases, because closing your mouth and reopening it makes a small popping noise.
quote: Don't close your mouth between phrases or sentences.

source.author: Karen Schaefer
source.title: Voicing Your Script: Tips and Techniques
source.publisher: Society of Environmental Journalists (sej.org conference materials)

advice: Don't breathe after every sentence by habit. Mark breaths where long sentences need them, and add a brief pause just before a complex or technical term so listeners are ready to catch it.
quote: A pause is especially effective before a word that's complex or highly technical in nature.

source.author: Marilyn Pittman, Paul Grabowicz
source.credentials: Based on lectures by Pittman at the UC Berkeley Graduate School of Journalism
source.title: Standups and Voice-overs
source.publisher: Berkeley Advanced Media Institute, UC Berkeley

advice: When you prepare a text to read, put brackets around word groups that must be said as one term, such as titles, names, or technical phrases, so a line wrap doesn't trick you into pausing inside them. Use a single slash for a short pause and a double slash for a longer one.
drill: Print your script in at least 14-point type. In pencil, bracket every multi-word term and add / and // pause marks, then read it aloud and check that no bracketed term got split.

source.author: Bill Brown
source.credentials: DTM; speech delivery coach in Gillette, Wyoming
source.title: Reading a Prepared Text

advice: An NPR correspondent's script habits: keep each line of script to just one line, double space between lines, and type an ellipsis wherever you need a reminder to stop and breathe, so the layout itself shows you where to pause.
quote: Use elipses…to remind yourself to stop and breathe.

source.author: NewsLab (advice from NPR correspondent Carrie Johnson)
source.title: Finding your voice

advice: In slower speech, a pause is the clearest signal that one thought group has ended. Practise grouping with something simple, like phone numbers, where pausing in the wrong place makes the listener write down the wrong number.
quote: In slow speech, the pause is the most obvious indicator that a thought group has ended.
drill: With a partner, read a 10-digit phone number grouped as 3-3-4 with a short pause between groups while your partner writes it down. Then read it with the pauses in the wrong places and see whether your partner gets confused.

source.author: Judy B. Gilbert
source.title: Teaching Pronunciation Using the Prosody Pyramid

advice: Learn grouping by studying skilled speakers: listen to a short talk with its transcript and mark a slash wherever each thought group ends. There is usually more than one acceptable split. What matters is that you group words on purpose to help the listener.
quote: The important thing is not where speakers divide the groups
drill: Play 60 seconds of a lecture or speech, mark the thought-group endings on the transcript with /, then read the transcript aloud pausing only at your marks.

source.author: Judy B. Gilbert
source.title: Teaching Pronunciation Using the Prosody Pyramid

advice: Pausing too often chops speech into groups that don't make sense, which makes listeners work harder and judge the speaker more harshly. The opposite mistake, barely pausing at all, often comes from overcorrecting, and it hides how your ideas connect.
quote: overly-frequent pausing can quickly become a serious problem because it breaks apart speech into illogical groups.

source.author: Timothy Kochem, Monica Ghosh, Lily Compton, Elena Cotos
source.title: Oral Communication for Non-Native Speakers of English – Thought Groups: Teacher's Corner

advice: Some word combinations usually belong in one group: an article with its adjective and noun ("the large molecule"), a preposition with its noun phrase ("in the graph"), and a verb with its object ("use a dictionary"). A fast speaker may pause only once in an utterance, while a slow speaker could pause up to four times.
quote: there is no one rule-governed method for dividing an utterance into thought groups.
drill: Pick a one-minute TED Talk clip and shadow it, matching only the speaker's pauses. Then record yourself and check that you never split a preposition from its noun or a verb from its object.

source.author: Agata Guskaroska, Erik Goodale, Timothy Kochem, Monica Ghosh, Lily Compton, Elena Cotos
source.title: Oral Communication for Non-Native Speakers of English (2nd ed.), Chapter 4: Thought Groups

advice: If you need thinking time, break your sentences into shorter thought groups. Each pause between groups gives you a moment to plan the next phrase at a spot where it sounds natural, which keeps you from stalling in the middle of one.
quote: it is better to use shorter thought groups because the pause can help you plan your next phrase
drill: Write four sentences about famous landmarks, split each into two or three thought groups with slashes, then say them aloud, linking the words inside each group and pausing only at the slashes.

source.author: Linda Lane
source.title: Introduction to Thought Groups (from Focus on Pronunciation)

advice: Pause right after signpost words like "Firstly" so listeners can hear the structure, and pause at the end of one section before you start the next.
quote: Speech without pauses and speech chunks can overwhelm the listener with 'too much information'.
drill: Take a speech transcript (the handout uses Kofi Annan), mark short pauses with / and section-change pauses with //, then read it aloud following your marks.

source.author: MaryAnn McDonald
source.title: Pronunciation 3 - Handout

advice: A long subject can be its own thought group. In "The short little dog / in the corner / is eating my new shoes," the short pauses come only between whole groups, never inside "the short little dog."
quote: A short pause between groups of words is an important way to distinguish one thought group from another.

source.title: A Short Introduction to English Pronunciation – Thought Groups and Sentence Stress

advice: Good places to start a new group are just before a "who/which/that" clause and just before "but," "and," or "because" ("The woman / who works in marketing / is my friend"). Bad places are right after "the," "a," or "my," and between "to" and its verb.
quote: Don't pause after articles or possessive pronouns.
drill: Practise one pattern at a time: first add pauses only before "who/which" clauses in five sentences, then only before "but/because," then combine both.

source.author: Annemarie
source.title: How to Group Words and Pause for Natural-Sounding English

advice: Inside a thought group, link the words into one smooth line with no tiny gaps between them. Put your breaks between groups instead. Don't model yourself on speakers who almost never pause, because the pauses are what help listeners follow.
quote: Within a thought group, we want all words to be part of one smooth line.

source.author: Rachel's English
source.title: Linking and Thought Groups – Spoken English

advice: Rate your own phrasing on a four-step scale used for reading fluency. The steps go from word-by-word, to choppy two- or three-word bursts, to a mix of run-on stretches and mid-sentence breaths, and finally to smooth phrasing in clause and sentence units.
quote: Reads with a mixture of run-ons, mid-sentence pauses for breath, and some choppiness.
drill: Record yourself reading a 150-word passage you haven't seen, then score it 1-4 on the phrasing scale. Reread it twice and score it again.

source.title: Measures of Prosody/Expression (includes Zutell & Rasinski's Multidimensional Fluency Scale)

advice: The length of the chunks you speak in tracks how skilled you are. In a national study of oral reading, the most fluent readers read in larger, meaningful phrase groups, and higher fluency went with higher reading proficiency, while the least fluent read word by word.
quote: Reads primarily in larger, meaningful phrase groups.
drill: Count the words between pauses in a 30-second recording of yourself. If most of your chunks are two or three words long, rehearse the passage until most run four words or more.

source.author: Sheida White
source.title: Listening to Children Read Aloud: Oral Fluency (NAEPfacts, Vol. 1, No. 1)
source.publisher: National Center for Education Statistics, U.S. Department of Education

advice: Research reviewed in this study found that better readers paused only briefly at commas and sentence ends, while weaker readers' pauses were inappropriately long and broke up the flow of the sentence. Less skilled adult readers also made more pauses in places that didn't fit. Keep pauses at small boundaries short.

source.author: Mara Breen, Lianne Kaswer, Julie A. Van Dyke, Jelena Krivokapić, Nicole Landi
source.title: Imitated Prosodic Fluency Predicts Reading Comprehension Ability in Good and Poor High School Readers

advice: Fill up with a low, slow breath that expands your whole ribcage, then let the air out steadily all the way to the end of the sentence, so you don't run dry and have to grab air in the middle.
quote: Inhale low and slow (360-degree expansion of the ribcage), exhale smoothly and consistently through to each sentence end.

source.author: Jillian Mitchell
source.credentials: Vocal coach with 20+ years of experience; founder of Voxsana
source.title: The Ins and Outs of Dynamic Speaking

advice: In poetry, a line break is not an automatic pause. When a sentence runs on past the end of a line, carry the thought straight into the next line and let the punctuation and meaning decide where you stop.
quote: Consider line breaks when shaping your delivery, and do not assume every line break requires a pause.
drill: Find the run-on lines in your poem (lines with no punctuation at the end). Read the poem once pausing at every line end and once pausing only at punctuation and meaning breaks, then compare the recordings.

source.title: Tips on Reciting

advice: Recitation judges reward pauses that make the meaning clearer or let an important moment land. They mark down pauses that drag on so long the piece loses momentum, so a dramatic pause should be deliberate and not stretched.
quote: Avoid rushing through important ideas or using drawn out pauses or slowing down so much that the poem loses momentum.

source.title: Tips on Reciting

advice: In poetry interpretation, mark the phrases (groups of words that express one thought) instead of reading line by line. A dramatic pause can be held longer than feels safe, as long as your mind stays on the poem while you hold it.
quote: The pause is one of the most effective tools for the interpreter.

source.author: Ruby C. Krider
source.credentials: National Forensic League Hall of Fame member
source.title: Interpretation of Poetry
source.publisher: National Forensic League archive (hosted at uvm.edu)

advice: Poetry reciters differ on line endings. Some pause at the end of a line even when the sentence runs on into the next one, while others keep the sentence together and pause elsewhere, such as at a comma inside the line. Choose your approach on purpose and use it consistently, rather than letting line ends decide for you.
quote: longer pauses appeared after the end of a verse.

source.author: Plinio A. Barbosa
source.title: The Dance of Pauses in Poetry Declamation

advice: In binder events like Prose, finish your thought before you turn the page, so the page turn doesn't create an accidental pause mid-sentence. Plan your silences as carefully as your loud moments.
quote: You always want to complete a thought before moving to a new page.
drill: Check where each page of your manuscript ends. If a page break falls inside a sentence, reformat so every page ends at a complete thought.

source.title: Prose Starter Kit

advice: Not every tiny gap is a pause. Fluency researchers usually count only silences longer than about a quarter of a second (250-300 ms). Micro-gaps of around 0.2 seconds or less are normal in connected speech, so focus on the longer mid-phrase silences and not on every small break.

source.author: Nivja de Jong
source.title: Analysis of fluency (LANGSNAP Workshop presentation)
source.publisher: LANGSNAP project, University of Southampton (web archive)

advice: When learners paused in the middle of a clause, the pause was often linked to swapping a word, rewording, or planning on the fly. If your recordings show mid-sentence stops, check whether you were changing your wording at that moment, and settle that phrasing in rehearsal so you don't rework it live.
quote: processes such as replacement, reformulation, and online planning
drill: Play back a recording and, at every mid-sentence pause, note whether the words right after it replaced or reworded what you had started. For each one, pick the final wording and say the whole sentence three times as one unbroken unit.

source.author: P. Tavakoli
source.title: Pausing patterns: differences between L2 learners and native speakers

advice: Learn where to pause by imitating a skilled speaker. After marking where they pause and which words they stress in a transcript, record yourself saying the same passage with the same pauses, check whether you paused only where you marked, and re-record, focusing on the spots you got wrong.
quote: Check your recording. Did you pause only where you marked "/" or "//"?
drill: Take a paragraph of your own speech, strip out all punctuation, and mark / for a short pause and // for a long one based only on meaning. Read it aloud from your marks, record it, and fix any spot where you paused inside a group.

source.author: Agata Guskaroska, Erik Goodale, Timothy Kochem, Monica Ghosh, Lily Compton, Elena Cotos
