source.title: Chapter 4. Thought Groups (Additional Activities), in Oral Communication for Non-Native Speakers of English, 2nd Edition

advice: Speakers are more likely to hesitate before a word that is hard to predict from the words before it. This held even when how common the word was was kept the same: among rare words, about 30% of hard-to-predict ones came after a hesitation versus about 15% of predictable ones. So the words to drill are the surprising, precise choices in each sentence, together with the words leading into them.
quote: Contextual probability had an effect on hesitation even when word frequency was held constant
drill: Underline the one word in each key sentence that a listener would least expect (a precise verb, a specific term, a striking adjective). Practise the three or four words before it plus the word itself as one smooth run until there is no gap.

source.author: Geoffrey W. Beattie, B. L. Butterworth
source.credentials: University of Sheffield; University of Cambridge
source.title: Contextual Probability and Word Frequency as Determinants of Pauses and Errors in Spontaneous Speech

advice: Even very short silences carry structure. In analyses of several sets of readings, most pauses of 0.13 to 0.25 seconds were tied to syntax, punctuation, or emphasis rather than to the mechanics of articulation. So place your brief breaks deliberately: at phrase boundaries, at punctuation, or where you want emphasis.
quote: The vast majority of these pauses are found to be psychological

source.author: Adolf E. Hieke, Sabine Kowal, Daniel C. O'Connell
source.title: The Trouble with "Articulatory" Pauses

advice: A stream of short pauses scattered through your sentences can make you sound choppy. In the political speeches these researchers analysed, most short pauses that were not tied to boundaries, punctuation, or emphasis came from one speaker, Carter, whose choppy, staccato style they said these pauses contributed to. Save brief breaks for boundaries and emphasis, and run the words in between together.
quote: Stylistically, his public speaking is characterized by a choppy, staccato presentation,
drill: Record a one-minute passage and mark every break, even tiny ones. Circle any break that is not at a phrase boundary or before a stressed word, then re-record joining the words across each circled spot.

source.author: Adolf E. Hieke, Sabine Kowal, Daniel C. O'Connell
source.title: The Trouble with "Articulatory" Pauses

advice: A break in the wrong place can do more harm than a missing one. In this study of garden-path sentences, listeners accepted sentences with an extra prosodic break that clashed with the grammar less often than sentences with a needed break left out. If you're unsure whether a pause belongs somewhere mid-sentence, leave it out rather than risk splitting the sentence in the wrong spot.
quote: Sentences with incongruent boundaries were accepted less than those with missing boundaries

source.author: Efrat Pauker, Inbal Itzhak, Shari R. Baum, Karsten Steinhauer
source.title: Effects of Cooperating and Conflicting Prosody in Spoken English Garden Path Sentences: ERP Evidence for the Boundary Deletion Hypothesis

advice: Listeners interpret each break by comparing it with the others in the sentence: whether a later break was bigger or smaller than an earlier one changed how listeners understood the sentence. Make your major breaks clearly longer than your minor ones so the structure of the sentence comes through.
quote: the interpretation of one prosodic boundary depends on the existence and relative size of other prosodic boundaries in the sentence.

source.author: Katy Carlson, Charles Clifton, Jr., Lyn Frazier
source.title: Prosodic Boundaries in Adjunct Attachment

advice: A well-placed break can rescue a sentence that listeners might otherwise misread. Kjelgaard and Speer found that a prosodic boundary in the right place removed the usual comprehension difficulty with temporarily ambiguous sentences. When a sentence could be heard two ways, put your break deliberately at the real grammatical joint.
quote: the appropriate occurrence of either type of prosodic boundary eliminated the usual difficulty
drill: Read your speech aloud slowly and flag any sentence where a listener could attach a phrase to the wrong part for a moment. Mark one clear break at the true joint in each, and test it on a friend who hasn't seen the script.

source.author: Katy Carlson, Charles Clifton, Jr., Lyn Frazier
source.title: Prosodic Boundaries in Adjunct Attachment

advice: Review your recording pause by pause. In this study, students watched a video of their presentation and were asked 'Why did you pause at that point?' at every pause. Pauses the researchers saw as planned were usually at clause ends, while unplanned ones were usually mid-clause. Sorting your own pauses this way shows which to keep and which to fix.
quote: Pauses we interpret as unplanned usually occur mid-clause.
drill: Watch a recording of a practice run and stop at every silence. Write down why you paused (breath, moving to the next point, emphasis, forgot what came next, searching for a word). Keep the first three kinds; target the others in your next rehearsal.

source.author: Heejin Chang, Scott Windeatt
source.title: Fluency issues in L2 academy presentations: Linguistic, cognitive and psychological influences on pausing behaviour

advice: Many unplanned pauses in student presentations came from content problems, such as having trouble remembering what to explain next, more than from language problems. If your stops cluster around complex material, rehearse what you will say about it, not just the exact wording.
quote: many of the pauses were linked to cognitive, i.e. content-related, rather than linguistic issues.

source.author: Heejin Chang, Scott Windeatt
source.title: Fluency issues in L2 academy presentations: Linguistic, cognitive and psychological influences on pausing behaviour

advice: If you don't know where you should be pausing, look at what your rushed speech looks like on paper. Write out a garbled sentence from your own recording with no spaces between words, then rewrite it with normal spacing. The contrast shows where your pauses belong.
quote: Often the clutterer must be taught to pause deliberately.
drill: Pick one hard-to-follow sentence from a recording of yourself. Write it as one unbroken string, then rewrite it with spaces and slashes at phrase breaks, and say the spaced version aloud with a short pause at each slash.

source.author: Kenneth O. St. Louis
source.title: Cluttering: Some Guidelines

advice: Speak louder. It's hard to be loud and fast at once, so more volume naturally slows you down.
drill: Read a paragraph at your normal volume, then at a strong projected volume, and compare the time each takes.

source.author: Joel Schwartzberg
source.title: How To Quit Talking Quickly

advice: Over-articulate, using your whole mouth. Clear consonants act like speed bumps and make you easier to understand.

source.author: Joel Schwartzberg
source.title: How To Quit Talking Quickly

advice: Each pause takes your speed back to zero. Even if you speed up again, regular pauses keep you from staying at full speed.

source.author: Joel Schwartzberg
source.title: How To Quit Talking Quickly

advice: Put questions to the audience into your talk. Nobody asks a question quickly, and waiting for answers resets your pace.

source.author: Joel Schwartzberg
source.title: How To Quit Talking Quickly

advice: Write 'PAUSE' in your notes where a point needs to sink in, and keep notes in short bullets so you think in separate chunks.
drill: Mark 'PAUSE' at five places in your outline and honor every one in rehearsal.

source.author: Joel Schwartzberg
source.title: How To Quit Talking Quickly

advice: If time runs short, cut lower-priority content instead of speeding up. Put your most important ideas first so cuts are easy.
quote: try to cut less important content, not speed up, because anything you rush will not be retained.

source.author: Joel Schwartzberg
source.title: How To Quit Talking Quickly

advice: Just being told 'slow down' rarely works. Rely on concrete tactics like volume, articulation and pauses instead.
quote: Your audience needs twice as long to receive your point as you need to make it.

source.author: Joel Schwartzberg
source.title: How To Quit Talking Quickly

advice: To get a feel for your pace, deliberately exaggerate speaking slowly and ask listeners how it came across. Often 'too slow' to you is about right to them.
drill: Present a minute at an exaggeratedly slow pace to a few people and ask whether it felt dull or just right.

source.title: Tips for fast speakers: How to slow down

advice: Make yourself pronounce the final consonants of words clearly. It reliably slows you down.
quote: Forcing yourself to strongly enunciate final consonants tends to slow a speaker down.

source.title: Tips for fast speakers: How to slow down

advice: Speak more slowly at the start, while the audience is still getting used to you and your topic.

source.title: Tips for fast speakers: How to slow down

advice: Slow down for complex material, and say a key sentence word by word for emphasis.

source.title: Tips for fast speakers: How to slow down

advice: Some speakers have a reasonable average pace but fire words in bursts. Fix that by slowing those phrases or moving where you pause.

source.title: Tips for fast speakers: How to slow down

advice: Practice a slower pace in everyday moments, like ordering at a restaurant, so it carries over to speeches.
drill: Next time you order food, speak at a deliberately slower pace.

source.title: Tips for fast speakers: How to slow down

advice: Speech-language pathologists treat pausing as a main tool for controlling rate. Adding pauses and slowing overall usually makes rushed speech clearer and more fluent.

source.title: Stuttering, Cluttering, and Fluency (Practice Portal)

advice: Talking very fast can make words run together and syllables drop out. Pauses in the right places help speech flow more smoothly.

source.title: Cluttering: Signs, Causes & Treatment

advice: Learn your actual rate in numbers, for example around 240 syllables per minute against about 200. Then you can tell what 'fast' really means for you.
drill: Count the syllables in a one-minute recording and compare against a normal-rate target.

source.title: From One Clutterer to Another… Strategies that Helped Me

advice: Tapping a finger on each syllable makes you aware of every syllable and evens out your rhythm.
drill: Read a paragraph aloud tapping one finger per syllable, then read it again without tapping at the same pace.

source.title: Cluttering Treatment: What Does It Consist Of? Basic Principles.

advice: Average speech runs about 150 words per minute, and closer to 120 suits listeners for whom the language isn't native. Time yourself to find your own number.
drill: Read a familiar passage for 10–15 seconds, count the words and work out your words per minute.

source.title: Presentation Skills Tip: Slowing Down the Fast Talkers

advice: Breathe from your diaphragm and speak on the out-breath instead of holding your breath. It steadies both your nerves and your pace.
drill: Before speaking, breathe in through your nose for 4 counts and out for 4 counts, several times.

source.title: Do You Talk Too Fast? 9 Ways To Slow It Down (with Science)

advice: When you notice you're speeding, interrupt yourself. Use the moment to pause, slow down and take control again.
drill: Read any text aloud focusing only on controlling your pace.

source.title: How to Stop Speaking Too Fast: Techniques to Slow Down and Engage Your Audience Better

advice: Talking too fast when presenting is very common. Consciously slow down, and use slow, deep breaths to calm your nerves.

source.title: Delivery and Q&A

advice: Even a small cut in pace helps. A modestly slower pace gives your brain time to keep up, so you use fewer fillers.

source.author: Andrew Dlugan
source.title: How to Stop Saying Um, Uh, and Other Filler Words

advice: Don't overcorrect. In field experiments, a brisk rate (about 195 words per minute) was judged more credible than a very slow one (about 100 words per minute).

source.author: Norman Miller, Geoffrey Maruyama, Rex J. Beaber, Keith Valone
source.title: Speed of speech and persuasion
source.publisher: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

advice: Researchers piloting a very slow rate (118 words per minute) found it too slow for the speaker to seem credible. If you're well under typical speeds, pick up the pace.

source.author: Stephen M. Smith, David R. Shaffer
source.title: Celerity and Cajolery: Rapid Speech May Promote or Inhibit Persuasion through its Impact on Message Elaboration

advice: In that experiment, very fast speech (about 220 words per minute) made listeners less able to tell strong arguments from weak ones. Slow down for your key reasoning.

source.author: Stephen M. Smith, David R. Shaffer
source.title: Speed of Speech and Persuasion: Evidence for Multiple Effects

advice: Match pace to content. Go slower for complex ideas like definitions and quicker for things the audience already knows. Time a full run-through to check.
drill: Time a complete out-loud rehearsal and compare it with your time limit.

source.title: Delivery
source.publisher: Central Michigan University Presentation Skills Center

advice: A noticeably slow rate can make it sound as if you don't know your speech well. Keep the introduction at a clear, confident rate and speed up in places to signal urgency.

source.title: Verbal Delivery (Chapter 8)

advice: Change speed on purpose. Speed up through a list of facts to show momentum, and slow right down, even softening your voice, for your biggest moment.
drill: Mark one list to speed through and one climax line to slow down in your speech, and rehearse the contrast.

source.title: Strategy: "Interping" Extemp

advice: Talking too slowly can bore listeners just as rushing loses them. Record yourself to check which way you lean.
drill: Record a two-minute practice and rate it yourself: too slow, about right, or too fast.

source.title: WC117: Public Speaking Tools

advice: Keep most of your talk at a normal conversational pace and change speed only for emphasis. An entire talk at a slow pace loses the audience.
drill: Rehearse with a metronome app set to your target pace.

source.title: Your speech pace: guide to speeding and slowing down

advice: If you slow down but fill the gaps with long thinking pauses, it drags. Knowing your material thoroughly removes the hesitations that make slow speakers seem stalled.
drill: Go through your notes and underline sentences you can deliver more briskly.

source.title: Question: What are some methods to improve the speed in which I'm talking during presentations?

advice: Nerves make you breathe less and talk faster, so your words get ahead of your thoughts and fillers appear. Breathing steadily keeps both in check.

source.author: Lisa B. Marshall
source.title: So, um, how do you, like, stop using filler words?

advice: Instead of watching the clock, concentrate on getting the feeling of each line across. Stressing key words and conveying emotion naturally lengthens your words and slows you down.
quote: do not focus on your speed. Instead, focus on communicating emotion.

source.author: Bill Brown
source.credentials: DTM; speech delivery coach, Gillette, Wyoming
source.title: Controlling Your Pace and Pitch

advice: Sounding fast is often more about short gaps between phrases than about how fast you form the words. Adding regular pauses can make you sound controlled even if your speaking rate barely changes.
quote: Instead, just introduce regular pauses—and keep your default speaking rate the same.
drill: Record a minute at your natural rate, then repeat it with a pause after every sentence and ask a listener which sounded more controlled.

source.title: The Myth About Fast Talkers | Public Speaking Tips

advice: Shape your pace across the whole speech: open slowly so listeners settle in, move to a brisker pace through the body, then slow down again to finish. A uniformly fast rate erases this structure.
quote: Generally, speeches should start slowly, gradually accustom the listener to a brisker pace, and then finish slowly.

source.author: Jason Baldwin
source.credentials: Graduate philosophy student, University of Notre Dame; coordinator of the LD division, Kentucky Institute
source.title: LD Rebuttals as Speeches
source.publisher: Rostrum (National Forensic League), Rostrum Library archive at University of Vermont

advice: Judges often complain about debaters going too fast but almost never about going too slow. When unsure, especially with lay judges, err toward a moderate, clear rate.
quote: I have never heard a judge complain that debaters spoke too slowly.

source.author: Jason Baldwin
source.credentials: Graduate philosophy student, University of Notre Dame; coordinator of the LD division, Kentucky Institute
source.title: LD Rebuttals as Speeches
source.publisher: Rostrum (National Forensic League), Rostrum Library archive at University of Vermont

advice: Racing to fit in everything you know makes you swallow words and drop endings. Include only what your answer needs so you can finish the time limit at an unhurried pace.
quote: swallowing words and dropping word endings all over the floor

source.author: Martha B. Ebeling
source.credentials: Extemp coach, Dayton Oakwood High School (OH); coached 23 national qualifiers in extemp
source.title: Ten Commandments for Effective Extemporaneous Delivery
source.publisher: Rostrum (National Forensic League), Rostrum Library archive at University of Vermont

advice: Some speakers rush to head off critique, talking so fast that listeners can barely keep up or interrupt. Slow down enough that your audience can think along with you and form their own questions.
quote: talk fast and deliver things so fast you can barely keep up

source.author: Kelly McGonigal (guest), Matt Abrahams (host)
source.credentials: McGonigal: lecturer, Stanford Graduate School of Business
source.title: Feeling Nervous? How Anxiety Can Fuel Better Communication
source.publisher: Stanford Graduate School of Business (Think Fast, Talk Smart)

advice: Nerves push most people to speed up, so a pace that feels fine alone may run fast under pressure. Time your practice runs in front of a real audience to find out your true performance pace.
quote: People often speak quickly when they're nervous or stressed, so watch for this.
drill: Do one timed run alone and one in front of friends; compare the two durations.

source.title: Public Speaking Presentations: Delivery

advice: The right rate depends on your listeners, not on a fixed number: slow enough that they understand you, fast enough to keep their attention. Too slow loses them just as surely as too fast.
quote: One should speak slowly enough to be understood and fast enough to sustain audience attention.

source.author: Wayne C. Mannebach
source.credentials: Former director of debate and forensics, Ripon College; English teacher, St. Mary Central High School (Neenah, WI)
source.title: Facts Alone Are Not Enough: A Plea for Coordinated Voice and Message
source.publisher: Rostrum (National Forensic League), Rostrum Library archive at University of Vermont

advice: If you sound slow when you're nervous, the cause may be hesitations rather than slow talking. In a small study, anxious speakers articulated just as fast as others but spent far more of their speaking time hesitating, so work on the gaps rather than trying to talk faster.

source.author: Zsuzsa Szánthó
source.title: Foreign language anxiety and filled pauses in spontaneous L2 speech
source.publisher: Proceedings of the 3rd International Symposium on Applied Phonetics (ISAPh 2021), ISCA Archive

advice: A slow pace works best as a spotlight, not a default. Slow down for the one or two ideas you most want remembered, and keep the rest of the talk moving, because a whole talk at a slow speed bores listeners.
quote: an entire talk at a slow pace will bore your audience.
drill: Highlight the two most important sentences in your speech. Deliver only those slowly, and deliver everything else at your normal conversational speed.

source.author: Dom Barnard
source.title: Average Speaking Rate and Words per Minute

advice: Judge your rate against the setting you are in. Presentations commonly run about 100-150 words per minute, audiobooks and radio about 150-160, and a sample of popular TED talks averaged about 173 (range 154-201). If you are well under the presentation range you are probably dragging, and if you are well over the TED range you are probably rushing.
drill: Record a 2-minute stretch of your speech, count the words, and divide by 2. Compare the number to the range for your setting.

source.author: Dom Barnard
source.title: Average Speaking Rate and Words per Minute

advice: Fast delivery creates energy at first, but kept up for minutes on end it wears listeners out. Use fast stretches in short bursts and then return to a moderate pace.
quote: after a minute or two, it stops being stimulating and becomes overwhelming.

source.author: Dom Barnard
source.title: Average Speaking Rate and Words per Minute

advice: A speaker who stays at one slow, even speed starts to sound monotone. Changing your speed from section to section keeps your voice sounding alive.
quote: Without pace variation, you're in danger of sounding monotone.

source.author: Dom Barnard
source.title: Average Speaking Rate and Words per Minute

advice: In a large study of online lecture videos, engagement generally rose as instructors spoke faster, and the faster speakers came across as more enthusiastic. Don't slow yourself down on purpose to seem careful. Let your natural energy set the speed.
quote: but rather to bring out their enthusiasm and reassure them that there is no need to artificially slow down.

source.author: Philip J. Guo, Juho Kim, Rob Rubin
source.title: How Video Production Affects Student Engagement: An Empirical Study of MOOC Videos
source.publisher: Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Learning at Scale (L@S 2014)

advice: Speed is a symptom of enthusiasm, not a substitute for it. If you sound slow and flat, speeding up mechanically won't fix it. Reconnect with why the content matters to you, and your rate will usually rise along with your energy.
quote: Thus, speeding up an unenthusiastic instructor might not improve engagement.
drill: Before a run-through, say aloud in one sentence why this topic excites you. Then deliver the opening and compare its rate with a cold run.

source.author: Philip J. Guo, Juho Kim, Rob Rubin
source.title: How Video Production Affects Student Engagement: An Empirical Study of MOOC Videos
source.publisher: Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Learning at Scale (L@S 2014)

advice: For recorded talks, part of what makes a slow speaker feel slow is dead air and filler. The researchers recommended cutting pauses and filler words in editing. Instructor rates in their videos ranged from about 48 to 254 words per minute, averaging about 156.
quote: and edit out pauses and filler words in post-production.
drill: Edit a recording of yourself by deleting every silence over about 2 seconds and every filler. Compare how long the edited and original versions run.

source.author: Philip J. Guo, Juho Kim, Rob Rubin
source.title: How Video Production Affects Student Engagement: An Empirical Study of MOOC Videos
source.publisher: Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Learning at Scale (L@S 2014)

advice: When researchers mechanically slowed recorded voices, listeners rated the speakers as less competent, and speeding voices up made them seem less benevolent (kind). If you tend to drag, a modest increase in rate can help you sound more capable, as long as you don't tip into rushing.

source.author: Bruce L. Brown, William J. Strong, Alvin C. Rencher
source.credentials: Language Research Center, Brigham Young University
source.title: Perceptions of personality from speech: effects of manipulations of acoustical parameters
source.publisher: Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 54(1), 29-35

advice: In this study, speaking rate explained far more of how competent a voice sounded than pitch did. Slower voices were rated less competent, and voices with less pitch movement lost ground on both competence and warmth. Being slow and flat at the same time is the combination to avoid.

source.author: Bruce L. Brown, William J. Strong, Alvin C. Rencher
source.title: Fifty-four voices from two: the effects of simultaneous manipulations of rate, mean fundamental frequency, and variance of fundamental frequency on ratings of personality from speech
source.publisher: Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 55(2)

advice: Don't assume talking faster automatically makes you more persuasive. When this study controlled for earlier methodological problems, the links between rate, credibility and persuasion were more limited and conditional than the simple 'faster is more convincing' story suggests.

source.author: W. Gill Woodall, Judee K. Burgoon
source.title: Talking fast and changing attitudes: A critique and clarification

advice: In a study of radio news, listeners rated 150 words per minute as slow and remembered the most when items were read at 170-190 words per minute. For spoken information, a brisk pace can help memory rather than hurt it.
quote: The news items that participants remembered best were delivered at a speed of 170 to 190 words per minute

source.author: Margarita Salas Guzman
source.title: Radio news: How the pace, density of broadcasts affect what audiences understand, remember

advice: Going slow through light material is the worst mix. In the same radio study, simple, low-information items read slowly were among the hardest to understand and the least remembered. When content is simple or familiar, move through it faster.
quote: were able to recall the least amount of information from clips of low density and low speed
drill: Label each section of your speech 'dense' or 'light.' Practice the light sections at a noticeably quicker pace than the dense ones.

source.author: Margarita Salas Guzman
source.title: Radio news: How the pace, density of broadcasts affect what audiences understand, remember

advice: Very high speed plus packed content overloads listeners. In the radio study, recall dropped for information-dense items read at about 230 words per minute. When a sentence carries many facts or numbers, give it more time.
quote: At 230 [words per minute], the listener is incapable of maintaining and processing the incoming information.

source.author: Margarita Salas Guzman
source.title: Radio news: How the pace, density of broadcasts affect what audiences understand, remember

advice: How fast you seem depends mostly on how much you pause, not on how fast you move your mouth. If you are told you sound slow, first cut the number and length of your pauses before trying to say the words themselves faster.
quote: Variations in the overall speed of talking were found to be variations in the amount of pausing.
drill: Measure two numbers from a recording: words per minute including pauses, and words per minute with the silences cut out. If only the first is low, your pauses are the problem.

source.author: Jürgen Trouvain
source.title: Tempo Variation in Speech Production: Implications for Speech Synthesis (Ch. 2, Sources of Tempo Variation)

advice: Use syllables per second as a benchmark. In Tauroza and Allison's measurements of British English, conversation ran about 4.4 syllables per second, radio and interviews about 4.2, and lectures were the slowest at about 3.2. If you measure below the lecture rate, you are slower than even careful academic speech.
drill: Count the syllables in a 30-second recording and divide by 30. Compare the result with 3.2 (lecture) and 4.2 (radio).

source.author: Jürgen Trouvain
source.title: Tempo Variation in Speech Production: Implications for Speech Synthesis (Ch. 2, Sources of Tempo Variation)

advice: Non-native speakers are often told to slow down, but research summarized here found native listeners judged slightly faster second-language speech as more understandable and less accented than the speaker's natural or slowed tempo. Only clearly too-fast speech was penalized. Slowing down a lot is not automatically a clarity fix.
quote: However, talking too fast resulted in a downgrading.

source.author: Jürgen Trouvain
source.title: Tempo Variation in Speech Production: Implications for Speech Synthesis (Ch. 2, Sources of Tempo Variation)

advice: Slowing down without adding vocal movement makes speech sound bored. Even speech synthesizers have this problem, and the suggested fix is more varied intonation. If you slow a passage down, let your voice rise and fall more so the slower speed sounds intentional, not tired.
quote: However, most present-day synthesisers bear the risk of sounding "bored" when speech tempo is reduced.

source.author: Jürgen Trouvain
source.title: Tempo Variation in Speech Production: Implications for Speech Synthesis (Ch. 8)

advice: Listeners tend to prefer faster speech, but only up to a point. Past a certain speed the benefit flips into a penalty. Aim for brisk, not breakneck.
quote: it is obvious that an overdose threshold will apply in speech rate as well

source.author: Radek Skarnitzl, Hana Hledíková
source.title: Prosodic Phrasing of Good Speakers in English and Czech

advice: Charismatic speakers don't hold one speed. A comparison of Steve Jobs and Mark Zuckerberg cited in this review found Jobs sped up and slowed down more sharply and varied his rate more. Build clear accelerations and decelerations into your delivery.
quote: documented a strong and symmetric acceleration and deceleration in speech rate and a higher variability in speech rate
drill: Pick one paragraph. Speed up steadily toward its key line, then slow down sharply as you say the key line.

source.author: Radek Skarnitzl, Hana Hledíková
source.title: Prosodic Phrasing of Good Speakers in English and Czech

advice: If your delivery is too slow and deliberate, break the habit by overshooting. Read the script as fast as you can, then read it again naturally. The second read usually comes out looser and quicker.
quote: Go fast — as fast as possible. Have them read the script at top speed, then try it again naturally.
drill: Read a 1-minute script at maximum speed, then immediately read it at a natural pace. Repeat three times.

source.title: The art of coaching vocal performance: How to help hosts and reporters own the mic

advice: If your words run together from speed, exaggerate in the other direction for practice. Read in a slow drawl, finishing every word before starting the next, then return to normal speed with that same completeness.
quote: Try a dramatic drawl. Have them read the script slowly and over-articulated, finishing each word before moving to the next.
drill: Read a paragraph in an exaggerated drawl, then read it at normal speed while keeping every word ending intact.

source.title: The art of coaching vocal performance: How to help hosts and reporters own the mic

advice: Mark your script for speed. Speed up through background or familiar material, and slow down when you introduce something new or important.
quote: It's fine to pick up the pace during background or familiar content.
drill: Mark '>' over background sentences and '<' over new or important sentences, then deliver the script following the marks.

source.title: Marking scripts can help you sound more natural on the radio

advice: Choose your speed to match what you are describing. Quick delivery suggests urgency or danger, and slow delivery suggests tension, finality or fear. A slow pace should be a choice made for meaning, not your default.
quote: By speaking slowly, you can suggest tension, finality or fear.

source.author: Bill Brown
source.title: Don't Race the Pace

advice: Rushing clips your words short and drains their feeling. Give the important words room by stretching them out instead of cramming more words into the same time.
quote: Speaking quickly limits or eliminates the lengthening of individual words, and, thus, limits expressiveness.

source.author: Bill Brown
source.title: Don't Race the Pace

advice: Practice a slower delivery against the clock. Take a section of your speech that takes 30 seconds and redeliver it in at least 40 seconds so you get used to the slower pace.
quote: try saying it in a minimum of 40 seconds
drill: Time a chunk that currently takes 30 seconds, then rehearse it until it lasts at least 40 seconds.

source.author: Bill Brown
source.title: Controlling Your Pace and Pitch

advice: For long listening, such as audiobooks or extended readings, being a little slow is safer than rushing. A somewhat deliberate pace lets listeners settle in, while a rushed read leaves them struggling to keep up.
quote: it's better for your narrator to err on the slower side than rush through the material

source.author: Scott Jacobi
source.title: 5 Tips for Choosing a Narrator

advice: In this lecture-video study, playing videos at 1.5x or 2x speed cost little comprehension, and performance fell only beyond 2x. Clear material doesn't need a very slow pace to be understood.
quote: minimal costs incurred by increasing video speed from 1x to 1.5x, or 2x speed, but performance declined beyond 2x speed.

source.author: Dillon H. Murphy, Kara M. Hoover, Karina Agadzhanyan, Jesse C. Kuehn, Alan D. Castel
source.title: Learning in double time: The effect of lecture video speed on immediate and delayed comprehension

advice: A naturally fast speaker is harder to follow than a recording sped up to the same length, and older listeners are hit hardest. If your audience includes older adults, such as parents or adult judges, don't count on them keeping up with your top speed.
quote: older listeners are at a much greater disadvantage when listening to natural fast speech.

source.author: Sandra Gordon-Salant, Danielle J. Zion, Carol Espy-Wilson
source.title: Recognition of time-compressed speech does not predict recognition of natural fast-rate speech by older listeners
source.publisher: Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 136(4), EL268-EL274

advice: Faster speech cut understanding more for older adults than for younger ones, and middle-aged listeners looked more like older listeners at the fastest rate tested. Your top speed may lose a broad part of an adult audience, not only elderly listeners.
quote: The reduction in speech recognition associated with faster rates of speech was greater for older adults than younger adults.

source.author: Anna R. Tinnemore, Lauren Montero, Sandra Gordon-Salant, Matthew J. Goupell
source.title: The recognition of time-compressed speech as a function of age in listeners with cochlear implants or normal hearing

advice: Classic time-compressed speech research (Foulke and Sticht, 1969, as cited in this report) found comprehension holds up well until rates far above normal speech, declining more steeply only above about 275 words per minute. A speaker at 110 words per minute has a lot of room to speed up before understanding suffers.
quote: a more rapid decline in comprehension occurs above 275 words per minute

source.author: Henry J. deHaan
source.credentials: U.S. Army Research Institute for the Behavioral and Social Sciences
source.title: A Speech-Rate Intelligibility/Comprehensibility Threshold for Speeded and Time-Compressed Connected Speech (Technical Paper 297)
source.publisher: U.S. Army Research Institute for the Behavioral and Social Sciences

advice: Listeners vary widely in how fast they can follow, so a speed that works for one person can lose another. When you speak to a group, pace for the slower listeners rather than the quickest.
quote: there is a wide range of variation in threshold values among subjects

source.author: Henry J. deHaan
source.credentials: U.S. Army Research Institute for the Behavioral and Social Sciences
source.title: A Speech-Rate Intelligibility/Comprehensibility Threshold for Speeded and Time-Compressed Connected Speech (Technical Paper 297)
source.publisher: U.S. Army Research Institute for the Behavioral and Social Sciences

advice: Speaking too slowly is not a safe default. Microsoft's rehearsal tool recommends about 100-165 words per minute and warns that a pace that is too slow loses the audience's interest, which also hurts understanding and memory.
quote: When you speak too slowly, the audience can lose interest in the material, which also can decrease comprehension and recall.
drill: Rehearse with a live pace meter, such as a presentation rehearsal tool, and look at the pace-over-time graph for stretches that sag below your target.

source.title: Suggestions from Speaker Coach

advice: A very slow pace can hurt your credibility, because audiences may read it as a sign that you don't care, don't know the topic, or didn't prepare.
quote: Speaking slowly may lead the audience to infer that the speaker is uninterested, uninformed, or unprepared

source.title: Communication in the Real World: An Introduction to Communication Studies (10.3 Vocal Delivery)

advice: A dragging pace undercuts your authority and can also push you past or short of a required speaking time. Aim for a conversational speed.
quote: If you speak too slow, you will not project authority or confidence.

source.author: Joshua Polanski, Dean Ward
source.title: What Not To Do: Speech Delivery

advice: In debate, a slow speaker usually has a preparation problem, not a voice problem: too little material prepared, or arguments not fully understood. Fix slowness by preparing more content and knowing your arguments in more depth.
quote: It is also possible to have a speed problem of going too slow, but this is unlikely.

source.title: Verbal Presentation (Parliamentary Debate guide)

advice: A pace that feels normal to you can be far too fast for judges. Use a metronome app and recordings to try different tempos and find a speed listeners can actually follow.
quote: Unquestionably, the biggest issue concerning vocal presentation is speed, and the biggest problem is going too fast.
drill: Set a metronome app and practice the same passage at two or three tempos. Record each one and choose the fastest version that still sounds clear on playback.

source.title: Verbal Presentation (Parliamentary Debate guide)

advice: Memorizing a speech word for word gives you a reason to race through it, so avoid memorizing. If you do have to memorize text, study how a slow-paced actor delivers lines.
quote: Memorizing gives you a reason to race through information, so avoid it.

source.author: Scott Schwertly
source.title: How to Slow Down Nervous, Speedy Speech

advice: If your delivery drags, pick the parts meant to build interest or energy and deliberately speed up there. Save the slower delivery for moments that should feel serious.
quote: try speeding up during parts of your speech that you want to drive audience interest or energy.

source.author: Amy Boone
source.title: Our Modern Pace: The Best Speakers Talk Faster

advice: Train a flexible rate with simple stories. Plan which passages of a children's story should go faster and which slower, read it aloud, and listen to how the speed changes the meaning.
quote: Then read it aloud and listen carefully to how speed alters interpretation.
drill: Mark a children's story with 'fast' and 'slow' passages, read it aloud, then swap the marks and read it again to hear the difference.

source.author: Susan Dugdale
source.title: Quick and easy effective tips for speaking rate

advice: Practice pacing on fact-heavy material. Read a dense news article aloud, slowing for the key facts and moving through the rest, and repeat until the mix of speeds feels right.
quote: Re-read aloud until you feel you have the mix of speeds right.
drill: Read a fact-heavy news article aloud twice: once normally, and once as if your listener knows nothing about the subject.

source.author: Susan Dugdale
source.title: Quick and easy effective tips for speaking rate

advice: Raise a slow rate in small steps. Start at a normal conversational pace with crisp articulation, then add about 10-20 words per minute at a time, and move up only once each step still sounds clear.
quote: Once you feel that your language is clear and crisp, slowly increase your speed in segments of 10–20 wpm.
drill: Record a passage at your current rate. Re-record it at +10-20 wpm, check the clarity, and repeat over several sessions.

source.author: Suzy Woltmann
source.title: How to Talk Fast: Exercises + Tips

advice: Don't put on a sudden burst of speed at your call to action, because it can make you seem rushed or nervous right when you need to sound sure. When you do change pace, shift smoothly rather than in jerky stops and starts.
quote: speaking hiccups (abrupt stops and starts)

source.author: Ray Anthony, Barbara Boyd
source.title: When to Adjust Your Speed in Innovative Presentations (Innovative Presentations For Dummies)

advice: In this informal analysis of TED talks, rates clustered around 153-168 words per minute, and anything roughly between 133 and 188 is a reasonable range. Treat that as a target band, not a single number to hit.
quote: It depends, but if you are anywhere close to the range of the speakers analyzed above (133 to 188 words/minute), you’re fine.

source.title: What is the Average Speaking Rate?

advice: Reading text aloud measures your reading rate, not your speaking rate. To know whether you are really slow or fast, time yourself giving an actual speech, ideally in front of listeners.
quote: this is not really your speaking rate. It's your reading rate.
drill: Time a full delivery of a real speech, without reading from a script, and divide the transcript's word count by the minutes.

source.title: What is the Average Speaking Rate?

advice: Slowing down isn't what makes clear speech clear. This research showed speakers can be highly intelligible at normal rates. If listeners struggle to understand you, work on articulation instead of dragging your pace.
quote: speaking slowly is not responsible for the high intelligibility of clear speech

source.author: Jean Christine Krause
source.credentials: Ph.D. thesis, MIT Dept. of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science
source.title: Properties of naturally produced clear speech at normal rates and implications for intelligibility enhancement

advice: Presenting is not the same as excited conversation. Audiences need a slower, steadier presenting rate (about 140-160 words per minute in this article) than many people use when chatting.
quote: It takes work to develop a slower presenting style, but you'll be a more effective speaker.

source.author: Denise Graveline
source.title: 5 ways to slow down your speech

advice: Find out why you rush before you try to fix it. Nerves, feeling short on time, and a racing mind each need a different remedy, and a recording will show you the exact spots where you speed up.
quote: Is it because you are nervous? Is it because you feel pressed for time?
drill: Watch a recording and mark each spot where you speed up. Next to each mark, write the likely cause: nerves, time, or racing thoughts.

source.author: Dave Aizer
source.credentials: Emmy Award-winning public speaking and media coach
source.title: Don't Talk Too Fast!

advice: Speakers tend to rush exactly where listeners need time most: transitions, internal summaries and the conclusion. Make those structural moments your planned slow-downs.
quote: Rushing the pacing of the speech; rushing key moments, such as transitions, internal summaries and conclusions.
drill: Underline every transition, summary and concluding line in your outline, and practice slowing down at each one.

source.author: A. Susan Owen
source.title: Delivery Tips
source.publisher: University of Puget Sound, Center for Speech and Effective Advocacy

advice: Talking slowly can cost you more than polish. When recordings were slowed by 30%, listeners judged the speakers less truthful, less fluent, less persuasive and more passive. If you speak slowly by habit, bringing your rate up toward normal may help you sound more credible and convincing.
quote: Slow-talking speakers were judged less truthful, less fluent, and less persuasive and were seen as more passive
drill: Record a one-minute answer at your habitual speed, then record it again aiming to finish about 20% sooner without cutting words. Play both to a friend and ask which speaker sounds more sure of what they are saying.

source.author: William Apple, Lynn A. Streeter, Robert M. Krauss
source.title: Effects of pitch and speech rate on personal attributions
source.publisher: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 37(5), 715-727

advice: Listeners judge competence and warmth differently. In this study, competence ratings rose steadily as speech got faster and fell as it got slower, while warmth (benevolence) peaked at the speaker's normal rate. If you are a slow speaker, getting back up to your normal rate should help on both counts. Speeding far past normal still costs some warmth.
quote: Ratings of competence were found to increase as rate increases and decrease as rate decreases, in a linear fashion.

source.author: Bruce L. Smith, Bruce L. Brown, William J. Strong, Alvin C. Rencher
source.title: Effects of Speech Rate on Personality Perception

advice: A very slow pace can send the wrong signal about you. Researchers note that listeners may read slow speakers as lacking confidence, and very slow speech may simply bore them. If you are told you sound unsure, check your speed as well as your words.
quote: Second, from a motivational perspective, very slow speech may elicit boredom

source.author: Joshua J. Guyer, Thomas I. Vaughan-Johnston, Leandre R. Fabrigar, Borja Paredes, Pablo Briñol, et al.
source.title: Vocal Speed and Processing of Persuasive Messages: Curvilinear Processing Effects

advice: Speeding up helps only in small doses. Across six studies with nearly 4,000 people, faster voices seemed more confident at first, but the benefit faded or even reversed beyond slight increases in speed. If you are slow, aim for a modest step up from your normal pace (tested speeds included about 10-15% faster), not a dramatic jump.
quote: faster voices were generally perceived as more confident
drill: Time a 30-second passage at your normal pace, then reread it trying to finish about 10% sooner (around 27 seconds). Stop there rather than pushing faster.

source.author: Joshua J. Guyer, Thomas I. Vaughan-Johnston, Leandre R. Fabrigar, Borja Paredes, Pablo Briñol, et al.
source.title: Vocal Speed and Processing of Persuasive Messages: Curvilinear Processing Effects

advice: Listeners tend to favor speakers who talk at about their own speed. In this study, speakers whose rate seemed similar to the listener's were rated more competent and more socially attractive than speakers who were slower or faster. Before a speech, notice how fast your audience or judge talks and keep your pace in that neighborhood.
quote: The participants judged speakers with speech rates similar to their own as more competent and socially attractive

source.author: S. Feldstein, Faith-Anne Dohm, C. Crown
source.title: Gender and speech rate in the perception of competence and social attractiveness

advice: Watch for audience signals that you are too slow. If listeners start finishing your sentences or cutting in to ask what your next point is, it may feel rude, but it is a signal to pick up the pace.
quote: sends an important signal that you need to increase your rate of delivery.

source.title: Rate of Delivery

advice: A slow speaker gives the audience's minds room to drift. Listeners can take in words faster than anyone can say them, so a very slow rate leaves spare thinking time that often goes elsewhere. Speed up through less important material so their attention stays with you.
quote: As listeners, we typically process words faster than a speaker can say them, leaving time for the mind to wander.

source.author: Jennifer Y. Abbott, Todd F. McDorman, David M. Timmerman, L. Jill Lamberton
source.title: Effectively Using Verbal, Nonverbal, and Televisual Delivery (Public Speaking and Democratic Participation, 2nd ed., ch. 18)

advice: Fit your speed to how much your listener already knows. When the topic is new to them, slow down to give them more time to think about your message.
quote: I will slow my rate of speech if my listener is unfamiliar with the subject I am talking about.
drill: With a stopwatch, time how long one paragraph takes at your normal rate. Then read the same paragraph clearly slower and clearly faster, and note how many seconds each version takes.

source.author: Rynette R. Kjesbo
source.title: Using an Appropriate Rate of Speech (Handy Handouts #351)

advice: Train your ear for specific speeds by reading along with text that scrolls at a set rate. Repeating the same passage at different speeds shows you how much a change in pace alters how you sound, and the pace graph afterwards shows whether you ran too fast, too slow, or too even.
quote: Start by selecting a speed to speak at, for example, 160 words per minute.
drill: Use a scrolling-transcript tool (or a teleprompter app) set to a fixed words-per-minute rate. Read the same passage at three settings, then pick the one that sounds most natural and practice holding it.

source.title: Measure and Test Your Speaking Pace: Online Exercise

advice: Your rate changes how the audience feels about you, even when it doesn't change what they remember. In this classroom study, slow, moderate and fast versions of the same lesson differed in students' ratings of the instructor's credibility and nonverbal immediacy and in students' affective learning, but not in recall or perceived clarity. Treat rate as a credibility tool, not just a comprehension one.

source.author: Brent K. Simonds, Kevin R. Meyer, Margaret M. Quinlan, Stephen K. Hunt
source.title: Effects of Instructor Speech Rate on Student Affective Learning, Recall, and Perceptions of Nonverbal Immediacy, Credibility, and Clarity

advice: For news-style delivery, many radio experts recommend 160-180 words per minute. When this study measured 40 European news bulletins, only the BBC fell in that band. The faster broadcasters also used fewer pauses, so speed and missing pauses tend to come together.
quote: Most authors addressing the medium of radio recommend a speech rate of between 160 and 180 words per minute (wpm).

source.author: Emma Rodero
source.title: A comparative analysis of speech rate and perception in radio bulletins

advice: Balance speed against how much each sentence carries. This radio study found the faster the delivery, the lighter the information should be, and the reverse. Recognition was best at about 170 words per minute for dense content and 190 for light content. Plan to slow toward 170 on fact-heavy passages and move toward 190 on simple ones.
quote: The higher the speed, the lower the information density should be, and vice versa.
drill: Highlight the three most fact-packed sentences in your script. Read them at roughly 170 wpm, and read the surrounding lighter material at roughly 190 wpm.

source.author: Emma Rodero
source.title: Influence of Speech Rate and Information Density on Recognition: The Moderate Dynamic Mechanism

advice: Don't copy TED-talk speed for every setting. In this corpus study, TED talks were significantly faster than university lectures. In the lectures, more lexically dense one-minute samples tended to be spoken more slowly, but there was no such link in TED talks, perhaps because TED talks are scripted. If you script a talk, mark the dense parts and deliberately slow down there.
quote: perhaps due to TED talks being a scripted genre.

source.author: Peter Wingrove
source.title: How suitable are TED talks for academic listening?
source.publisher: Journal of English for Academic Purposes, 30, 79-95

advice: In a lecture study, students heard the same material at about 100, 150 or 200 words per minute. Slower delivery went with better comprehension, and the faster the lecture, the less important students judged the topic to be. Racing through material can make it seem less important as well as harder to follow.
quote: Slower delivery correlated with higher student comprehension.

source.author: Julia Hinde
source.title: Fast talkers lose their audience

advice: About 150-160 words per minute is a comfortable speed for listeners. Nervous speakers often run faster, so check a section of your talk against the clock.
quote: A comfortable speed of talking for listeners is approximately 150 – 160 words per minute.
drill: Pick a passage of about 150 words from your talk and practise until delivering it takes at least one full minute and still sounds natural.

source.title: Speaking clearly
source.publisher: The University of Melbourne, Academic Skills

advice: Measure your rate instead of guessing it. Use dictation software to transcribe one minute of your presentation, count the words, and compare the total with a benchmark (this guide lists 100-120 wpm for formal presentations). Then decide whether you need to slow down or speed up.
quote: The single biggest mistake inexperienced speakers make is speaking too fast.
drill: Turn on speech-to-text (e.g., Dictate in MS Word), deliver one minute of your talk, and count the words. Repeat after each rehearsal and log the number.

source.title: Delivering an Oral Presentation (Public Speaking)

advice: Learn your own speed-up ratio. This presenter knows she speeds up in front of an audience, so a 13.5-minute practice run becomes her 12-minute talk. Time every rehearsal, compare it with the real talk, and use that ratio to plan.
quote: when I time 13.5 minutes, I know that my actual presentation will be a perfect 12 minutes.

source.author: Iris van Zelst
source.credentials: Patience Cowie research fellow, University of Edinburgh
source.title: Presentation skills – 2. Speech
source.publisher: EGU Blogs (Geodynamics Division), European Geosciences Union

advice: If you present in a second language, adjust your speed to that language. Some languages tend to run faster than others, and this presenter suggests that matching the usual pace of the language you are speaking makes your accent less noticeable.
quote: If you match the pace of the language you are speaking, your accent will be less noticeable

source.author: Iris van Zelst
source.credentials: Patience Cowie research fellow, University of Edinburgh
source.title: Presentation skills – 2. Speech
source.publisher: EGU Blogs (Geodynamics Division), European Geosciences Union

advice: Don't slow down just by chopping your sentences up with extra pauses. In this clear-speech study (listeners with hearing loss or in noise), inserting pauses into conversational sentences lowered intelligibility, and deleting pauses from clear sentences lowered it too. Adding gaps is not a shortcut to being understood.
quote: Manipulation of pause structure reduced scores both when additional pauses were introduced into conversational sentences

source.author: Rosalie M. Uchanski, Sunkyung S. Choi, Louis D. Braida, Charlotte M. Reed, Nathaniel I. Durlach
source.title: Speaking clearly for the hard of hearing IV: Further studies of the role of speaking rate
source.publisher: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research, 39(3), 494-509

advice: When you read poetry aloud, paint each image for your listeners and give them time to picture and think about it before you move on. Don't rush past a vivid line; let it register before the next one starts.
quote: s/he must give them time to picture and think about what the poet has written.
drill: Mark the three strongest images in your piece. Read it aloud, silently counting 'one' after each image before going on, then record and check that the gaps sound intentional rather than hesitant.

source.author: Tony Figliola
source.credentials: Established a speech program at Holy Ghost Prep (PA)
source.title: Oral Interpretation of Literature: Prose and Poetry Reading
source.publisher: Rostrum (National Forensic League), via UVM Rostrum Library

advice: Picture your speaking rate as a speedometer and keep your speech below the 'speed limit'. This cluttering handout suggests visual aids like this for monitoring your rate, after first working on slowing down.
quote: Use visual aids such as a speedometer for monitoring the rate of speech.
drill: Draw a simple speedometer with a 'speed limit' mark. Have a partner point to where your speed is while you practise, and give yourself a 'ticket' each time you go over the limit.

source.author: Kevin Stuckey
source.title: Cluttering (Handy Handouts #210)

advice: When fast speech makes long words collapse, practise by exaggerating the stressed syllable in each word while still pronouncing every syllable. The aim is to learn to monitor your own speech, so you hear when syllables are being squeezed out.
quote: Have the person who clutters exaggerate stressed syllables in words and articulate all syllables.
drill: List ten long words from your speech (e.g., 'responsibility', 'particularly'). Say each three times with an exaggerated stressed syllable and every syllable clear, then once at normal delivery.

source.author: Kevin Stuckey
source.title: Cluttering (Handy Handouts #210)

advice: Even fluent speakers produce roughly six disfluencies per 100 words in spontaneous speech, more when nervous or the topic is hard. Judge your progress against that, not against perfection.

source.author: Lisa B. Marshall
source.title: Um, How Do I Stop, Ya Know, Using Um and Ah?

advice: Keep your filler reports from each speech and compare them over time to see which habits are fading.

source.author: Yue Yin
source.credentials: Professor of educational psychology, University of Illinois Chicago
source.title: Less Filler, More Substance

advice: A well-planned speech with a clear beginning, middle and end means you spend less time searching for thoughts, which cuts fillers and blanks.

source.author: Yue Yin
source.credentials: Professor of educational psychology, University of Illinois Chicago
source.title: Less Filler, More Substance

advice: Internalize your ideas instead of memorizing words. Memorizing word for word leaves no other route when one word slips.

source.author: Diane Windingland
source.title: What Was I Saying?

advice: Pauses mark where one idea ends and the next begins, standing in for punctuation your audience can't see. More complex material needs more pauses.

source.author: Andrew Dlugan
source.title: Speech Pauses: 12 Techniques to Speak Volumes with Your Silence

advice: Record and listen back to your practice runs, not just to check content, so you hear how you actually sound.

source.title: How to Overcome Your Fear of Public Speaking

advice: Practicing out loud under realistic conditions, with time signals, builds fluency far more than silent review.
drill: Ask a practice judge for time signals and deliver the full speech aloud.

source.author: Jordan Phillips
source.title: Commentary Extemp Starter Kit

advice: Slowing down and pausing improve how clearly you're understood, a principle behind rate control in fluency therapy.

source.title: Cluttering Updated

advice: If your talk sounds stiff and memorized, the fix is more rehearsal, not less. Keep going past the stage where it sounds recited until it sounds natural.
quote: When a speaker sounds too rehearsed, they're not done rehearsing.

source.title: Rehearsals (TEDx Organizer Guide)

advice: Use a loop of recording a run-through, transcribing it, editing it and running it again. Seeing your actual words on paper exposes rough spots that you miss while you're speaking.
quote: Record, transcribe, edit, repeat.

source.title: Rehearsals (TEDx Organizer Guide)

advice: Plan far more practice than feels necessary. One guideline is about an hour of rehearsal for each minute you'll speak.
quote: The optimal ratio of preparation to performance is one hour of practice for every minute of presentation.

source.author: Noah Zandan
source.credentials: CEO and co-founder of Quantified Communications
source.title: How to Stop Saying “Um,” “Ah,” and “You Know”

advice: Retelling the same talk several times reduces hesitation. In Nation's original 4/3/2 study, speakers hesitated less in each retelling and even used more complex sentences.
quote: He found that the number of hesitations decreased in the retellings, and that sentences were more complex.

source.author: N. de Jong (PI), L.K. Halderman, C.A. Perfetti
source.credentials: Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam; University of Pittsburgh
source.title: Fostering fluency in second language learning (summarizing Nation, 1989, 'Improving speaking fluency', System 17)
source.publisher: LearnLab (Pittsburgh Science of Learning Center) research wiki

advice: The 4/3/2 drill builds fluency by repeating the same talk under shrinking time. Give a talk on a familiar topic for four minutes, then again in three minutes and finally in two minutes, each time to a new listener. Vary your wording between rounds so you don't lock in mistakes.
quote: talk to a partner about a familiar topic for four minutes, then repeat the talk in three minutes
drill: Give your speech to three different listeners in 4, 3, then 2 minutes, keeping all the main points each time.

source.author: Tim Stoeckel
source.credentials: Professor, Department of International Studies and Regional Development, University of Niigata Prefecture
source.title: Repeated Reading with Retelling: A Multi-Skilled Fluency Activity
source.publisher: English Teaching Forum (U.S. Department of State)

advice: Shrinking the time limit across repetitions (4/3/2) seems to produce more durable fluency gains than repeating at the same length each time. Researchers found gains in speed and pausing that lasted on a later test.
quote: the 4/3/2 activity (repeating a monologue task with increasing time pressure) can lead to robust fluency development.

source.author: Mai Ngoc Tran, Kazuya Saito
source.title: Effects of the 4/3/2 Activity Revisited: Extending Boers (2014) and Thai & Boers (2016)
source.publisher: Language Teaching Research (accepted manuscript, UCL Discovery)

advice: When you rehearse, fix one problem at a time, and practice that single fix several times in a row before moving on to the next one.
quote: We recommend practicing one solution at a time, but doing so a few times in a row.

source.author: George Sun, Andee Wallace, Sarah Bening
source.title: Public Speaking: How to Practice Effectively

advice: Start rehearsing early and step up how often you do it as the date gets closer. TED's schedule runs from first rehearsals about four months out, to every two weeks at two months, weekly in the final month, then dress rehearsals one or two days before.
quote: The key to a great talk is to start rehearsing as early as possible.

source.title: Prepare speakers and program (TEDx Organizer Guide)

advice: Build breaks into a long rehearsal schedule. TED suggests stepping away from a talk for a week or two now and then, and taking a full break about two weeks before the event, before coming back for dress rehearsals.
quote: 2 weeks out: Take a break. (Don’t think about the talk.)

source.title: Prepare speakers and program (TEDx Organizer Guide)

advice: Rehearse with a countdown clock in front of you, and keep going until you hit your time every single run, not just once.
quote: Time yourself. Practice with the clock winding down in front of you.
drill: Set a visible countdown timer for your time limit. Run the speech until you finish within 10 seconds of the target on three runs in a row.

source.title: Speaker Guide

advice: Treat practicing aloud as editing. Saying the speech out loud is when you find the awkward phrases you'd trip over, so rewrite those lines until they come out smoothly.
quote: Practicing aloud is the 'editing' of public speaking
drill: Read your draft aloud once. Mark every spot where you stumble or restart, rewrite those sentences in simpler spoken wording, and read it again.

source.title: How Do I Work on My Public Speaking Skills to Communicate My Research?
source.publisher: Derek Bok Center for Teaching and Learning, Harvard University

advice: In extemp, spend about half of your prep time practicing the delivery, not writing. Keep a log of how you use your 30 minutes so you can see whether choosing topics or building the speech is eating into your speaking practice.
quote: Students should designate approximately 1/2 of their preparation time for practicing delivery.
drill: For your next five practice preps, note the minute you finish choosing a topic, finish outlining, and start speaking aloud. Adjust until about 15 minutes are left for delivery.

source.author: University Interscholastic League (preface by Jana Riggins, UIL State Speech Director)
source.title: Informative and Persuasive Speaking Handbook, 2024-25

advice: Work your way down to contest prep time. Beginners can start with overnight (or longer) preparation, then move to the real 30-minute limit and practice with it often, so speaking on short prep becomes routine.
quote: Initially, let students have overnight to prepare a speech, or longer if necessary.

source.author: University Interscholastic League (preface by Jana Riggins, UIL State Speech Director)
source.title: Informative and Persuasive Speaking Handbook, 2024-25

advice: Don't aim for zero hesitation. Even highly proficient and native speakers still pause and hesitate, and some hesitations help listeners get ready for complex content. Focus on the hesitations that break up your phrases, not on every pause.
quote: At higher levels of proficiency, pauses and hesitations will still occur (as in native speech).

source.author: Nivja H. De Jong
source.title: Fluency in Second Language Testing: Insights From Different Disciplines

advice: Repeating the same talk made speakers more fluent whether or not the time limit shrank, but the shrinking time limit seemed to undercut gains in accuracy. When you're trying to clean up errors, repeat at the same length rather than racing a shorter clock.
quote: Fluency improved under both task conditions

source.author: Frank Boers
source.title: A Reappraisal of the 4/3/2 Activity

advice: In repeated retellings, much of the extra smoothness came from speakers reusing exact word strings from their first version. So your first run's phrasing tends to carry over: plan your key sentences carefully before you start repeating the talk.
quote: A strikingly high amount of verbatim duplication of word strings from the participants' first version of their monologues in subsequent versions

source.author: Frank Boers
source.title: A Reappraisal of the 4/3/2 Activity

advice: The direction of the time limit changes what repetition trains. Shrinking (4-3-2) or constant (2-2-2) time improved fluency, while expanding time (2-3-4) gave more complex output at the cost of fluency and accuracy. Choose shrinking or constant time when smooth delivery is the goal.
quote: the expanding time condition leads to more complex output at the expense of fluency and accuracy

source.author: Benjamin Thanyawatpokin, Carl Vollmer
source.credentials: Ritsumeikan University; Ritsumeikan Uji Junior and Senior High School

advice: Don't count on shadowing alone to make your own off-the-cuff speech more fluent. In a small classroom study of eight learners, a semester of shadowing practice produced no significant change in speaking speed, pausing, self-corrections or filled pauses in their one-minute speeches.
quote: The results of the analysis did not show any significant improvements.

source.author: Yuka Muraoka
source.title: Shadowing and Fluency: How does Shadowing Practice Promote Fluency in the EFL classroom?
source.publisher: 恵泉女学園大学紀要 (Keisen University Bulletin), No. 29, pp. 93-112

advice: Keep practicing over long breaks. Students' speaking scores rose during the semester but plateaued or slipped over the summer, while those who kept up regular shadowing-based self-practice made small fluency gains.
quote: Mean scores improved during the spring semester but either plateaued or declined during the summer break.

source.author: Noriko Nakanishi
source.title: Temporal Dynamics of EFL Learners' Oral Proficiency: Effects of Coursework and Self-Training Using Shadowing-Based Tasks

advice: Build the stamina to keep talking with very little prep. Practice long speeches with just one minute of prep and seven minutes of speaking, and modify the format as needed for novices.
quote: 1 minute of prep, 7 minutes of speaking.
drill: Draw a random topic, prep for 1 minute, and speak for 7 minutes without stopping. Novices can shorten the speaking time and build up.

source.author: Ananth Veluvali
source.title: Extemp Drill List

advice: Separate rate, the speed of your words, from pace, the speed of your ideas. Pacing is about how much time you give each segment of the talk. Time each section and aim for roughly equal time on each main idea.
quote: Rate refers to the speed of words, whereas pace refers to the speed of ideas (the overall pace of talk).
drill: During a timed run-through, have a partner note the clock time when you start the introduction and each main point, then compare the durations.

source.title: Delivery

advice: Short, frequent practice beats long, rare sessions. Recording yourself for about 10 minutes a day helps more than one 2-hour session a week, and listening back right away and again a day later helps you catch problems.
quote: You will improve more quickly if you record yourself 10 minutes per day than if you try to do 2 hours once a week
drill: For one week, record a 10-minute talk on a topic from your speech every day. Listen once immediately and once 24 hours later, noting each stop inside a sentence.

source.title: Pronunciation Strategies: Improve Your Spoken English

advice: In this study of spontaneous speech, the points where independent judges agreed a new semantic unit began tended to coincide with the start of a new temporal cycle of speech and silence, and those units often spanned several clauses and more than one sentence. Plan your talk as multi-sentence idea chunks rather than sentence by sentence.
quote: It is argued that a theory of speech generation must contain provision for semantic integration at the suprasentential level.

source.author: B. Butterworth
source.title: Hesitation and semantic planning in speech

advice: Check yourself again a few weeks after training. In one study, nine social-work students, divided into three small groups, learned to notice their disfluencies and use a replacement response. All of them cut disfluencies, and 2.5 to 6 weeks later, six of the nine were at least 80% below their starting rate. Re-record yourself to see whether your own gains are holding.
quote: At follow-up 2.5 to 6 weeks after training, six of nine participants achieved a reduction of at least 80 percent from baseline.
drill: Three to six weeks after a practice block ends, record a fresh 3-minute talk and compare its fillers per minute with your very first recording.

source.author: Anja Göhring, Christoph Bördlein
source.credentials: Technical University of Applied Sciences Würzburg-Schweinfurt (THWS)
source.title: Using Brief Habit Reversal to Decrease Speech Disfluencies in Public Speaking. A Systematic Replication

advice: Match a replacement action to each habit. In habit-reversal studies covered by one review, speakers practised a 3-second silent pause in place of 'um' or 'uh', held the tongue still in a set position for 3 seconds instead of a tongue click, and started the sentence again without 'like' when 'like' was misused.
quote: 3–second silent pause for filled pauses; placing the tongue in a certain position and holding for 3 seconds for tongue clicks
drill: Pick one habit. In a 3-minute practice talk, each time you catch an 'um' starting, stop and stay silent for a slow count of three, then go on.

source.author: Pauline Menjot, Lamia Bettahi, Anne-Lise Leclercq, Nancy Durieux, Angélique Remacle
source.title: Interventions That Target or Affect Voice or Speech Production During Public Speaking: A Scoping Review

advice: Don't expect general delivery training to cut your fillers. In one study, four speakers trained online in public-speaking behaviours improved those behaviours, and an expert rated them as more effective speakers, yet their rate of disfluencies didn't change. If fillers are your problem, give them their own targeted practice.
quote: Although remote video-based BST was effective for all participants, it did not produce a change in the rate of speech disfluencies.

source.author: Matthew M. Laske, Florence D. DiGennaro Reed
source.title: The efficacy of remote video-based training on public speaking

advice: Cutting fillers is not the whole job. In a small study, online awareness training reduced two speakers' disfluencies, but expert ratings of how effective they were did not improve, and some got worse. Ratings did rise after separate training in broader public-speaking behaviours, using speech outlines. Work on fillers alongside your other delivery skills.
quote: Although expert ratings of perceived public speaking effectiveness improved following BST, the ratings did not improve and some worsened following AT.

source.author: Matthew M. Laske, Florence D. DiGennaro Reed, J. Turner B. Braren
source.title: The efficacy of remote video-based behavioral skills training and awareness training on public speaking performance

advice: Start counting before you start fixing. In a small replication with four social-work students, three were already using fewer filled pauses during the baseline phase, before any training began. Log your fillers per minute from your very first recording, so you can see what is really changing, and when.
quote: three of the four participants showed a decrease in response frequency already during the baseline.
drill: Record a 2-minute talk on three separate days before trying any technique, and write down your fillers per minute each time.

source.author: Christoph Bördlein, Anja Sander
source.title: Habit Reversal to Decrease Filled Pauses in Public Speaking: A Partial Replication

advice: Train your filler habits for online talks too. In a small thesis study, three graduate students received awareness training over a video call. Their targeted disfluencies in virtual speeches dropped and stayed low for two weeks and with a small audience, and two kept a low rate in a talk at a professional seminar.
quote: two participants maintained a low rate of speech disfluencies during a speech delivered during a professional seminar.
drill: Give a 3-minute talk to a friend over a video-call app, count your fillers per minute, and compare with the same talk given in person.

source.author: Jason Alexander Church
source.credentials: M.A. thesis, Applied Behavioral Science, University of Kansas
source.title: Reduction of Speech Disfluencies Through Online Awareness Training

advice: An instant cue may help more than a report afterwards. In one study, 24 university participants had six daily 25-minute conversations with either a sound from smart glasses each time they said an unwanted word (such as a filler) or an app that reviewed the talk afterwards. Both helped. Eight days after training ended, the instant-cue group did better, about 40% below its starting rate.
quote: Both approaches were effective in reducing the occurrence of unwanted words, but WSCoach appears to be more effective in the long run.
drill: For six days in a row, hold a 20-minute conversation in which a partner taps the table the moment you say a filler. A week later, record one conversation with no taps and count.

source.author: Youpeng Zhang, Nuwan Janaka, Ashwin Ram, Peilin Yin, Yang Tian, Shengdong Zhao, Pierre Dragicevic
source.credentials: City University of Hong Kong, with National University of Singapore, Saarland University, Zhejiang University, Guangxi University and Inria
source.title: WSCoach: Wearable Real-time Auditory Feedback for Reducing Unwanted Words in Daily Communication
source.publisher: Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies

advice: Expect live filler alerts to feel distracting at first. In one study, an instant sound cue was rated more distracting than an app that reviewed talks afterwards, but most users got used to it within a few days, though not everyone did. If a live cue keeps breaking your train of thought, switch to reviewing recordings afterwards, which also cut unwanted words in that study.
quote: Although it initially caused some distraction, most adapted within three sessions, after which the distraction became negligible.

source.author: Youpeng Zhang, Nuwan Janaka, Ashwin Ram, Peilin Yin, Yang Tian, Shengdong Zhao, Pierre Dragicevic
source.credentials: City University of Hong Kong, with National University of Singapore, Saarland University, Zhejiang University, Guangxi University and Inria
source.title: WSCoach: Wearable Real-time Auditory Feedback for Reducing Unwanted Words in Daily Communication
source.publisher: Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies

advice: Try practising with a live signal. In one classroom study, helpers dropped a penny in a jar right after each 'um', 'uh', 'like' or 'you know', and those students used fewer fillers in their first speech than classes with no live signal. Pennies for speaking too fast worked about as well, and neither raised speech anxiety or lowered how competent students felt.
quote: immediate feedback effectively reduces filler word use during speeches in initial exposures and does not adversely impact state and trait anxiety
drill: During a 2-minute practice talk, have a friend drop a coin into a cup right after each 'um', 'uh', 'like' or 'you know'.

source.author: Michael Hazel, Colleen McMahon, Nancy Schmidt
source.title: Immediate Feedback: A Means of Reducing Distracting Filler Words during Public Speeches

advice: Fillers can be catching. In an experiment with 100 public-speaking students, those who heard a sample speech full of 'um' and 'uh' just before giving their own used more fillers themselves, without noticing. Just before you practise or present, listen to a filler-free speaker rather than one full of fillers.
quote: Students who heard a speech with excessive vocal fillers used more vocal fillers in their own speech.
drill: If you warm up by listening to a model talk before a practice run, pick two minutes of a fluent speaker who rarely says 'um', then record yourself straight away.

source.author: W. Benjamin Myers, Theresa A. Wadkins
source.credentials: University of Toledo; University of Nebraska at Kearney
source.title: Vocal Fillers, Contagion Effects, and, um, Overlooked Pedagogical Opportunities in the, uh, Public Speaking Classroom

advice: If a friend or an app signals your fillers, agree first on what the signal means. In one small experiment, a tone, a light or a word given right after each speech stumble did nothing for three of four volunteers until they were told what it marked. Then their disfluencies dropped substantially.
