quote: When the contingency was pointed out to these subjects through instructions, however, presentation of the stimuli was then followed by substantial reductions in disfluencies.
drill: Before a practice talk, tell your partner: 'Tap the table once each time I say um or uh.' Repeat the rule back so you both know exactly what the tap means.

source.author: Gerald M. Siegel, Bruce Hanson
source.title: The Effect of Response-Contingent Neutral Stimuli on Normal Speech Disfluency
source.publisher: Journal of Speech and Hearing Research

advice: Begin each practice by deciding to cut your fillers and stumbles. In a 1960s study of college students reading aloud, one group was simply asked to reduce their disfluencies, with no feedback or reward, and their disfluencies dropped markedly. A clear intention costs nothing, so state it before every run-through.
quote: Instructions to one group of subjects to decrease disfluencies resulted in a marked attenuation of the response, even though no contingencies were arranged.
drill: Before each recording, say out loud: 'This time I pause instead of saying um.' Now and then record one run without saying it and compare the two filler counts.

source.author: Gerald M. Siegel, Richard R. Martin
source.title: Punishment of Disfluencies in Normal Speakers
source.publisher: Journal of Speech and Hearing Research

advice: Live correction seems to help most when you stumble a lot. In a study of 59 college adults speaking freely, hearing 'wrong' in an earphone after each disfluency significantly cut disfluencies for those who had many, but not for those who already had few. Speaking rate stayed stable. If your filler count is already low, this kind of drill may add little.
quote: A significant (p < 0.05) decrease in disfluencies was obtained from Baseline to Treatment for high level Contingent subjects.

source.author: Gerald M. Siegel, Richard R. Martin
source.title: Verbal Punishment of Disfluencies During Spontaneous Speech

advice: A reminder works best when it follows an actual filler. In one study, hearing 'wrong' right after each disfluency cut disfluencies sharply, while the same word played at random times had no significant effect. Disfluencies rose again once the cue stopped, so end each practice with a few cue-free minutes to check what sticks.
quote: Contingent presentation resulted in a sharp decrease in disfluencies during Segment 2, and an increase in disfluencies during Segment 3.
drill: Practise for 5 minutes with a partner tapping after each filler, then 3 minutes with no taps. Count fillers in each part separately.

source.author: Gerald M. Siegel, Richard R. Martin
source.title: Verbal Punishment of Disfluencies in Normal Speakers
source.publisher: Journal of Speech and Hearing Research

advice: Try a points game: start with points and lose one for each filler or stumble. In one study, five college students spoke over 10 to 17 sessions, and during the penalty phase each disfluency cost a penny, shown on a screen. Four cut their disfluencies to very low levels, the change mostly held after the penalty stopped, and it partly carried over to reading aloud.
quote: Disfluencies were suppressed and kept at very low levels for four of the subjects during the punishment procedures, and there was general resistance to extinction.
drill: Start each 5-minute practice talk with 20 points and lose one for every 'um', 'uh' or repeated word. Log your score daily and try to keep more points each time.

source.author: Gerald M. Siegel, Joanne Lenske, Patricia Broen
source.title: Suppression of normal speech disfluencies through response cost

advice: Try a 'time-out' drill in practice: after each filler or stumble, stop and stay silent for 10 seconds before going on. In one small study, three adults speaking freely had to fall silent for 10 seconds after each disfluency, across 14 sessions, and all three cut disfluencies almost to zero early on and stayed there. Keep it for practice: 10 seconds is long in a real talk.
quote: disfluency rate reduced essentially to zero during the early treatment sessions and remained at that low level throughout the experiment.
drill: In a 5-minute practice talk, have a partner raise a hand at each 'um' or false start (or catch them yourself); each time, stop, count silently to ten, then carry on.

source.author: Richard R. Martin, Kamala Rangaswamy
source.title: The Effects of Time-Out From Speaking on the Disfluency Rates of Normal Speakers

advice: Practise as if it counts. In one study of 40 college adults, people were most disfluent in the situations they rated least important, and stumbled more in casual conversation than when talking to a TV camera as if to an audience. The authors suggest that caring more made them monitor their speech more closely. Treat each practice run as a real talk, not a casual chat.
quote: It appeared that as subjects became more concerned about their speech, they monitored it more carefully and thus became more fluent.

source.author: Patricia A. Broen, Gerald M. Siegel
source.title: Variations in Normal Speech Disfluencies

advice: Silent stops seem to count more than 'um's when listeners rate your fluency. A review of 22 second-language studies found that how often learners paused silently was strongly linked to lower fluency ratings, while how often they said 'uh' or 'um' was only weakly linked. Pauses inside a clause showed the strongest link in the few studies that checked. Work on mid-sentence silent stops before chasing every 'um'.
quote: The effect size of silent pauses approached large (r = –.57), while that of filled pauses was regarded as being small (r = –.24).
drill: Record a one-minute answer. Count silent stops inside sentences and 'um's separately, then redo it aiming to cut the silent mid-sentence stops first.

source.author: Shungo Suzuki, Judit Kormos, Takumi Uchihara
source.title: The Relationship Between Utterance and Perceived Fluency: A Meta-Analysis of Correlational Studies

advice: Your 'um's in a new language may partly be your personal style. In a study of 51 adult learners of Dutch, how often each person said 'uh' or 'um' in their first language strongly predicted how often they did so in Dutch. Record yourself in your first language as a baseline. The authors even speculate that becoming more fluent may mean changing how you speak in every language.
quote: It was found that all fluency measures could, to a certain extent, be predicted on the basis of L1 fluency behavior
drill: Tell the same one-minute story in your first language and in English, count the fillers in each, and compare your English count with your own first-language baseline.

source.author: Nivja H. De Jong, Rachel Groenhout, Rob Schoonen, Jan H. Hulstijn
source.title: Second language fluency: Speaking style or proficiency? Correcting measures of second language fluency for first language behavior

advice: A hesitation helps listeners remember only the word right after it. In four experiments, three kinds of hesitation each made a word more memorable, but only when the hesitation came immediately before that word at the end of the sentence. Put your key word last, and if you need a beat, take it right before that word rather than earlier in the sentence.
quote: only manifesting when the disfluency immediately preceded a critical memory probe word at the end of the sentence
drill: Write three sentences that end with your key term. Say each one with a short silent beat just before the key term, then without the beat, and listen back.

source.author: Evgeniia Diachek, Sarah Brown-Schmidt
source.title: The effect of disfluency on memory for what was said
source.publisher: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition

advice: A short silence can do an 'um's job for your listener. In a brain-recording study, a silent pause before a word changed how listeners processed it much as 'er' had in earlier work, and in a surprise memory test they recognised words heard after silent pauses more often. Before an important or unexpected word, try a brief silent pause instead of a filler.
quote: listeners were more likely to recognise words which had been encountered after silent pauses
drill: Read a paragraph aloud and underline two key words. Before each, pause silently for about half a second instead of saying 'um'.

source.author: Lucy J. MacGregor, Martin Corley, David I. Donaldson
source.title: Listening to the sound of silence: disfluent silent pauses in speech have consequences for listeners

advice: Don't add 'um's on purpose to make your points stick. An earlier English study found that fillers helped listeners recall a story, but two web-based follow-ups could not repeat this: German listeners remembered the fluent version better, and English listeners showed no reliable difference. Treat any memory benefit from fillers as uncertain.
quote: Our results could not replicate the findings of the original study: in fact, the opposite effect was found for German.

source.author: Beeke Muhlack, Mikey Elmers, Heiner Drenhaus, Jürgen Trouvain, Marjolein van Os, Raphael Werner, Margarita Ryzhova, Bernd Möbius
source.title: Revisiting Recall Effects of Filler Particles in German and English

advice: When you mention something again, say it smoothly. In an eye-tracking experiment, a hesitant 'thee, uh...' before a noun drew listeners toward an object that had not been mentioned yet, while a fluent 'the' drew them toward the one already mentioned. A hesitation before a familiar item can briefly send listeners looking for something new.
quote: with a disfluent article, they were biased toward an object that had not been mentioned
drill: Retell a short story in which the same person or object comes up several times. Say every repeat mention with no 'uh' before it.

source.author: Jennifer E. Arnold, Michael K. Tanenhaus, Rebecca J. Altmann, Maria Fagnano
source.title: The Old and Thee, uh, New

advice: A pause or 'um' can make a true statement sound like a lie. In a two-person guessing game, listeners treated statements containing pauses, filled or silent, as untruthful, yet speakers who paused were actually more likely to be telling the truth. When being believed matters, prepare your key facts so you can state them without hesitating.
quote: When producing false statements, speakers are less likely to produce the cues that listeners associate with lying.
drill: Write down three facts you will need to state in an interview or meeting, and say each one aloud in one smooth go, five times.

source.author: Jia E. Loy, Hannah Rohde, Martin Corley
source.title: Cues to Lying May be Deceptive: Speaker and Listener Behaviour in an Interactive Game of Deception

advice: Hesitations can cancel out a strong argument. In a listening experiment on a topic that mattered to listeners, messages containing hesitations, hedges or tag questions produced less favourable attitudes and worse views of the speaker, and strong arguments were no more persuasive than weak ones once any of these markers was present. Rehearse your best points until they come out without hesitation.
quote: strong arguments were no more persuasive than weak arguments when the message contained any of these markers
drill: Pick your strongest point and say it five times, until you can deliver it with no 'uh' or 'um' before or inside it.

source.author: Kevin L. Blankenship, Thomas Holtgraves
source.title: The Role of Different Markers of Linguistic Powerlessness in Persuasion
source.publisher: Journal of Language and Social Psychology

advice: In mock job interviews, fewer fillers went with better ratings. In an analysis of 138 recorded mock interviews with university students, scored by independent raters, candidates who spoke more fluently and used fewer filler words such as 'uh', 'umm' and 'like' tended to be rated as better candidates. Practise your answers to common interview questions until they come out with few fillers.
quote: our framework recommends to speak more fluently, use fewer filler words
drill: Record your answer to 'Tell me about yourself', count the fillers, and re-record until the count drops.

source.author: Iftekhar Naim, Md. Iftekhar Tanveer, Daniel Gildea, Mohammed Ehsan Hoque
source.title: Automated Analysis and Prediction of Job Interview Performance

advice: If 'like' is your habit, cut it first. In a simulated hiring study, 176 students and professionals saw an interviewee who overused 'like' as less professional and were least likely to want to hire or recommend them, compared with versions using 'uh' or neither. In an interview, overusing 'like' may cost you more than 'uh' does.
quote: less likely to recommend the interviewee for hiring if the interviewee overused the word "like" compared to "uh" or control
drill: Record a two-minute interview answer and count 'like' and 'uh' separately. Work on 'like' first.

source.author: Brenda Russell, Jenna Perkins, Heather Grinnell
source.title: Interviewees' Overuse of the Word “Like” and Hesitations: Effects in Simulated Hiring Decisions

advice: When you mean yes, start with yes. In a collection of recorded phone calls, replies to invitations, offers and requests began with 'um' or 'uhm' far more often when they were refusals (19.4%) than when they were acceptances (5.7%). Starting a yes with 'um' may make it sound like a no is coming, so lead with your answer.
quote: the frequency of nonlexical hesitations particles “u(h)m” is greater in dispreferred actions than in preferred actions (19.4% and 5.7%, respectively)
drill: Have a partner ask you quick requests ('Can you join us on Friday?'). Answer each with 'Yes, ...' or 'Sure, ...' immediately, with no 'um' first.

source.author: Kobin H. Kendrick, Francisco Torreira
source.title: The Timing and Construction of Preference: A Quantitative Study

advice: In one small study, 'um' marked planning what to say next more than hunting for words. When 15 students retold a story, fillers were far more likely just before a new sentence or story event, and unlike silent pauses they were not tied to rarer words. If your 'um's cluster where sentences or new points begin, focus on planning your next idea rather than on vocabulary.
quote: fillers and silent pauses occurred most when difficult material was still being planned. Fillers were associated only with conceptual difficulties
drill: Retell a film or a book chapter from a list of its main events. Afterwards, mark each 'um': did it come where a new sentence or event began, or in the middle of one?

source.author: Scott H. Fraundorf, Duane G. Watson
source.title: Alice's adventures in um-derland: psycholinguistic sources of variation in disfluency production

advice: Topic changes are filler hot spots. In descriptions spoken by two Dutch speakers, 50 of 64 phrases that opened a new paragraph-sized section contained a filled pause, against 176 of 438 phrases elsewhere. Plan the first sentence of each new point before you reach it, so you can start it cleanly.
quote: 50 out of 64 phrases following a strong boundary have one or more FPs, compared with only 176 out of 438 following a weak one
drill: List your talk's main points and write the opening sentence of each. Practise only the transitions: finish one point, then say the next opening sentence with no 'um'.

source.author: Marc Swerts, Anne Wichmann, Robbert-Jan Beun
source.credentials: Institute for Perception Research (IPO), Eindhoven; University of Central Lancashire
source.title: Filled pauses as markers of discourse structure
source.publisher: Proceedings of the 4th International Conference on Spoken Language Processing (ICSLP 96), ISCA

advice: 'Um's may rise when you start watching your own speech. In two experiments, making speakers feel evaluated or self-conscious sharply increased their 'um's. The authors link 'um' to paying close attention to your own words, not simply to nerves. When you practise, keep your attention on your listener and your message rather than checking each word as you say it.
quote: anxiety may increase ums not when it makes the speech task harder but when it causes the speaker to pay attention to the speech

source.author: Nicholas Christenfeld, Beth Creager
source.title: Anxiety, alcohol, aphasia, and ums
source.publisher: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

advice: An accent doesn't stop an 'uh' from helping your listener. In a Dutch study with scripted stories, listeners were better at remembering a word that came right after an 'uh', and this held for a highly proficient non-native speaker with a clear accent as well as for a native speaker. So a single 'uh' need not throw you: carry on rather than stopping to apologise.
quote: We observed beneficial effects of both native and non-native disfluencies on listeners’ recall accuracy

source.author: Hans Rutger Bosker, Jade Tjiong, Hugo Quené, Ted Sanders, Nivja H. de Jong
source.credentials: Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics, Nijmegen; UiL OTS, Utrecht University
source.title: Both native and non-native disfluencies trigger listeners’ attention
source.publisher: Disfluency in Spontaneous Speech: DiSS 2015, an ICPhS Satellite Meeting (Edinburgh)

advice: Listeners may read your 'uh' differently if you have an accent. In a Dutch eye-tracking study, a native speaker's 'uh' made listeners expect a less common object, but a closely matched 'uh' from a non-native speaker did not. So with an accent, an 'uh' before a rare word may give listeners less of a hint. Practise the less common words you need until you can say them smoothly.
quote: when participants listened to disfluent non-native speech, no anticipation of low-frequency referents was observed
drill: List five less common words you need for your topic and say each one in a full sentence until it comes out without an 'uh' before it.

source.author: Hans Rutger Bosker, Hugo Quené, Ted Sanders, Nivja H. de Jong
source.credentials: Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics; Utrecht Institute of Linguistics OTS, Utrecht University
source.title: Native ‘um’s elicit prediction of low-frequency referents, but non-native ‘um’s do not

advice: A ready-made phrase can help you through a planning moment. In a four-week course for university English learners, one class was taught to notice their pausing, use time-buying words such as 'well' and 'let me think', and avoid needless self-corrections. That class gained more in speed and in run length between pauses than a class without this training, though the phrases were only one part of it.
quote: using lexical fillers (e.g. well) and longer lexical chunks (e.g. let me think) and practising them in conversations
drill: Pick two time-buying phrases, such as 'let me think' and 'the main point is'. Answer five unexpected questions, using a phrase instead of a long silence or an 'um' while you plan.

source.author: Parvaneh Tavakoli, Colin Campbell, Joan McCormack
source.title: Development of Speech Fluency Over a Short Period of Time: Effects of Pedagogic Intervention

advice: Expect more 'uh' and 'um' when the situation feels formal. In a large corpus, speakers who retold the same car accident used more filled pauses in a voice message to the police than in one to a friend, in English, German and Russian alike. Rehearse the formal version of what you need to say, not just the casual one.
quote: Overall the FP frequency was higher in the formal compared to the informal situations in all languages
drill: Explain the same event twice: once as a voice message to a friend, once as a message to an official. Compare the filler counts and practise the formal version.

source.author: Marlene Böttcher, Margaret Zellers
source.title: Do you say uh or uhm? A cross-linguistic approach to filler particle use in heritage and majority speakers across three languages

advice: Abandoning a sentence partway costs listeners more than repeating a word. In listening experiments with natural speech, words right after a false start took listeners longer to pick out, while words after a spontaneous repeat did not. In the Dutch tests this happened only when the false start came mid-sentence; in the English test, early false starts slowed listeners too. Settle how a sentence will run before you start.
quote: False starts in the middle of a sentence cause more processing trouble than false starts in the beginning, and repetitions cause no trouble at all.
drill: Record a one-minute answer and mark each sentence you abandoned partway. Redo it, taking a silent beat before each sentence so any change of plan happens before you start speaking.

source.author: Jean E. Fox Tree
source.title: The Effects of False Starts and Repetitions on the Processing of Subsequent Words in Spontaneous Speech

advice: When you work on restarts, tackle false starts first. In one listening study with computer-generated sentences, 40 listeners rated a speaker who began a phrase and then switched wording ('is known, um, is called') as less competent than one who repeated a small word ('the, um, the') or a short phrase ('is called, um, is called'). The researchers suggest that cutting false starts may help you sound more competent.
quote: False starts were found to have the greatest negative impact
drill: In a recording, count false starts (switching words mid-phrase) separately from simple repeats. On the next take, aim to cut the false starts first.

source.author: Ambika Kirkland, Marcin Włodarczak, Joakim Gustafson, Éva Székely
source.credentials: KTH Royal Institute of Technology; Stockholm University
source.title: Evaluating the Impact of Disfluencies on the Perception of Speaker Competence Using Neural Speech Synthesis
source.publisher: Proceedings of the 20th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences (ICPhS 2023), Prague

advice: If you expect to stumble, a brief, honest apology for being nervous may soften how listeners judge your repeated words. In a small listening experiment with computer-generated lecture clips, repeated words made the speaker seem less competent, but when each clip included a short apology for being anxious, that drop in competence ratings largely disappeared. This is one study with synthetic voices, so treat it as an option.
quote: When participants heard that the speaker was anxious about giving a lecture, the effect of repetitions on competence was eliminated

source.author: Ambika Kirkland, Joakim Gustafson, Éva Székely
source.credentials: Division of Speech, Music & Hearing, KTH Royal Institute of Technology
source.title: Pardon my disfluency: The impact of disfluency effects on the perception of speaker competence and confidence

advice: When you correct a wrong word, try stressing the new word, as in 'turn left, er, RIGHT'. Among self-corrections by Dutch speakers describing colored patterns, about half of the fixes for real errors were stressed this way (72% for opposites like left and right), against 19% of fixes that only refined a word that wasn't wrong. The authors see this stress as marking the old word as rejected.
quote: repairs were marked when the original utterance had been actually erroneous, rather than simply less appropriate than the repair
drill: Describe a route aloud and plant three deliberate slips, such as 'the red, er, the BLUE door'. Practise stressing each corrected word clearly, then carry straight on.

source.author: Willem J. M. Levelt, Anne Cutler
source.title: Prosodic Marking in Speech Repair

advice: Repeated words are something listeners notice. In one study, native and advanced non-native English listeners rated and commented on learners narrating picture stories; pausing, self-repetition, speech rate and fillers made up three-quarters of their negative timing-related comments. So work on repeats like 'I I think' or 'the the' alongside your pauses.
quote: Pausing, self-repetition, speech rate, and fillers accounted for three-quarters of the negative temporal impressions recorded by listeners
drill: Play back one minute of a recording and tally your repeated words. Re-record the same minute, aiming to say each word once, and compare the tallies.

source.author: Marian J. Rossiter
source.title: Perceptions of L2 Fluency by Native and Non-native Speakers of English

advice: Decide in advance what you'll call the key things you mention, especially things with more than one possible name. In a Dutch experiment where people described networks of pictures, pictures that people tend to name in different ways led to more pauses and more self-corrections than pictures with one obvious name. The authors conclude that trouble finding a word can itself cause disfluencies.
quote: there were more pauses and more self-corrections in the low name agreement condition than the high name agreement condition
drill: Before a practice talk, list the five or six things you'll mention most and pick one name for each. Stick to those names during the run.

source.author: Robert J. Hartsuiker, Lies Notebaert
source.title: Lexical Access Problems Lead to Disfluencies in Speech

advice: Sort your restarts into two kinds: corrections fix a wrong word or form; false starts drop a fine phrase to say it another way. In 2-minute talks by 56 learners of English, lower-intermediate speakers paused silently inside corrections more often than advanced speakers, but not inside false starts. The authors suggest false starts may reflect momentary trouble shaping the idea, so planning ideas may help more than grammar work.
quote: This suggests that false starts depend less on proficiency level, and may reflect temporary problems with conceptual encoding
drill: In a transcript of your talk, mark each restart C (fixing a wrong word or form) or F (dropping a fine phrase to say it another way). If F's dominate, note your next point's key words before each section and try again.

source.author: Simon A. Williams, Malgorzata Korko
source.credentials: University of Sussex; University of Middlesex
source.title: Pause behavior within reformulations and the proficiency level of second language learners of English

advice: Compare your restart count only across recordings of the same kind of task. In a study of 42 university learners of English in Barcelona, self-corrections differed between task types, rose when route directions involved many similar-looking landmarks, and barely differed between weaker and stronger learners. On that harder route, learners made fewer errors while correcting themselves more, which the author reads as closer attention to accuracy.
quote: Results show an overall effect of Task Complexity on self-repairs behavior across task types, with different behaviors existing among the three task types.
drill: Log the task type with each recording (story, directions, opinion) and compare restart counts only within the same type, week to week.

source.author: Roger Gilabert
source.title: Effects of manipulating task complexity on self-repairs during L2 oral production
source.publisher: IRAL - International Review of Applied Linguistics in Language Teaching

advice: Record yourself telling the same kind of story in your first language too. In a study of 58 adult learners of English, how often they corrected themselves in English was predicted by how often they did so in their first language, together with attention control, while English proficiency did not predict it. So part of your restart count may be personal style, not a language gap.
quote: while proficiency was not a significant predictor of L2 self-repair behavior, attentional control and L1 repair frequency together explained 40% of the variance
drill: Tell the same two-minute story in your first language and in English, count self-corrections in each, and use the first-language count as a rough baseline.

source.author: Michael Zuniga, Daphnée Simard
source.title: Factors Influencing L2 Self-repair Behavior: The Role of L2 Proficiency, Attentional Control and L1 Self-repair Behavior

advice: A rise in self-corrections during practice is not always a bad sign. In a three-day practice study with 50 Japanese university learners of English, those with stronger attention control and memory for speech sounds corrected themselves more afterwards. Many corrections fixed small forms, like 'help' to 'helped', and the author tentatively reads the rise as closer self-monitoring. Judge a rise by what you fix, not only by the count.
quote: It is thus tentatively argued that the increase in repair frequency may be a sign of positive L2 developmental change
drill: After a practice session, list each self-correction and what it fixed: a word ending, a word choice, or a whole phrase. If most are quick fixes of word forms, a higher count may reflect closer checking rather than worse speaking.

source.author: Yuichi Suzuki
source.title: Individual differences in memory predict changes in breakdown and repair fluency but not speed fluency: A short-term fluency training intervention study

advice: Don't do all your practice runs back to back. In a classroom study with Japanese university learners of English, telling the same story six times in a row cut pauses the most, but right afterwards those learners repeated words more often on a new story. Splitting the runs with about 45 minutes of other activity reduced that. Spread your repeats across the day or week.
quote: inserting other activities for periods as short as 45 minutes can reduce the drawbacks of massed repetition
drill: Plan six run-throughs of a two-minute talk as three in the morning and three in the evening, with other work in between, instead of six in a row.

source.author: Yuichi Suzuki, Keiko Hanzawa
source.credentials: Kanagawa University; Tokyo University of Science
source.title: Massed Task Repetition Is a Double-Edged Sword for Fluency Development: An EFL Classroom Study

advice: Collect ready-made four- and five-word phrases for things you often talk about, such as 'I agree with the idea', and practise saying them aloud. In a study of 50 Japanese university learners of English, those who used more of these longer, tightly linked phrases repaired their speech less often. It's a link, not proof of cause.
quote: This indicates that as participants produce more four-five-word MI sequences, they repair their speech less frequently.
drill: Write five four- or five-word phrases you could use on your next topic, such as 'the main reason is that'. Say each aloud several times, then use them in a one-minute talk.

source.author: Dan Hougham, Jon Clenton, Takumi Uchihara
source.title: Disentangling the contributions of shorter vs. longer lexical bundles to L2 oral fluency

advice: When you have to speak on an unfamiliar topic, take time to plan first. In a study of second-language speakers, both planning time and a familiar topic made speech more fluent; planning helped more and across more measures, and having planning time helped make up for not knowing the topic well.
quote: The availability of planning time also helped to compensate for lack of content familiarity.
drill: Pick a topic you know little about. Jot down key points and words first, then talk for two minutes; compare with an unplanned try on a similar topic.

source.author: Gavin Bui, Zeping Huang
source.credentials: Hang Seng Management College, Hong Kong; Hong Kong Baptist University
source.title: L2 fluency as influenced by content familiarity and planning: Performance, measurement, and pedagogy

advice: Even one minute of planning before you speak can help. In a small study of 31 learners of German, accuracy improved with just 1 minute of planning but not with more, while fluency grew with longer planning (groups had 1, 5 or 10 minutes). Use a minute to settle your first points; take longer when smooth flow matters most.
quote: Accuracy of speech improved with only 1 minute planning but did not increase with more planning time.
drill: Before your next practice answer, set a one-minute timer to note your opening point and two supporting points, then speak.

source.author: Uta Mehnert
source.title: The Effects of Different Lengths of Time for Planning on Second Language Performance

advice: How often you stop may matter more to listeners than how long each stop lasts. Pooling 22 studies of second-language speech, researchers found fluency ratings were linked more closely to how often speakers paused than to how long their pauses were, and pauses inside clauses showed the strongest links. So count your mid-sentence stops and work on bringing that number down.
quote: Perceived fluency was strongly associated with speed and pause frequency, r = |.59–.62|; moderately with pause duration, r = |.46|
drill: Record a one-minute answer and mark every silent stop inside a sentence. Re-record the same answer three times, trying to lower that count each time.

source.author: Shungo Suzuki, Judit Kormos, Takumi Uchihara
source.title: The Relationship Between Utterance and Perceived Fluency: A Meta-Analysis of Correlational Studies

advice: Listeners may judge your fluency partly by how long your pauses last, even when that says little about your vocabulary. In a study of learners of Dutch, the average length of their pauses inside sentences was not linked to their vocabulary scores, but it was clearly linked to how fluent listeners rated them. So pause length is worth working on even if your vocabulary is strong.
quote: The correlations between log duration of pauses and perceived fluency, on the other hand, are always much higher
drill: Find the three longest stops in a recording, note the word or idea you were reaching for each time, and rehearse those spots until you can say them without the gap.

source.author: Nivja H. De Jong, Hans Rutger Bosker
source.credentials: Utrecht Institute of Linguistics OTS, The Netherlands
source.title: Choosing a threshold for silent pauses to measure second language fluency
source.publisher: Proceedings of Disfluency in Spontaneous Speech, DiSS 2013 (ISCA Archive; TMH-QPSR 54(1), pp. 17-20)

advice: Not every pause is a problem. In one study of 32 people taking an English speaking test, rated from elementary (A2) to advanced (C1), the number of silent pauses at clause ends was about the same at every level, though the lowest level's pauses were longer. Pauses inside clauses were more frequent at the two lower levels. So focus on cutting mid-clause stops and keeping clause-end pauses short.
quote: The number of end-clause silent pauses did not distinguish the different levels
drill: In a recording, label each stop as end-of-clause or mid-clause. Rehearse the phrases where the mid-clause stops happen, and check that the end-of-clause ones stay short.

source.author: Parvaneh Tavakoli, Fumiyo Nakatsuhara, Ann-Marie Hunter
source.credentials: University of Reading (Tavakoli); University of Bedfordshire (Nakatsuhara); University of Leeds (Hunter)
source.title: Aspects of Fluency Across Assessed Levels of Speaking Proficiency

advice: Expect your pauses to change more slowly than your speed. In a four-week study with 37 university English learners, the group given extra fluency training ended up speaking faster and in longer stretches between pauses, but the number and length of their silent pauses barely changed. Keep tracking your pauses over a longer stretch of practice, and don't give up when they lag behind.
quote: the development of breakdown fluency, i.e. silence and pausing, is slower and less sensitive to pedagogic intervention
drill: Retell a short picture story and record it. Listen back and mark where your speech broke down, then record the same story again. The learners in this study did this kind of task as weekly homework.

source.author: Parvaneh Tavakoli, Colin Campbell, Joan McCormack
source.title: Development of Speech Fluency Over a Short Period of Time: Effects of Pedagogic Intervention

advice: Languages can differ in pausing habits, so model your pauses on fluent English speakers, not your first language. In a study of 30 Russian speakers of English, the more advanced group had matched the length of their English pauses to the native norm, though even they paused more often in English than in Russian. The author suggests following the target language's pausing norms may make speech sound more fluent.
quote: adherence to the target language pausing norms may lead to the perception of nonnative speech as more fluent and nativelike
drill: Shadow one minute of a fluent English speaker talking informally, copying where and how long they pause. Then record your own version of the same content and compare the pauses.

source.author: Anastasia Riazantseva
source.title: Second Language Proficiency and Pausing: A Study of Russian Speakers of English

advice: To make a key word stand out, stretch the word itself and add a short pause next to it. When Swedish speakers in one study repeated a phrase with more and more emphasis, they lengthened the key word and, mostly at the highest levels of emphasis, added pauses beside it. Those pauses averaged under a fifth of a second, so an emphasis pause can be brief.
quote: pausing – in combination with increased word duration – appears as a powerful means used to make words extra prominent
drill: Say one sentence three times with more emphasis on its key word each time: first with light stress, then with the word stretched, then stretched with a brief pause next to it. Record all three and compare.

source.author: Eva Strangert
source.title: Emphasis by Pausing
source.publisher: Proceedings of the 15th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences (ICPhS 2003), Barcelona, pp. 2477-2480

advice: A pause before a punch line is a common assumption, but one study found no sign of it. In 20 recorded joke performances, the researchers found no evidence that punch lines came after a pause, and speakers didn't speed up or slow down around them, whether the joke was prepared or spontaneous. So you can keep your normal rhythm going into the funny line.
quote: The other common assumption is that punch lines are preceded by pauses. Our data show no evidence supporting this claim
drill: Practise a short funny story at an even pace and deliver the last line without stopping before it. Record it and check that your rhythm stays the same into the punch line.

source.author: Salvatore Attardo, Lucy Pickering
source.title: Timing in the performance of jokes
source.publisher: Humor: International Journal of Humor Research

advice: If you talk fast, give listeners catch-up time by pausing at the ends of clauses and sentences. In one experiment with 27 young adults, adding silent pauses at those points to sped-up stories (twice as long at sentence ends), until the stories were back to their original length, brought recall close to normal-speed levels and reduced signs of listening effort. Earlier work they cite found random pauses did little.
quote: inserting silent pauses at linguistically salient points within a time-compressed narrative (“time-restoration”) returns recall accuracy to a level approximating that for a normal speech rate
drill: Read a paragraph aloud at your natural speed, but stop briefly at each comma and clause end and a little longer at each full stop. Record it, then compare it with a run-through without those stops.

source.author: Ryan M. O'Leary, Jonathan Neukam, Thomas A. Hansen, Alexander J. Kinney, Nicole Capach, Mario A. Svirsky, Arthur Wingfield
source.credentials: Department of Psychology, Brandeis University; Department of Otolaryngology, NYU Langone Medical Center
source.title: Strategic Pauses Relieve Listeners from the Effort of Listening to Fast Speech: Data Limited and Resource Limited Processes in Narrative Recall by Adult Users of Cochlear Implants

advice: When your listeners are still learning English, lengthen the pauses between short phrases instead of stretching out your words. In a study with lower-intermediate Japanese university students, passages with pauses of about half a second between short phrases were understood better than versions with 0.2-second pauses, even when the words themselves were spoken faster and the overall speed was the same.
quote: learners scored higher in listening to faster speech if longer pauses are inserted than in listening to slower speech with shorter pauses
drill: Mark a short text into phrases of about five to eight syllables. Read it at your normal word speed, holding a clear half-second silence at each mark, and record it for a listener who is learning English.

source.author: Kosuke Sugai, Shigeru Yamane, Kazuo Kanzaki
source.credentials: Kindai University; Kansai University; Osaka Electro-Communication University
source.title: The Time Domain Factors Affecting EFL Learners’ Listening Comprehension: a Study on Japanese EFL Learners
source.publisher: ARELE: Annual Review of English Language Education in Japan, vol. 27, pp. 97-108 (The Japan Society of English Language Education)

advice: When you want listeners to hear a clear break between two ideas, use a real silence, not only a change in pitch. In a listening experiment with Mandarin sentences, listeners detected a phrase break 81% of the time when it was marked only by a pause, compared with 58% when marked only by a stretched final syllable and 57% when marked only by a pitch reset.
quote: Pause was a more powerful perceptual cue than both final lengthening and pitch reset

source.author: Xiaohong Yang, Xiangrong Shen, Weijun Li, Yufang Yang
source.credentials: Institute of Psychology, Chinese Academy of Sciences; Shanghai Normal University
source.title: How Listeners Weight Acoustic Cues to Intonational Phrase Boundaries

advice: Try matching each pause to the size of the break in your content: longer between big sections than between sentences, and shorter before a sentence giving the cause or result of the last. When 20 Dutch speakers read news reports aloud for imagined listeners who had to understand them fully, pauses grew with the size of the break in the text's structure, and causally linked parts had shorter pauses.
quote: Pauses between segments which are related in a causal way are shorter than pauses between segments which are related in a non-causal way.
drill: Take a short text, mark each break as major (new topic) or minor (new sentence), and underline sentences that give a cause or result. Read it aloud with longer pauses at major breaks and shorter ones before the underlined sentences, and record it.

source.author: Hanny den Ouden, Leo Noordman, Jacques Terken
source.credentials: Tilburg University; Eindhoven University of Technology
source.title: The Prosodic Realization of Organizational Features of Texts

advice: When you read aloud, try pausing less often but letting the pauses you do take run a little longer. In a study of Portuguese poetry recitations by 20 non-professional readers and 2 actors, listeners rated the whole recitations as more pleasant when they had longer and less frequent pauses, and they preferred the actors' readings.
quote: recitations with longer pause durations and lower pausing rates are more pleasant when our participants listen to the whole poem declamation
drill: Record a short poem or paragraph twice: once pausing at every comma and line end, once grouping it into fewer, larger chunks with slightly longer pauses between them. Ask a listener which they prefer.

source.author: Plinio A. Barbosa
source.credentials: Department of Linguistics, University of Campinas, Brazil
source.title: Pleasantness and Wellbeing in Poem Declamation in European and Brazilian Portuguese Depends Mostly on Pausing and Voice Quality

advice: A prepared talk can carry more silence than off-the-cuff speech; put it at phrase and clause breaks rather than filling it. In French recordings, carefully prepared political speeches had 50% more total silent-pause time than interviews, most silent pauses fell at clause or phrase boundaries, and audible hesitations, frequent in interviews, were almost absent from the speeches.
quote: The total time of silent pauses was 50% greater in political speeches than in either type of interview.
drill: Record the same two-minute talk twice, once off the cuff and once after preparing it. In the prepared take, replace each 'um' with a silent break at the end of a phrase.

source.author: Danielle Duez
source.title: Silent and Non-Silent Pauses in Three Speech Styles

advice: In conversation, the gap before your answer counts toward how fluent you sound. In two listening experiments, answering slowly after a long gap lowered fluency ratings for both native and non-native speakers, while jumping in fast and cutting into the question lowered ratings only for native speakers. When someone asks you something, aim to start your answer without a long silence.
quote: in nonnative speech, only too “reluctant” answers led to lower fluency ratings
drill: Have a friend ask you ten quick questions, or play recorded ones. Record your answers and check how long you stay silent before starting each one.

source.author: Marjolein van Os, Nivja H. de Jong, Hans Rutger Bosker
source.credentials: Saarland University (van Os); Leiden University (de Jong); Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics (Bosker)
source.title: Fluency in Dialogue: Turn-Taking Behavior Shapes Perceived Fluency in Native and Nonnative Speech

advice: If you mean yes to a request, or you agree with someone's opinion, reply promptly: even a gap of about a second can sound reluctant. Listeners in the United States, Italy and Japan rated speakers as less willing to comply or agree the longer the silence before the reply (gaps of 0, 0.6 or 1.2 seconds), though the three groups differed in how much agreement they expected.
quote: Ratings significantly decreased within each language group at longer inter-turn silences, indicating a generalized response to the gaps

source.author: Felicia Roberts, Piera Margutti, Shoji Takano
source.title: Judgments Concerning the Valence of Inter-Turn Silence Across Speakers of American English, Italian, and Japanese

advice: If your listeners are still learning the language, avoid fast speech, but you don't need to go very slowly. In one study of lower-intermediate adult learners, passages delivered at about 200 words per minute were understood significantly less well, while slowing from 150 to 100 brought no significant gain. The author called the findings tentative, but for such listeners aim nearer 150 than 200.
quote: Results showed that moderately fast speech rates resulted in a significant reduction in comprehension
drill: Time yourself reading a 150-word paragraph aloud. If you finish well under a minute, read it again and stretch it to about one minute.

source.author: Roger Griffiths
source.title: Speech Rate and NNS Comprehension: A Preliminary Study in Time-Benefit Analysis

advice: If you have a strong accent, speaking fast may cost you more than it costs others. In a small study of passages read by three Chinese speakers of English and one American, native English listeners understood every speaker less at a fast rate than at a regular rate, but the drop was largest for the most heavily accented speaker. Keep to a regular pace while you work on pronunciation.
quote: speaking rate is more critical for the comprehension of heavily accented speech
drill: Record the same paragraph at your normal pace and at a fast pace. Ask a friend to write down what they caught from each version, and compare.

source.author: Janet Anderson-Hsieh, Kenneth Koehler
source.title: The Effect of Foreign Accent and Speaking Rate on Native Speaker Comprehension

advice: When a non-native listener isn't following you, longer pauses alone may not help. In one study, native English speakers retold a short film to a native and to a non-native partner. A slight majority slowed down for the non-native partner by pausing longer, not by talking more slowly. Those who got the story across hadn't changed their rate; those who struggled had added significantly more pause time.
quote: the subjects who successfully communicated the story to NNSs did not adjust their speech rate

source.author: Tracey M. Derwing
source.title: Speech Rate Is No Simple Matter: Rate Adjustment and NS–NNS Communicative Success

advice: Slower isn't always better for listeners who are learning English. In one study, English learners rated how suitable the pace was in stories read by native speakers and by Mandarin speakers of English. Computer-slowed or sped-up versions mostly didn't improve the ratings, but listeners tended to rate sped-up versions of the slowest Mandarin speakers better. If you speak very slowly by habit, try edging your pace up.
quote: In general, the modifications did not result in improvements in the ratings.
drill: Record a one-minute story at your usual pace, then retell it a little faster (about 55 seconds). Ask a listener which pace sounded more comfortable to them.

source.author: Tracey M. Derwing, Murray J. Munro
source.title: What speaking rates do non-native listeners prefer?

advice: When you speak fast to language learners, where you put the key word may matter. In one study of sentences sped up by computer, recall dropped as listeners' proficiency dropped. Native listeners focused on key content words, but learners tended to recall more words from the start or end of a sentence. When you must talk quickly to learners, putting the key word first or last may help.
quote: both learner groups tended to recall more words they had heard in initial or final sentence position
drill: Take three sentences from your talk and rewrite each so the most important word comes first or last. Say both versions aloud and notice which word stands out.

source.author: Linda Conrad
source.title: The Effects of Time-Compressed Speech on Native and EFL Listening Comprehension

advice: Speaking more clearly can make you easier to understand, even if your accent stays the same. In one study, proficient non-native speakers who switched from a conversational to a deliberately clear speaking style in their second language were understood significantly better in noise by both native and non-native listeners, while their accent was rated the same. Aim to be understood; that doesn't require sounding native.
quote: while intelligibility was improved, the presence of foreign accent remained constant in both speaking styles
drill: Read five sentences twice, first in your everyday style and then as clearly as you can, and record both. Ask a friend to listen with some background noise and say which version was easier to catch.

source.author: Rajka Smiljanić, Ann R. Bradlow
source.credentials: Department of Linguistics, University of Texas at Austin (Smiljanić); Department of Linguistics, Northwestern University (Bradlow)
source.title: Bidirectional clear speech perception benefit for native and high-proficiency non-native talkers and listeners: Intelligibility and accentedness
source.publisher: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 130(6), 4020-4031

advice: Use your first-language pace as your personal yardstick. In a study of 86 bilinguals from ten language backgrounds, the group spoke English more slowly than their first language, but people who talked fast in their first language also tended to talk faster in English. Compare your English pace with your own natural speed, not only with native speakers.
quote: within the bilingual group, L1 speaking rate significantly predicted L2 speaking rate
drill: Tell the same one-minute story in your first language and then in English. Time both versions and note whether the English one slows down in the pauses or in the words themselves.

source.author: Ann R. Bradlow, Midam Kim, Michael Blasingame
source.title: Language-independent talker-specificity in first-language and second-language speech production by bilingual talkers: L1 speaking rate predicts L2 speaking rate
source.publisher: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 141(2), 886-899

advice: With older listeners, make sentences easier to follow rather than slowing right down. In experiments with older adults, adding explanations and using fewer clauses tucked inside other clauses helped them, while short sentences, a slow speaking rate and high pitch did not, and led them to report more communication problems. Keep a natural pace, add brief explanations, and avoid tucking one clause inside another.
quote: The use of short sentences, a slow rate of speaking, and high pitch resulted in older adults' reporting more communication problems.
drill: Find a sentence in your talk with a clause tucked into the middle, such as 'The plan, which we agreed on last week, starts Monday.' Say it so each idea comes in turn: 'We agreed on the plan last week, and it starts Monday.' Keep your normal pace.

source.author: Susan Kemper, Tamara Harden
source.title: Experimentally disentangling what's beneficial about elderspeak from what's not

advice: What makes you easy to understand may change as your English grows. In a study of 120 Japanese learners of English describing pictures, native listeners' ease-of-understanding ratings were linked at beginner to intermediate levels to an optimal speech rate, rich vocabulary and varied prosody (stress, rhythm and intonation), and at higher levels more to accurate sounds, good prosody and correct grammar. Early on, your pace deserves attention.
quote: optimal rate of speech, appropriate and rich vocabulary use, and adequate and varied prosody were important for beginner to intermediate levels

source.author: Kazuya Saito, Pavel Trofimovich, Talia Isaacs
source.title: Second language speech production: Investigating linguistic correlates of comprehensibility and accentedness for learners at different ability levels

advice: Being easy to understand and sounding less accented are linked to different things. When 58 US undergraduates rated lectures by 11 international teaching assistants, how easy the speakers were to understand was mostly associated with speaking rate, while accent ratings were best predicted by pitch range and word stress. If being understood is your main goal, your pace is a good first thing to check.
quote: Accent ratings were best predicted by pitch range and word stress measures whereas comprehensibility scores were mostly associated with speaking rates

source.author: Okim Kang
source.title: Relative salience of suprasegmental features on judgments of L2 comprehensibility and accentedness

advice: If you present in a second language, expect a slower pace and plan to cover less. In one study, 14 fluent Swedish speakers gave the same presentation in English and in Swedish: their English was 23% slower, and in the same amount of time it carried significantly less information. When your time is fixed, cut material so the talk fits.
quote: Speaking rate was found to be 23% slower when using English.
drill: Time one practice run of your talk in English. If it runs over your time limit, cut a point and time it again.

source.author: Rebecca Hincks
source.title: Speaking rate and information content in English lingua franca oral presentations

advice: When you practise speaking clearly, tell yourself to 'overenunciate', saying each word with exaggerated care, rather than just 'speak clearly'. In one study, 12 speakers said sentences in their usual way and under three clear-speech instructions. Overenunciating gave the biggest gain in how much listeners understood through background babble, ahead of speaking as if to someone with a hearing impairment, and then speaking clearly.
quote: the overenunciate condition was associated with the greatest intelligibility benefit, followed by the hearing impaired and clear conditions
drill: Say the same three sentences in your normal style and then while overenunciating every sound. Record both and play them back with a fan or radio running in the background.

source.author: Jennifer Lam, Kris Tjaden
source.credentials: University at Buffalo, State University of New York
source.title: Intelligibility of Clear Speech: Effect of Instruction
source.publisher: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research, 56(5), 1429-1440

advice: Whether talking fast makes you sound credible may depend on your audience. A study comparing Korea and the United States found that fast delivery raised a speaker's credibility in the US, and for women speakers in Korea, but slow delivery worked better for Korean men. Before you speed up to sound credible, think about what your listeners expect.
quote: slow delivery is more effective in increasing the credibility of Korean male speakers

source.author: Hyun O. Lee, Franklin J. Boster
source.credentials: Wake Forest University (Lee); Michigan State University (Boster)
source.title: Collectivism-Individualism in Perceptions of Speech Rate: A Cross-Cultural Comparison

advice: What your speed says about you may depend on what your listeners are used to. In one study of men's voices, a fast voice conveyed power and competence to Americans but not to Koreans, while Koreans living in the United States, like Americans, linked faster speech with competence. Think about your listeners' background and experience before you speed up to impress.
quote: A fast voice conveyed power and competence to Americans, but not to Koreans.

source.author: Ying Peng, Leslie A. Zebrowitz, Hoon Koo Lee
source.title: The Impact of Cultural Background and Cross-Cultural Experience on Impressions of American and Korean Male Speakers

advice: If you sound slow and flat, speed may not be the first thing to fix. In a small Swedish study, 12 listeners ranked computer-edited versions of a slow, monotonous politician's speech: a livelier pitch (higher, with a wider range) helped most, removing slips and repetitions came second, and speeding up (5% faster, with shorter hesitation pauses) came third. Try working on the rise and fall of your voice first.
quote: Modifying F0 dynamics produced the greatest effects
drill: Record a paragraph in your usual voice, then again at the same speed but letting your pitch rise and fall more on key words. Compare which sounds more engaging.

source.author: Eva Strangert, Joakim Gustafson
source.credentials: Department of Language Studies, Umeå University (Strangert); Department of Speech, Music and Hearing, KTH, Stockholm (Gustafson)
source.title: What Makes a Good Speaker? Subject Ratings, Acoustic Measurements and Perceptual Evaluations

advice: Your own sense of how you come across can be off. In one study, 134 international students rated their accent and how easy they were to understand right after telling a picture story in English. Those whom listeners rated hardest to understand or most accented overrated themselves; those rated best underrated themselves. So compare your impression with outside feedback, such as a listener's view or your measured numbers.
quote: speakers at the low end of the accentedness and comprehensibility scales overestimated their performance; speakers at the high end of each scale underestimated it
drill: Before you play back a recording, rate your own pace and clarity from 1 to 5. Then listen back, check the measured pace, and see how close your guess was.

source.author: Pavel Trofimovich, Talia Isaacs, Sara Kennedy, Kazuya Saito, Dustin Crowther
source.title: Flawed self-assessment: Investigating self- and other-perception of second language speech

advice: Plan with notes, then put the notes away and speak. In one study of 32 pre-intermediate learners of English, those given 10 minutes to plan, with notes taken away before speaking, made about half as many pauses of a second or longer as those with no planning. In a picture-story task, planners also guided on content, words, grammar and order made about 8 such pauses, against about 30 without planning.
quote: The most striking result here is in terms of the number of pauses and the amount of total silence.
drill: Choose a story to tell. Spend up to 10 minutes noting what happens, in what order, and the key words and sentence patterns you'll need. Put the notes out of sight, then record the story.

source.author: Pauline Foster, Peter Skehan
source.title: The Influence of Planning and Task Type on Second Language Performance

advice: Match your planning to your goal. In one study of second-language speakers giving a monologue, those who planned beforehand spoke more fluently and with more varied words than those who planned carefully as they spoke, while careful planning during speech improved accuracy. If smooth delivery matters most, do your thinking before you start; if correctness matters most, give yourself time to plan as you speak.
quote: The pre-task planners also produced more fluent and lexically varied language than the on-line planners.
drill: Take two similar prompts. For one, plan for 5 minutes and then speak; for the other, skip planning but speak slowly and carefully. Compare which recording flows better and which has fewer mistakes.

source.author: Fangyuan Yuan, Rod Ellis
source.title: The Effects of Pre-Task Planning and On-Line Planning on Fluency, Complexity and Accuracy in L2 Monologic Oral Production

advice: Don't count on a minute or two of planning to rescue a test answer. In a study of 90 candidates doing IELTS-style speaking tasks, 1 or 2 minutes of planning made no significant difference to their scores or to their speech. Interviewers noticed that many candidates seemed lost while planning or too anxious to use what they had prepared.
quote: Neither the analysis of the scores, nor the discourse analysis revealed any significant differences in performance according to the amount of planning time provided.
drill: Answer two similar test-style questions for 2 minutes each, one after a minute of planning and one with none. Compare the recordings to see whether the minute really helps you.

source.author: Catherine Elder, Gillian Wigglesworth
source.title: An investigation of the effectiveness and validity of planning time in Part 2 of the IELTS Speaking Test
source.publisher: IELTS Research Reports, Volume 6 (IELTS Australia and British Council)

advice: To make gains last, repeat the same talk instead of switching topics every time. In one classroom study, 24 English learners recorded 4-, 3- and 2-minute speeches in each of three sessions. Fluency rose during training whether they kept one topic or used three, but it held up on later tests only for those who repeated the same speech.
quote: fluency improved for both groups during training but was maintained on posttests only by the students who repeated their speeches.
drill: In one session, record a talk for 4 minutes, then the same talk in 3 minutes, then in 2 minutes, without changing the topic.

source.author: Nel de Jong, Charles A. Perfetti
source.credentials: Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam; University of Pittsburgh
source.title: Fluency Training in the ESL Classroom: An Experimental Study of Fluency Development and Proceduralization

advice: When you practise several stories, finish all the repeats of one before moving to the next. In one study, learners of English told cartoon stories over three days, either the same story three times each day (A-A-A, then B-B-B, then C-C-C) or rotating stories (A-B-C each day). On a later test with a new story, the same-story group had improved more: they spoke faster, with shorter pauses inside sentences.
quote: blocked practice resulted in greater fluency development (faster articulation rate and shorter mid-clause pause duration) than did interleaved practice.
drill: Pick three short picture stories. Day 1: tell story A three times. Day 2: story B three times. Day 3: story C three times.

source.author: Yuichi Suzuki
source.title: Optimizing Fluency Training for Speaking Skills Transfer: Comparing the Effects of Blocked and Interleaved Task Repetition

advice: Choose a practice schedule you can keep: daily and weekly both worked. In one study of 116 Japanese learners of English, four sessions, each with 3 minutes of planning and then one picture story told three times in a row, brought similar gains whether held a day or a week apart: fewer pauses inside sentences than untrained learners on tests 7 and 28 days later. Speaking speed didn't improve.
quote: indicating that short- and long-spaced conditions were equally effective for developing L2 fluency.
drill: Run four sessions, a day or a week apart. In each, plan for 3 minutes, then tell one new picture story three times in a row without breaks.

source.author: Joe Kakitani, Judit Kormos
source.title: The effects of distributed practice on second language fluency development

advice: Repeating a speaking task helps fluency, though not as much as other skills. A 2025 meta-analysis of second-language task-repetition studies found repetition improved fluency less than it improved sentence complexity and accuracy. Studies with longer gaps between repeats tended to show smaller fluency gains, so for a smoother repeat, do it while the first attempt is still fresh.
quote: Fluency and lexical complexity, while positively influenced by TR, exhibit smaller gains, suggesting that TR primarily enhances structural aspects of language.
drill: Tell a 2-minute story, tell it again right away while it is fresh, and compare the two recordings.

source.author: Mahmoud Abdi Tabari, Jingyuan Zhuang, Mahsa Farahanynia
source.title: Task repetition and L2 oral performance: A meta-analysis

advice: Keep one practice story and retell it regularly. In one six-month study of 30 intermediate learners of English, a group that repeated the same narrative task every two weeks, 11 times in all, then did better on a new task, an interview, than a comparison group without this practice, in fluency and complexity, though not in accuracy.
quote: the benefits of massed repetitions of the same task transfer to performance of a new task but not necessarily in all areas of performance.
drill: Pick a story you can tell in about 2 minutes. Retell and record it every two weeks, and now and then answer interview-style questions on a new topic to test the carry-over.

source.author: Mohammad Javad Ahmadian
source.title: The effect of 'massed' task repetitions on complexity, accuracy and fluency: does it transfer to a new task?

advice: Try shadowing with your phone: play a short recorded dialogue, speak along with it, and record yourself. In one eight-week study, 16 learners shadowed at least four times a week for 10 minutes or more. Listeners later rated their unscripted speech as easier to understand and more fluent, though their accent ratings did not change significantly.
quote: Results indicated that the participants improved significantly on all speaking measures apart from accentedness
drill: Four times a week, spend 10 minutes speaking along with a short recorded dialogue, recording yourself as you go.

source.author: Jennifer A. Foote, Kim McDonough
source.title: Using shadowing with mobile technology to improve L2 pronunciation

advice: Learn whole phrases from model conversations, then use them when you speak. In a small five-week study of volunteer English classes in the US, a class that learned ready-made phrases (like 'I can't stand it when...') from recorded conversations and their transcripts, and practised using them, made larger gains in speaking speed and in how long they talked between pauses than a comparison class, though it started out weaker.
quote: We conclude that explicitly teaching formulaic sequences may lead to increased use of such phrases and also increased fluency.
drill: Find a transcript of a conversation on your topic. Underline five ready-made phrases, listen to the audio while reading, then record yourself talking on the topic using each phrase.

source.author: Michael McGuire, Jenifer Larson-Hall
source.title: Teaching Formulaic Sequences in the Classroom: Effects on Spoken Fluency

advice: As you read and listen, notice and collect common word combinations (collocations and set phrases), then reuse them. In one small study of 32 college English majors, students taught to notice such phrases over 22 hours of lessons were rated more proficient in an interview by two raters who didn't know their group, and phrase counts tracked those ratings.
quote: Both perceived the experimental group as more proficient than the control group.
drill: Each time you read or listen to something in English, write down three useful word combinations, then use them in your next practice recording.

source.author: Frank Boers, June Eyckmans, Jenny Kappel, Hélène Stengers, Murielle Demecheleer
source.credentials: Erasmus College of Brussels; University of Antwerp; Université Libre de Bruxelles
source.title: Formulaic sequences and perceived oral proficiency: putting a Lexical Approach to the test

advice: Study your own fluency, then practise on purpose. In a four-week study of B2-level English students at a UK university, a group that learned about speed, pausing and repair, practised short thinking phrases like 'well' and 'let me think', and at home recorded a story retelling, listened for breakdowns and re-recorded it, spoke faster and in longer stretches between pauses than a comparison group. Pausing was slower to change.
quote: the EG produced statistically more fluent language, demonstrating a faster speech and articulation rate, longer runs, and higher phonation time ratios.
drill: Retell a short picture story and record it. Listen back and mark where your flow broke down (long stops, repeats, self-corrections), then record the same retelling again.

source.author: Parvaneh Tavakoli, Colin Campbell, Joan McCormack
source.title: Development of Speech Fluency Over a Short Period of Time: Effects of Pedagogic Intervention

advice: Memorise short stories and retell them, repeat useful phrases, shadow recordings and try speed drills. In an 18-week study of 64 Persian-speaking university students, a group that spent 6 of its 18 class hours on this kind of fluency training improved more in rated fluency than a group doing only general speaking practice, and was still clearly above its starting level a month later.
quote: The findings revealed that the fluency training significantly enhanced the EFL students’ speech fluency.
drill: Memorise a 1-minute story, retell it from memory, then retell it again a little faster than feels comfortable.

source.author: Mahmood Yenkimaleki, Vincent J. van Heuven
source.credentials: Bu-Ali Sina University; Leiden University; University of Pannonia
source.title: Effect of pedagogic intervention in enhancing speech fluency by EFL students: A longitudinal study

advice: Rehearse in front of real people, and a bigger group if you can. In a study of students giving a videotaped speech, those who reported practising before an audience earned higher scores than those who practised without one, and practising before larger audiences went with higher scores. The study compared students' own reports, so other differences between them may explain part of this.
quote: Students who practiced their speech before an audience received higher evaluation scores than did students who practiced without an audience.
drill: Before the real talk, do at least one full run-through in front of friends or family, and invite a few more people if you can.

source.author: Tony Smith, Ann Bainbridge Frymier
source.title: Get 'Real': Does Practicing Speeches Before an Audience Improve Performance?

advice: Pauses to find a word are more likely when you build a phrase word by word. In one study of spoken English, pausing during word search was significantly more frequent in freely built phrases than in ready-made ones, which the author reads as a sign that ready-made phrases are stored and recalled whole. For topics you often discuss, collect the ready-made phrases and practise each as one piece.
quote: pausing was significantly more frequent in connection with lexical search in computed as compared to prefabricated structures
drill: List 10 phrases you use when talking about your work or studies (for example 'one of the main reasons', 'at the end of the day'). Say each one five times as a single smooth unit, then talk for one minute about what you do, using at least four of them.

source.author: Britt Erman
source.title: Cognitive processes as evidence of the idiom principle

advice: Common word combinations go with fewer mid-sentence stops. In a study of 56 learners taking an English speaking test (levels B1 to C1), those who used more high-frequency word combinations articulated faster, and those whose speech held a larger share of such combinations paused less often in the middle of clauses. Learn the frequent phrases for your usual topics as whole units.
quote: high-frequency n-grams correlated positively with articulation rate; (b) n-gram proportion correlated negatively with frequency of mid-clause pauses
drill: Take a question such as 'What is the best way to relax after work?'. Start your answer by reusing a phrase from it ('The best way to relax after work is...') and keep going for one minute. On a second try, say the same opening in your own words.

source.author: Parvaneh Tavakoli, Takumi Uchihara
source.credentials: University of Reading; University of Western Ontario
source.title: To What Extent Are Multiword Sequences Associated With Oral Fluency?

advice: Ready-made phrases go with smoother speech even in a first language. In a study of 45 native Polish speakers giving monologues, those who used more set phrases spoke faster, with longer runs between pauses and more of their time filled with speech. It is a correlation, which the author treats as preliminary evidence that set phrases support fluency. Build up set phrases for topics you often talk about.
quote: a higher concentration of formulaic material in output is associated with faster speed of speech, longer stretches of speech between pauses
drill: Record one minute on a familiar topic. In the transcript, underline the set phrases you used, add three more you know that fit the topic, and record the minute again using them.

source.author: Ewa Guz
source.credentials: John Paul II Catholic University of Lublin
source.title: Formulaic Sequences as Fluency Devices in the Oral Production of Native Speakers of Polish

advice: Say a set phrase as one smooth unit and put any pause after it, not inside it. Phrases like 'the thing is' and 'the trouble is' are often spoken as one intonation unit, often with a pause after them, while a break inside them ('The trouble, is...') sounds unnatural, notes a chapter reviewing research on how set phrases are pronounced.
quote: They are often articulated in one intonation unit and/or are followed by a pause.
drill: Say 'The thing is,', 'The point is,' and 'What I mean is,' each as one unit, pause briefly, then finish the sentence. Do five different endings for each opener.

source.author: Phoebe Lin
source.credentials: Department of English, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University
source.title: Formulaic language and speech prosody
source.publisher: Routledge (in A. Siyanova-Chanturia & A. Pellicer-Sánchez (Eds.), Understanding Formulaic Language: A Second Language Acquisition Perspective, pp. 78-94)

advice: Set phrases can help fluency in more than one way. In a study that followed ESL learners' spoken story retellings over six months, five uses emerged, including stringing several phrases together to stretch a run of speech and using filler phrases and self-talk. Practise joining two or three phrases you know well into one unbroken run.
quote: use of multiple formulas to extend a run; reliance on one formula; use of self-talk and filler formulas
drill: Answer three everyday questions, each starting with two linked set phrases, for example 'To be honest, the main thing is...' or 'As far as I know, most people...'. Keep talking for 30 seconds each without stopping.

source.author: David Wood
source.title: Uses and Functions of Formulaic Sequences in Second Language Speech: An Exploration of the Foundations of Fluency

advice: Borrow phrases from a model of the kind of talk you want to give. In a case study, a Japanese learner heard native speakers tell personal stories, marked their hesitations on the transcript, shadowed each recording at least eight times, then told her own stories. After six weeks her speech rate rose about 14% and her runs between pauses grew about 26%, with many phrases taken from the models.
quote: Results indicate a strong increase in fluency after six weeks of focused instruction
drill: Find a one-minute recording, with transcript, of someone telling a personal story. Mark where they pause, underline the phrases between pauses, shadow it eight times, then tell your own similar story using three of their phrases.

source.author: David Wood
source.title: Effects of focused instruction of formulaic sequences on fluent expression in second language narratives: A case study

advice: Being able to recall a phrase may come before using it freely, the author suggests. In a 6-week class study in Japan, a phrase-focused fluency workshop (shadowing, rebuilding a heard text, role-plays) clearly improved students' recall of the target phrases, but their fluency and their use of those phrases in a recorded role-play did not rise significantly more than a regular class's. Keep using new phrases in unscripted talk.
quote: perhaps suggests that productive recall precedes free productive speaking use
drill: After learning five new phrases, give three unscripted one-minute talks on different topics and tick each phrase when you manage to use it naturally.

source.author: Haidee Thomson
source.credentials: Hokusei Gakuen University Junior College, Japan
source.title: Building Speaking Fluency with Multiword Expressions

advice: When you retell something you have read or heard, reuse its phrases on purpose and check their exact wording. In a small study, international students in New Zealand who read and heard a short story and then retold it reused many single words but very few multiword expressions, and the phrases they did borrow often came out incomplete or altered.
quote: transfer from input to output at the level of phraseology cannot at all be taken for granted
drill: Before retelling a short article, underline five useful phrases and say each aloud three times. Record your retelling, then compare each phrase with the original and fix any changed words.

source.author: Hien Hoang, Frank Boers
source.credentials: Quy Nhon University, Vietnam; Victoria University of Wellington, New Zealand
source.title: Re-telling a story in a second language: How well do adult learners mine an input text for multiword expressions?
source.publisher: Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching

advice: Learn the most common spoken word combinations as early as the most common words. In a 10-million-word corpus of spoken British English, 84 combinations were as frequent as words in the top 1,000, such as 'a bit', 'as well', 'a lot of', 'in fact', 'at the moment', 'have a look' and 'in terms of'.
quote: There are in fact many, and these deserve the same kind of attention given to high frequency words.
drill: Say one true sentence about your week with each of 'a bit', 'as well', 'in fact', 'at the moment', 'have a look' and 'in terms of'. Then use three of them in a one-minute talk.

source.author: Dongkwang Shin, Paul Nation
source.title: Beyond single words: the most frequent collocations in spoken English

advice: Have ready-made phrases for agreeing, disagreeing and asking what someone means.
