Among 54 ESL students at a US university, those given four lessons with real recorded examples of routines like 'That's true', 'Yeah, but...' and 'What do you mean...?' significantly raised their use in a simulated group discussion, while a test-only group barely changed. Agreement plus 'but' ('That's true, but...') served as a way to disagree.
quote: both corpus searches and the use of corpus excerpts led to a significant increase in the oral production of pragmatic routines
drill: Write 10 opinions on cards. Draw one, read it aloud, and reply within two seconds by agreeing ('That's true'), disagreeing ('That's true, but...') or asking ('What do you mean by...?').

source.author: Kathleen Bardovi-Harlig, Sabrina Mossman, Yunwen Su
source.title: The effect of corpus-based instruction on pragmatic routines

advice: Keep sentence frames ready for common jobs, such as giving an example ('For example, ...') or comparing ('Compared to ...', 'On the other hand, ...'), and fill the gaps with words from the question. In a small study of 36 recorded answers by US school English learners in grades 5 to 8, answers with more set phrases, counting ones taken from the question, tended to have longer fluent runs.
quote: the use of formulaic sequences is a significant predictor of fluency in the data set
drill: For five practice questions, answer each in 45 seconds using one example frame and one comparing frame, reusing words from the question in the gaps.

source.author: Jennifer François, Mohammed Albakry
source.title: Effect of formulaic sequences on fluency of English learners in standardized speaking tests

advice: If one small phrase like 'I think', 'so' or 'also' fills your talk, widen your set. Among Chinese and Korean ESL speakers on a university speaking test, lower-level speakers leaned on a few such markers, while higher-level speakers spread their use more evenly across many, as native speakers did. One possibility the author raises is that heavy 'I think' use works like a filler.
quote: Learners at lower levels of proficiency tend to use only a small repertoire of PMs that includes I think, so, and also
drill: Transcribe one minute of your speech and count each marker ('I think', 'so', 'also', 'well'). If one dominates, record again, swapping half of them for others such as 'I'd say', 'in my view' or 'besides'.

source.author: Colleen Neary-Sundquist
source.title: The use of pragmatic markers across proficiency levels in second language speech
source.publisher: Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching

advice: A pause beside 'now' or 'by the way' at a topic change is normal, but a 'you know' may signal a stumble. In 15 hours of native English and French speech, structuring markers tended to sit beside pauses at major boundaries, linking markers such as 'because' rarely came with false starts, and check-in markers like 'you know' were more often found with false starts and cut-off words.
quote: interpersonal DMs are associated to disruptions of utterances in the form of truncations and false-starts
drill: In a transcript of your recording, circle every 'you know' and check the words around it for a restart or a cut-off word. Re-record those sentences after planning each one in full.

source.author: Ludivine Crible
source.title: Discourse markers and (dis)fluency in English and French: Variation and combination in the DisFrEn corpus

advice: Not every small word is a filler to delete. In a study of Norwegian lower-secondary pupils taking a paired English speaking test, the more fluent pupils used more 'smallwords', such as 'well' and 'right', and a wider range of them, moving toward young native speakers' use. When reviewing a recording, a well-placed 'well' or 'right' can be part of fluent speech.
quote: In terms of quantity and range, there was found to be no doubt that fluency and smallword use were correlated.
drill: Listen to two minutes of a fluent speaker chatting and note each 'well', 'right' or 'I mean'. Then retell what they said, using two of those words where they fit.

source.author: Angela Hasselgreen
source.title: Testing the Spoken English of Young Norwegians: A Study of Test Validity and the Role of 'Smallwords' in Contributing to Pupils' Fluency
source.publisher: Cambridge University Press (Studies in Language Testing 20)

advice: Practise new discourse markers aloud, and keep coming back to them. In a small UK study of Chinese learners, a class that practised markers like 'Right', 'Anyway' and 'As I was saying' in drills and role-plays used more of them in a speaking test right afterwards than a class that only studied them, though its gain was not significantly bigger. Eight weeks later the groups no longer differed significantly.
quote: statistically significant differences between the PPP group and III/control groups in terms of a higher mean usage of the target DMs
drill: Role-play a phone call in which you are interrupted: open with 'Right, ...', pick up again with 'As I was saying, ...' and wrap up with 'Anyway, ...'. Repeat it on three different topics, then again a week later.

source.author: Christian Jones, Ronald Carter
source.credentials: University of Central Lancashire; University of Nottingham
source.title: Teaching spoken discourse markers explicitly: A comparison of III and PPP

advice: In one study, listeners rated trivia statements as less likely to be true when a non-native speaker read them. The authors traced this to the extra effort of understanding the accent, not to prejudice. Listeners made aware of that difficulty corrected for a mild accent but not a heavy one. Later studies are mixed; the useful lesson is to make your speech easy to follow.
quote: People judged trivia statements such as “Ants don’t sleep” as less true when spoken by a non-native than a native speaker.
drill: Record three short facts and ask someone who has not heard you before to repeat them back. Re-record any fact they did not catch the first time.

source.author: Shiri Lev-Ari, Boaz Keysar
source.title: Why don't we believe non-native speakers? The influence of accent on credibility

advice: Don't assume your accent makes people doubt what you say. A careful 2024 repeat of a UK study found no difference in how much British listeners believed trivia statements from Polish-accented and British speakers, or in how well they understood them. The authors note that such accent effects have been small in earlier studies. When listeners can follow you easily, there may be no credibility cost.
quote: We did not reproduce the original pattern of results, observing no effect of speaker accent or exposure on comprehension or veracity.
drill: Say two facts to a listener and ask them to write them down. If they catch every word, spend your practice time on delivery rather than on hiding your accent.

source.author: Samantha Barlow, Greg Beardsley, Zéta Bsharah, Robin Crofts, Carlos De La Rosa, Andrea Gutierrez, Carlie Highfill, Amy Gail Wade Johnson, Caroline Johnson, Jacob Johnson, Isaac Leyva Cardenas, Jordan Taylor Martinez, Nathaniel Todd Miller, Riley Monroe Murray, Sylvia Page, Taylor Petersen, Irina Ramos, Rayvin Rhodes, Phoebe Vainuku, Brenan M. Wednesday, Emma Corrine Farnsworth, Seung Kyung Kim, Rachel Hayes-Harb
source.title: The effects of exposure and explicit stereotypes on veracity judgments of Polish-accented English speech: A preregistered close replication and extension of Boduch-Grabka & Lev-Ari (2021)

advice: Accent bias in hiring shows up across many studies, and it isn't only about clarity. A review combining 139 results found standard-accented candidates were rated more hireable, especially for communication-heavy jobs, yet how easy candidates were to understand did not significantly change the size of the bias. Keep working on clarity for your listeners, but don't blame yourself for a bias that clarity alone may not remove.
quote: candidates' relative comprehensibility was not a significant moderator of hiring bias

source.author: Jessica L. Spence, Matthew J. Hornsey, Eloise M. Stephenson, Kana Imuta
source.title: Is Your Accent Right for the Job? A Meta-Analysis on Accent Bias in Hiring Decisions

advice: In one study, accented candidates giving the same scripted answers as native speakers were less often recommended for a manager job, and lower ratings of their 'political skill' (reading what others want, building networks) statistically accounted for the gap. Rather than trying to erase an accent, the authors suggest tackling that doubt head-on in interviews, for example by showing how you win support and fight for resources.
quote: its effects on assessments of the speakers' political skill are something that speakers can actively mitigate
drill: Prepare one short story about a time you won people's support or secured resources for a project, and rehearse telling it out loud.

source.author: Laura Huang, Marcia Frideger, Jone L. Pearce
source.credentials: University of Pennsylvania (Wharton School); Holy Names University; University of California, Irvine
source.title: Political skill: Explaining the effects of nonnative accent on managerial hiring and entrepreneurial investment decisions

advice: Make your speech easier to process and listeners may rate you more kindly. In experiments with a Mandarin-accented speaker, listeners who saw subtitles, or who already knew what the message was about, found the speech easier to follow and rated the speaker more favorably. So when you can, it may help to show captions or key words on your slides and to preview your main point before the details.
quote: Compared to the unsubtitled/unfamiliar conditions, the subtitled/familiar conditions increased listeners’ fluency, elicited more positive affect, and resulted in more favorable language attitudes.
drill: For your next talk, write a two-sentence preview and choose three key words to put on screen or say first.

source.author: Marko Dragojevic
source.title: Extending the fluency principle: Factors that increase listeners’ processing fluency positively bias their language attitudes

advice: Listeners tune in to a new accent quickly. In lab tests with Spanish- and Chinese-accented English, native English listeners processed accented sentences more slowly at first, but the gap shrank within about a minute, sometimes after just two to four sentences. So consider opening with a greeting or a simple preview, and save your most important point until listeners have tuned in.
quote: processing speed is initially slower for accented speech than for native speech but that this deficit diminishes within one minute of exposure
drill: Write a two- or three-sentence warm-up opening (a greeting, who you are, your topic) and practise it until it flows.

source.author: Constance M. Clarke, Merrill F. Garrett
source.title: Rapid adaptation to foreign-accented English
source.publisher: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America

advice: A strong accent does not automatically make you hard to understand. In one study, native English listeners put many ratings of Mandarin speakers' English at the 'heavily accented' end, yet the speech was mostly highly intelligible and rated easy to understand. Aim to be understood, not to sound native: when you practise, ask 'Did they catch every word?' rather than 'Did I sound foreign?'
quote: a strong foreign accent does not necessarily reduce the comprehensibility or intelligibility of L2 speech
drill: Have a friend write down what you say for 30 seconds, then practise only the words they missed.

source.author: Murray J. Munro, Tracey M. Derwing
source.credentials: Simon Fraser University; University of Alberta
source.title: Foreign Accent, Comprehensibility, and Intelligibility in the Speech of Second Language Learners

advice: To sound clearer and more fluent when speaking freely, practise the big patterns of speech, not only single sounds. In a 12-week study of English learners, both pronunciation-trained groups improved on short sentences, but only the group taught general speaking habits and prosody (stress, rhythm, intonation) also improved in comprehensibility and fluency when telling unscripted stories.
quote: only the global group showed improvement in comprehensibility and fluency in the narratives
drill: Read a short paragraph aloud, marking the stressed word in each phrase, then retell it without the text, keeping the same stress and rhythm.

source.author: Tracey M. Derwing, Murray J. Munro, Grace Wiebe
source.credentials: University of Alberta; Simon Fraser University
source.title: Evidence in Favor of a Broad Framework for Pronunciation Instruction

advice: Three habits went with how easy listeners found learners to understand. In a small study of 30 Japanese learners of English, their rate of 'um/uh', silent pauses inside clauses, and articulation rate (speed between pauses) best predicted native listeners' ratings, together accounting for nearly half the differences in ratings. Their fluency in Japanese did not add to this, so these English habits may be worth targeting directly.
quote: filled pause ratio, silent pauses within clauses, and articulation rate as the strongest L2 predictors of comprehensibility
drill: Record a one-minute answer, count your 'um/uh's and any pauses in the middle of a phrase, then record it again, moving the pauses to the ends of clauses.

source.author: Dion Clingwall, Gavin Brooks, Jon Clenton
source.credentials: Prefectural University of Hiroshima; Kyoto University of Foreign Studies; Hiroshima University
source.title: Investigating the Comprehensibility Paradigm: Key Fluency Predictors in L1 English Speakers’ Evaluations of Japanese Speakers’ L2 English

advice: A filler may cost the most in the middle of a sentence. In an experiment with a synthetic voice, adding 'uh' made the speaker sound less confident, and more so mid-sentence ('the more uh, accurate version') than at the start ('Uh, I think...'). Versions with no filler sounded most confident. So if you need to hesitate, do it before you start the sentence, not halfway through.
quote: stimuli were rated as sounding most confident when no filler was present, and most hesitant with a medial filler
drill: Answer five quick questions. If you need thinking time, take it before your first word, then say the whole sentence without an 'uh' in the middle.

source.author: Ambika Kirkland, Harm Lameris, Éva Székely, Joakim Gustafson
source.title: Where’s the uh, hesitation? The interplay between filled pause location, speech rate and fundamental frequency in perception of confidence

advice: Listeners can hear how sure you are. In a Dutch study, answers given with low confidence tended to come after a longer delay, with fillers like 'uh' and a rising, question-like tone, and listeners could pick up the speaker's certainty from sound alone. When you do know an answer, give it straight away and let your voice fall at the end.
quote: low FOK answers are typically longer than high FOK answers, and tend to contain more marked auditory cues (fillers, longer delay, and high intonation)
drill: Ask a friend ten easy questions about your work or studies. Answer each with no 'uh' before it and a falling tone on the last word.

source.author: Marc Swerts, Emiel Krahmer
source.title: Audiovisual prosody and feeling of knowing

advice: Sounding unsure and sounding less honest share the same voice cues. French listeners in lab experiments heard made-up words with altered pitch, loudness and speed; rising pitch, quieter syllable starts and a slower rate made the speaker seem less certain and less honest. English and Spanish listeners heard certainty the same way. When you mean it, let your pitch fall at the end and start words at full volume.
quote: listeners' perceptions of the certainty and honesty of other speakers from their speech are based on a common prosodic signature
drill: Say five factual sentences twice, once ending with a rising tone and once with a falling tone. Record both and listen for which sounds surer.

source.author: Louise Goupil, Emmanuel Ponsot, Daniel Richardson, Gabriel Reyes, Jean-Julien Aucouturier
source.credentials: STMS UMR 9912 (CNRS/IRCAM/SU), Paris; University of East London; University College London
source.title: Listeners’ perceptions of the certainty and honesty of a speaker are associated with a common prosodic signature

advice: When recommending something, let your voice show conviction. In four experiments, speakers who tried to persuade through their voice were more persuasive, even when listeners noticed the attempt; they sounded more confident without seeming less sincere. A cross-study analysis and a follow-up test found they spoke louder and varied their volume. The effect was small, but the authors suggest speaking moderately louder and raising your volume on key points.
quote: communicators tend to speak louder and vary their volume during paralinguistic persuasion attempts, both of which signal confidence and, in turn, facilitate persuasion
drill: Read a short recommendation aloud twice, the second time a little louder with extra volume on the two most important words. Compare the recordings.

source.author: Alex B. Van Zant, Jonah Berger
source.title: How the voice persuades
source.publisher: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

advice: When you want people to see how capable you are, let them hear you. In experiments, people acting as employers, and professional recruiters, rated job candidates as more competent, thoughtful and intelligent, and were more interested in hiring them, when they heard a pitch rather than read the same words. Adding video did not change this. Where you can, make your case out loud.
quote: These evaluators rated a candidate as more competent, thoughtful, and intelligent when they heard a pitch rather than read it
drill: Turn your strongest written pitch into a 60-second spoken version, record it, and listen back as if you were the employer.

source.author: Juliana Schroeder, Nicholas Epley
source.credentials: Booth School of Business, University of Chicago
source.title: The Sound of Intellect: Speech Reveals a Thoughtful Mind, Increasing a Job Candidate's Appeal

advice: Bad sound makes good content seem worse. When identical conference talks were played with heavy echo, or radio interviews sounded like a bad phone line, listeners rated the talk or interview, the speaker and the research less favorably. Before you record or present online, reduce echo, use a decent microphone or headset, and test your sound. If the line is still bad, the authors suggest saying so.
quote: viewers thought that the talk was worse, the speaker less intelligent and less likeable, and the research less important
drill: Record the same 20 seconds in two places, a bare room and a room with soft furnishings, and keep the setup that sounds clearer.

source.author: Eryn J. Newman, Norbert Schwarz
source.credentials: University of Southern California; Australian National University
source.title: Good Sound, Good Research: How Audio Quality Influences Perceptions of the Research and Researcher

advice: Nerves can come with more 'um's and silent pauses. In a study of Dutch teenagers learning English, a graded task with an outside teacher raised their anxiety and their 'um's. Seven who listened back said their pauses under pressure were mostly about what to say next, not which word to use. If it's the message, plan your points; if it's a missing word, practise saying it another way.
quote: participants reported more issues related to the content of the message in the high-anxiety condition compared to the low-anxiety condition.
drill: Play back a nervous take and mark each long pause or 'um' as M (I didn't know what to say next) or W (I couldn't find the word). Fix the bigger pile first.

source.author: Myrthe M. S. J. Rood, Nivja H. de Jong
source.credentials: Rijnlands Lyceum Sassenheim (Rood); Leiden University Graduate School of Teaching & Leiden University Centre for Linguistics, Leiden University (de Jong)
source.title: A mixed-methods study on the effects of manipulated speaking anxiety on L2 utterance and L2 cognitive fluency
source.publisher: Journal of the European Second Language Association

advice: Aim your calming tools at the moments just before you start and at your first minute. In a study of college students giving speeches, the rise in anxiety from rest to the start of the speech and the change during the first minute together accounted for 68% of the differences in overall anxiety during the speech, while changes in the last minute added nothing significant.
quote: both sensitization and habituation 1 were significant predictors, together accounting for 68% of the variance in overall state anxiety scores during speech performance.
drill: Rehearse your first 60 seconds until you could say them half asleep, and do your calming routine right before you press record.

source.author: Ralph R. Behnke, Chris R. Sawyer
source.title: Public speaking anxiety as a function of sensitization and habituation processes

advice: Do several practice runs in a row, not just one. In a small study, 19 adults gave three short talks to a virtual audience in one session. They began the second and third talks less distressed than the first, and the authors concluded that three talks in a row were needed for distress to settle. They warn that a single run may simply confirm your fear.
quote: An increase in distress during the second scenario indicated that three consecutive speech performances were critical in achieving habituation.
drill: Record the same one-minute talk three times in a row. Rate your nerves from 0 to 10 before each take, and don't stop after a rough second take.

source.author: Marcel Takac, James Collett, Kristopher J. Blom, Russell Conduit, Imogen Rehm, Alexander De Foe
source.title: Public speaking anxiety decreases within repeated virtual reality training sessions

advice: Spend five minutes breathing slowly right before you speak. In a trial with 66 young adults, box breathing (in 4 seconds, hold 4, out 4, hold 4) or a slow sigh twice a minute (in through the nose for 3 seconds, out through pursed lips for 6), done before a stressful mock job talk and for one minute after, gave smaller rises in heart rate and anxiety than normal breathing.
quote: brief breathing practice can buffer acute physiological stress responses
drill: Set a five-minute timer before you record. Breathe in for 4, hold for 4, out for 4, hold for 4, and repeat until the timer ends.

source.author: Matthew J. McAllister, M. Hunter Martaindale, Nate Sutton, Judith P. Andersen
source.credentials: Metabolic & Applied Physiology Laboratory, Department of Health & Human Performance, Texas State University
source.title: Box breathing and prolonged exhalation reduces markers of physiological stress reactivity in response to a virtual trier social stress test

advice: Slow breathing can calm you, but don't expect it to carry your talk. In a study of 120 Dutch university students, a 12-minute guided slow-breathing video (about six breaths a minute, longer out-breaths) lowered anxiety right after the exercise and kept heart-rate variability higher during a three-minute speech. But their anxiety during the speech was no lower than a control group's, and observers did not rate their speeches better.
quote: the slow breathing intervention significantly increased HRV immediately after the intervention, during the public speaking task, and during the recovery and reduced state anxiety
drill: Before a take, breathe in for 4 seconds and out for 6 (six breaths a minute) for five minutes, then rehearse your opening once.

source.author: Rüya Akdağ, Mariska E. Kret, Evin Aktar, Milica Nikolić
source.credentials: Department of Cognitive Psychology, Institute of Psychology, Leiden University
source.title: A proof of concept study on digital interventions for reducing socio-evaluative stress and anxiety in youth

advice: Hiding your nerves works worse than rethinking the situation. Before you speak, take a realistic view: this is practice, and a shaky take has no lasting cost. In one study, 202 students facing an impromptu speech to a camera were told to hide their feelings, rethink the situation, or accept their anxiety. The hiders' heart rates rose more than the others', and they felt more anxious than the rethinkers.
quote: the Suppression group showed a greater increase in heart rate from baseline than the Reappraisal and Acceptance groups.
drill: Before your next recording, sit for one minute with your eyes closed and tell yourself: this is practice, and nothing bad happens if this take is shaky. Then record.

source.author: Stefan G. Hofmann, Sanna Heering, Alice T. Sawyer, Anu Asnaani
source.title: How to handle anxiety: The effects of reappraisal, acceptance, and suppression strategies on anxious arousal

advice: Read a pounding heart as your body getting ready to help you, not as a sign you're failing. In one study, people told before a speech that their stress arousal was beneficial showed less shame and anxiety, less avoidant body language, and were rated slightly better (a marginal difference) than people given no instructions.
quote: Arousal reappraisal participants exhibited less shame and anxiety, less avoidant nonverbal signaling, and performed marginally better than no instruction controls.
drill: When you feel your heart racing before a take, say quietly: 'This is energy for my talk.' Then start speaking.

source.author: Miranda L. Beltzer, Matthew K. Nock, Brett J. Peters, Jeremy P. Jamieson
source.title: Rethinking butterflies: The affective, physiological, and performance effects of reappraising arousal during social evaluation

advice: Coach yourself by name. Just before you speak, think through your nerves using your own name or 'you' ('Ana, you've prepared this') instead of 'I'. In one study, people who prepared for a five-minute speech this way were rated by observers as better speakers than those who used 'I', showed less distress, and brooded less about the speech afterwards.
quote: Compared with the first-person group, the non-first-person group performed better according to objective raters in both studies.
drill: Before your next take, spend 30 seconds talking to yourself by name: 'Why is [name] nervous? [Name], you know this topic.' Then record.

source.author: Ethan Kross, Emma Bruehlman-Senecal, Jiyoung Park, Aleah Burson, Adrienne Dougherty, Holly Shablack, Ryan Bremner, Jason Moser, Ozlem Ayduk
source.title: Self-talk as a regulatory mechanism: How you do it matters
source.publisher: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

advice: Before you speak, remind yourself of three facts: pre-talk nerves are normal; listeners notice your nerves less than you think and watch you less closely than you fear; and nerves don't have to hurt your talk. In one study, students who read a message like this before a graded class talk felt less anxious beforehand and less physically tense during it, and said it eased their worry about nerves.
quote: those who received the inoculation message reported significantly lower pre-task anxiety
drill: Write the three facts on a card and read them aloud before each recording.

source.author: Ben Jackson, Josh Compton, Ashleigh L. Thornton, James A. Dimmock
source.credentials: School of Sport Science, Exercise and Health, The University of Western Australia
source.title: Re-Thinking Anxiety: Using Inoculation Messages to Reduce and Reinterpret Public Speaking Fears

advice: Before a talk you dread, vividly imagine it: nerves at the start, then the nerves fading and the talk going well. In a study of 43 people with moderate speaking anxiety, anxiety before a virtual-reality talk dropped after a 4-minute imagery exercise like this but not in a no-exercise group, and distress eased during the talk while the other group's rose. It didn't raise willingness to present.
quote: Anticipatory anxiety reduced in the positive mental imagery group, but not in the control group.
drill: Close your eyes for four minutes before recording. Picture your nerves at the start of the talk, then picture them fading and the talk going well, in as much detail as you can. Then record.

source.author: Elze Landkroon, Eva A.M. van Dis, Katharina Meyerbröker, Elske Salemink, Muriel A. Hagenaars, Iris M. Engelhard
source.title: Future-Oriented Positive Mental Imagery Reduces Anxiety for Exposure to Public Speaking

advice: When nerves turn your attention inward, point it at your listeners: look at their faces as you talk. In one study, highly socially anxious people practised talks to a virtual audience while trained to focus outward. Anxiety fell whether they focused on faces or on objects in the room, but focusing on faces also brought more eye contact and more positive feelings.
quote: with particular advantages of an external social focus concerning eye contact to the audience and positive affect
drill: Practise a talk to a friend or a video call. Each time you notice yourself checking how you sound, move your eyes back to a face.

source.author: Theresa F. Wechsler, Michael Pfaller, Rahel E. van Eickels, Luise H. Schulz, Andreas Mühlberger
source.credentials: Department for Psychology, Clinical Psychology and Psychotherapy, University of Regensburg
source.title: Look at the Audience? A Randomized Controlled Study of Shifting Attention From Self-Focus to Nonsocial vs. Social External Stimuli During Virtual Reality Exposure to Public Speaking in Social Anxiety

advice: If speaking makes you very anxious, don't trust your gut rating of how a talk went. In one study, people diagnosed with social phobia rated their own short impromptu speech worse than people without the diagnosis rated theirs, yet the audience's overall ratings of the two groups did not differ. Before deciding you did badly, ask a listener to rate the same talk, or check your recording and numbers.
quote: social phobics rated their own performance worse than did nonclinical controls, and there was a significantly greater discrepancy between self and other ratings
drill: After a recording, rate yourself 1 to 5 for how confident you sounded. Ask someone else to rate the same recording, then compare.

source.author: Ronald M. Rapee, Lina Lim
source.credentials: Department of Psychology, University of Queensland
source.title: Discrepancy between self- and observer ratings of performance in social phobics

advice: Prepare before you watch your own recording. First predict in detail what you think you'll see, picture yourself giving the talk, then watch the video as if the speaker were a stranger. In one study, people who did this before viewing a video of their speech rated their performance higher than people who simply watched it.
quote: Participants who received cognitive preparation prior to the video feedback made higher ratings of their overall performance
drill: Before playing back a take, write down three things you expect to see, such as 'my voice will shake'. Watch it as if it were someone else, and check each prediction.

source.author: Allison G. Harvey, David M. Clark, Anke Ehlers, Ronald M. Rapee
source.credentials: Department of Psychiatry, University of Oxford
source.title: Social anxiety and self-impression: cognitive preparation enhances the beneficial effects of video feedback following a stressful social task

advice: If using a new language makes you anxious, you may be underrating yourself. In a study of 37 English-speaking young adults with varied French skills, more anxious learners rated their ability lower than calmer learners with the same actual skill, while calmer learners tended to overrate theirs. Don't skip a speaking task because it feels beyond you: try it, record it, and decide from the result.
quote: anxious students tended to underestimate their competence relative to less anxious students, who tended to overestimate their competence.
drill: Pick three speaking tasks you think you can't do yet, such as explaining your job in one minute. Record an attempt at each and decide from the recordings.

source.author: Peter D. MacIntyre, Kimberly A. Noels, Richard Clément
source.title: Biases in Self-Ratings of Second Language Proficiency: The Role of Language Anxiety

advice: Recall your language progress often. In one study, 88 Chinese university students of English were randomly split. For 30 days, one group took a calming breath, recalled in detail the progress they had made in English since starting university, and wrote it down; most did this at least once a day. Their English classroom anxiety fell, while the other group's stayed the same. The drop was small.
quote: levels of anxiety decreased significantly over time in the experimental group but remained stable in the control group
drill: Most days for a month, take a slow breath and write down, in detail, one thing you can now say or understand in your new language that you couldn't before.

source.author: Yinxing Jin, Jean-Marc Dewaele, Peter D. MacIntyre
source.credentials: School of Foreign Languages, Hainan Normal University; Birkbeck College, University of London; Department of Psychology, Cape Breton University
source.title: Reducing anxiety in the foreign language classroom: A positive psychology approach

advice: If speaking to a group in your new language scares you, practising with a virtual audience may feel less threatening. In a small study of 20 university students with intermediate English, those who gave eight short practice talks in a VR headset to a virtual audience reported lower language anxiety than those who spoke to real people over Zoom.
quote: practicing speaking in VR was associated with statistically significant lower FLA scores, compared with speaking practice using Zoom.

source.author: Regina Kaplan-Rakowski, Alice Gruber
source.credentials: Department of Learning Technologies, University of North Texas (Kaplan-Rakowski); The Center for Languages and Intercultural Communication, Augsburg Technical University of Applied Sciences (Gruber)
source.title: The impact of high-immersion virtual reality on foreign language anxiety

advice: Make practice harder in small steps that you choose. In a small pilot study without a comparison group, students with high speaking anxiety gave 20-minute talks to a virtual class and could raise the challenge every four minutes, for example a bigger audience or tougher reactions. As they raised it, their heart rate and anxiety fell, and their speaking anxiety was still lower a month later.
quote: Participants increased their exposure to virtual social threat during each VRET session, which coincided with a reduction in heartrate and self-reported anxiety and arousal.
drill: Build a ladder: talk alone to your phone, then on a video call to one friend, then to two or three people. Move up a rung when the current one feels manageable.

source.author: Preethi Premkumar, Nadja Heym, David Joseph Brown, Steven Battersby, Alexander Sumich, Bethany Huntington, Rosie Daly, Eva Zysk
source.credentials: Division of Psychology, London South Bank University
source.title: The Effectiveness of Self-Guided Virtual-Reality Exposure Therapy for Public-Speaking Anxiety

advice: If fear of speaking holds you back, an online or VR programme is worth trying. A review of 30 randomized trials found that psychological programmes for fear of public speaking delivered online, by computer or in VR (7 of 62) worked about as well as face-to-face ones. In cognitive and behavioural programmes, people kept improving after the programme ended, so measure your progress over weeks, not one day.
quote: Interventions using technology-assisted modes of delivery are equally effective as traditional face-to-face interventions in reducing FoPS.

source.author: Omid V. Ebrahimi, Ståle Pallesen, Robin M. F. Kenter, Tine Nordgreen
source.credentials: Department of Clinical Psychology, Faculty of Psychology, University of Bergen
source.title: Psychological Interventions for the Fear of Public Speaking: A Meta-Analysis

advice: Practise with a partner and correct each other as you talk: say the right version, or give a quick prompt like 'Pardon?' or 'You need past tense' so your partner fixes it. In a 10-week study of Japanese university English classes, pairs taught to do this became more accurate and spoke faster, while pair practice without corrections improved speed only.
quote: After one semester of intervention, the two CF groups improved in both overall accuracy and fluency, measured as unpruned and pruned speech rates
drill: Swap short stories with a partner for five minutes. Each time you hear a mistake, either say the sentence correctly or say 'Pardon?' so the speaker can fix it, then carry on. Change partners and repeat.

source.author: Masatoshi Sato, Roy Lyster
source.title: Peer interaction and corrective feedback for accuracy and fluency development: Monitoring, practice, and proceduralization

advice: Before rating your own recording, try rating a few other speakers. In one study of 40 international students, about 15 minutes of rating and discussing three sample recordings (weak, middle and strong) helped some students rate their own speech more like outside listeners did, mainly those whose self-ratings were already fairly accurate. For those whose self-ratings were far off, it didn't help and may even have made things worse.
quote: peer-assessment appeared to mainly benefit L2 speakers with initially good self-assessment skills
drill: Find three short recordings of other learners at different levels. Rate each from 1 to 10 for how easy it is to follow and say why. Then rate your own recording the same way.

source.author: Aki Tsunemoto, Pavel Trofimovich
source.title: Self-assessment of second language comprehensibility: The roles of peer-assessment and metacognition

advice: When you listen back, check fluency on purpose. In one study of advanced learners of English, those rating how easy their own story was to understand said they paid attention mainly to pronunciation and the plot, not grammar or fluency, and their self-ratings were often too high or too low. Play your recording once just for pauses, fillers and restarts.
quote: learners reported paying attention to pronunciation and the story plot rather than grammar or fluency
drill: Play your last recording three times: once for content, once only for pauses and fillers, and once only for restarts. Keep a tally for each pass.

source.author: Mireia Ortega, Joan C. Mora, Ingrid Mora-Plaza
source.title: L2 Learners’ Self-Assessment of Comprehensibility and Accentedness: Over/Under-Estimation, Effects of Rating Peers, and Attention to Speech Features
source.publisher: Proceedings of Pronunciation in Second Language Learning and Teaching (Virtual PSLLT), Iowa State University Digital Press

advice: Don't just watch your recording; score it. In one study, students who filled in a scoring checklist for the recording of their first presentation scored higher on their second presentation, including for timing and speaking skills, than students who were only encouraged to watch themselves. Both groups also got teacher and peer feedback.
quote: the students who completed the self-assessment rubric received higher scores than the other group
drill: After each recording, score yourself from 1 to 5 on pace, mid-sentence pauses, fillers and restarts, and write one specific fix to try next time.

source.author: Sian M. Ritchie
source.title: Self-assessment of video-recorded presentations: Does it improve skills?

advice: Reviewing your own video is a start, not the whole job. In a study of 144 first-year university students giving presentations, those who got feedback from a teacher improved their presenting the most, while those who only reviewed their own video with a scoring guide improved the least. When you can, ask an experienced listener for comments too.
quote: Results demonstrated the superiority of teacher feedback for encouraging students' presentation behaviour
drill: Once a week, send one recording to a teacher, tutor or skilled friend and ask for one thing to keep and one thing to change.

source.author: Stan van Ginkel, Judith Gulikers, Harm Biemans, Martin Mulder
source.title: The impact of the feedback source on developing oral presentation competence

advice: Video of yourself speaking is a useful feedback tool. A review that pooled 12 published studies of public speaking classes found that students who got feedback through videotapes of their speeches gained more speaking skill and gave speeches with better content, and the video feedback did not significantly raise their anxiety.
quote: no statistically significant increase in anxiety is experienced by students when video technology is utilized in the classroom to provide feedback
drill: Video yourself giving a two-minute talk, watch it back, note your fillers and long pauses, then record the talk again.

source.author: John Bourhis, Mike Allen
source.title: The role of videotaped feedback in the instruction of public speaking: A quantitative synthesis of published empirical research

advice: Write out your recordings yourself rather than working from a transcript someone else made. In a study of two English-for-academic-purposes classes, students who transcribed and improved their own role-play seemed to keep their corrected forms more accurate when they did the task again, including four weeks later, than a class that worked from teacher-made transcripts.
quote: the self-transcribing procedure was more effective in helping the learners to maintain higher rates of accuracy in the forms highlighted
drill: Pick one minute of a recording and type it out yourself, word for word. Correct the errors you find, then record the same talk again.

source.author: Tony Lynch
source.title: Learning from the transcripts of an oral communication task

advice: Treat automatic filler counts as a rough guide. When researchers tested an automatic 'uhm' detector on learner speech in Dutch and English, it found 56-65% of the filled pauses that human annotators marked, and only about a third of the sounds it flagged were real fillers. Watch your trend across sessions, and listen back to check a few flagged spots.
quote: 65% of the Dutch manually annotated filled pauses and 56% of the English manually annotated filled pauses were indeed correctly classified
drill: Pick three spots your app counted as fillers, play each one, and mark whether it was really an 'um' or 'uh'.

source.author: Nivja H. de Jong, Jos Pacilly, Willemijn Heeren
source.title: PRAAT scripts to measure speed fluency and breakdown fluency in speech automatically
source.publisher: Assessment in Education: Principles, Policy & Practice

advice: Automatic feedback doesn't have to be perfect to help. In a one-session pronunciation study with 30 native speakers of Chinese learning English, feedback that was right two times in three improved the practised words about as much as fully accurate feedback, while feedback right only one time in three helped less. If a tool's flags look mostly right to you, keep using it.
quote: machine feedback can be beneficial even when it is ‘good enough’ (i.e., not 100% accurate)

source.author: Alif Silpachai, Reza Neiriz, MacKenzie Novotny, Ricardo Gutierrez-Osuna, John M. Levis, Evgeny Chukharev
source.credentials: Radboud University; Iowa State University; Texas A&M University
source.title: Corrective feedback accuracy and pronunciation improvement: Feedback that is ‘good enough’

advice: Speech-to-text software can be a stricter listener than people. In one study, 15 learners of French read texts aloud: the software got fewer of their words right than everyday native listeners did, but the two scores rose and fell together. So speech-to-text gives a rough check on how clearly you speak, but a missed word doesn't always mean people couldn't follow you.
quote: The results reveal that ASR transcription accuracy was lower than that of human transcribers.
drill: Once a week, read the same short paragraph into a dictation app. Count the words it gets wrong and watch that number over a month.

source.author: Elena Shimanskaya
source.title: Comparing L2 intelligibility for learners of French: Automatic speech recognition versus human listeners

advice: Expect your recorded voice to sound strange, and listen anyway. While you talk, you also hear your voice through the bones of your head, which makes it sound lower to you than it sounds to others. A recording leaves that part out. So don't let the odd sound put you off; listen for your pauses, fillers and pace.
quote: Although it is the sound we associate most with ourselves, it is perceived as strange when played back in a recording.

source.author: Pavo Orepic, Oliver Alan Kannape, Nathan Faivre, Olaf Blanke
source.credentials: École polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL); Université Grenoble Alpes
source.title: Bone conduction facilitates self-other voice discrimination

advice: Keep a written log of your practice numbers. In a review of 138 experiments on many kinds of goals (not speaking in particular), people who were helped to track their progress did better at reaching their goals, and tracking helped more when progress was written down or shared with others. After each session, note your fillers, pauses and pace.
quote: progress monitoring had larger effects on goal attainment when the outcomes were reported or made public, and when the information was physically recorded
drill: After each practice, log the date, fillers per minute, mid-sentence pauses and words per minute. Show the log to a friend once a week.

source.author: Benjamin Harkin, Thomas L. Webb, Betty P. I. Chang, Andrew Prestwich, Mark Conner, Ian Kellar, Yael Benn, Paschal Sheeran
source.title: Does monitoring goal progress promote goal attainment? A meta-analysis of the experimental evidence
